What the decree actually changes

Guatemala’s Congress approved Decreto 18-2026 on 29 July 2026, amending Decreto 15-98, the Ley del Impuesto Único Sobre Inmuebles — the IUSI, the single annual tax on real estate collected by municipalities. President Bernardo Arévalo signed it on 28 August, and the Diario de Centro América published it the same day. Publication started every clock in the reform.

The headline: the IUSI rate on residential and mixed-use property is now zero. Mixed use covers a home with a small business attached, a common arrangement in Guatemala. Whatever your house is worth, the annual bill from the town hall disappears once the change takes effect.

Commercial property moves the other way. Buildings used for business pay three per thousand of assessed value up to Q500,000, about US$65,580; six per thousand up to Q1 million, about US$131,161; and nine per thousand above that. Conversions here use the Banco de Guatemala reference rate of Q7.62422 per dollar for 29 August.

The timetable now running

The gazette text staggers three clocks. The ban on conditioning municipal services on IUSI payment takes effect 60 days after publication, in late November 2026. The IUSI changes themselves — the zero rate for homes and the new commercial table — take effect 90 working days after publication, which Congress’s first secretary calculates as 8 January 2027; until then, owners must keep paying 2026 and prior-year bills under the old rules. The income-tax and stamp-duty changes are dated 1 January 2027.

Inside that window, four bodies must rebuild their systems: the municipalities, the finance ministry, the SAT tax agency and the cadastre directorate. Expect uneven implementation across 340 municipalities — some will update bills promptly, others will need chasing.

What foreign owners should do now

Keep your registration current. The zero rate removes the bill, not the registry: the duty to register the property with your municipality stays in force, and an unregistered property remains the classic source of fines and paperwork trouble at sale time.

If you are selling, the decree helps twice. Individuals are exempted from the 10 percent tax on the capital gain, effective 1 January 2027, removing a cost that used to be priced into every private sale. Combined with the zero IUSI, the carrying and exit costs of a Guatemalan home both fall.

If you own commercial space, budget the other way. A shop or office assessed above Q1 million moves to nine per thousand — the sharpest end of the new table. And if a municipality ever threatens to cut your water, rubbish collection or street lighting over a disputed bill, the decree now expressly bars that tactic.

Why the town halls are unhappy

Finance minister Jonathan Menkos puts the loss to municipalities at about Q1.2 billion a year, roughly US$157.4 million, and says the constitutional transfer formula cannot be reopened to replace it. The partial offset is a 3 percent stamp duty on second and subsequent property transfers, routed to municipalities through the SAT.

The impact is wildly uneven. An analysis by Icefi, the Central American fiscal studies institute, found 45 of 340 municipalities collected nothing at all in 2025 and reckons roughly 300 come out ahead once the stamp duty flows. Five heavy losers sit in and around the capital, where values are highest: Guatemala City, Mixco, Villa Nueva, Santa Catarina Pinula and San Miguel Petapa. The municipalities’ association, ANAM, has warned that local finances are at risk.

Could the courts stop it?

Objections are already on record. Icefi’s director called the law technically flawed and noted it passed without opinions from the finance ministry or the SAT; a development-foundation economist argues the different treatment of residential and commercial property could be unconstitutional.

One case is already at the Constitutional Court — filed by the Cabal caucus on 12 May 2026 — but it targets the original IUSI statute, not this decree. No separate action against Decreto 18-2026 itself has been reported. Plan on the reform taking effect, and treat any court surprise as exactly that.

When does Guatemala’s property tax on homes actually end?

The decree was published on 28 August 2026. The zero IUSI rate for residential and mixed-use property takes effect 90 working days later, on 8 January 2027 — until then, 2026 bills still stand. A ban on cutting municipal services over unpaid tax starts in late November 2026, and the new commercial rate table also begins on 8 January 2027.

Do foreign owners in Guatemala still pay the IUSI?

Once the change takes effect, no — the zero rate applies to residential and mixed-use property regardless of the owner’s nationality. What does not disappear is registration with the municipality. Commercial property keeps paying, at three, six and nine per thousand across value bands, with the top rate above Q1 million, about US$131,161.

What changes if I sell a property in Guatemala?

Individuals are exempted from the 10 percent tax on the capital gain. Municipalities, for their part, are barred from cutting water, rubbish collection or street lighting over unpaid tax — and a 3 percent stamp duty on second and subsequent transfers now flows to them through the SAT to offset their lost IUSI revenue.

World.title: Brazil’s Gripen F Makes Its First Flight With an Air Force Pilot Aboard
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · DEFENCE

Key Facts — First flight The Gripen F first flight ran 40 minutes from Linköping on 28 August 2026.

— Crew Saab’s Jakob Högberg flew with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos.

— Order Brazil contracted 36 jets in 2014, 28 single-seat F-39E and eight two-seat F-39F.

— Budget The 2026 federal line for the programme is about R$2.1 billion (US$403.8 million).

— Schedule The last of the 36 aircraft is now due for delivery in 2032.

The Gripen F first flight opens a test campaign that must finish before the jet reaches Brazil.

Saab flew the two-seat Gripen F for the first time on Friday, with a Brazilian Air Force test pilot aboard. The sortie lasted 40 minutes from the company airfield at Linköping in Sweden.

A Gripen in flight. The two-seat Gripen F, built only at Linköping in Sweden, flew for the first time on Friday. Photo: Milan Nykodym, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Flickr.

What Saab confirmed about the Gripen F first flight

The aircraft took off at 09:40 local time and stayed airborne for 40 minutes, Saab said. The sortie checked the fighter’s core systems and its initial flight performance.

Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg flew the aircraft with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Lieutenant Colonel Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos. The company did not publish the airframe’s registration, nor the altitudes and speeds flown.

No matching notice appeared on the Brazilian Ministry of Defence news pages on the day of the flight. Brazilian aviation titles carried the same departure time and the same two pilot names.

Cavok, a Brazilian aviation outlet, reported the same 09:40 departure and roughly 40 minutes aloft. It described the Gripen F first flight as the opening of a wider test campaign.

Saab’s release carries the reference CU 26-034 and links to video of the departure. It gives no serial number for the airframe, a detail Brazilian outlets also left out.

Why the two-seat version matters to Brazil

The Gripen F is the two-seat version of the single-seat Gripen E, built to Brazilian requirements. It shares sensors, avionics, mission systems, weapons and logistics with the aircraft already in service.

Saab says the second cockpit lets a crew divide the workload during complex missions. The rear seat can manage sensors, mission systems and weapons rather than simply carrying an instructor.

For the Air Force the aircraft shortens the path from a training aeroplane to a front-line fighter. Pilots convert on the same platform they will fly in combat, cutting the need for an interim jet.

Brazilian reporting says the two-seater drops the 27 millimetre Mauser cannon carried by the single-seat version. The space it occupies is needed for the systems that sit behind the second cockpit.

Where the F-39 programme stands today

Brazil signed with Saab in 2014 for 36 aircraft, 28 single-seat F-39E and eight two-seat F-39F. Saab announced the deal at 39.3 billion Swedish kronor (about US$4.05 billion at 2014 values).

Ten aircraft were in service by late 2025, with one more kept for test work in Brazil. The first jet assembled in the country, registered FAB 4109, was rolled out in March 2026 as the twelfth.

The single-seaters fly with the 1st Air Defence Group at Ala 2, the Anápolis wing in Goiás. That unit, known as the Jaguar Squadron, shares the base with Embraer KC-390 transport aircraft.

Sweden builds 13 single-seaters and all eight of the two-seaters, according to Brazilian trade reporting. The other 15 single-seat jets are assembled at Embraer’s plant in Gavião Peixoto, São Paulo.

The Air Force has already flown the type abroad, sending six F-39E jets across the Andes to Chile this year. That deployment, for the Salitre 2026 exercise, was the fighter’s first large multinational outing.

The Embraer assembly line at Gavião Peixoto

Gavião Peixoto holds the only Gripen production line outside Sweden, according to Saab’s own account. The site also hosts the Gripen design and development centre that opened there in 2016.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva attended the March rollout of the first Brazilian-built fighter. Defence Minister José Múcio Monteiro and the Air Force commander were also at the ceremony.

Saab counts more than 350 Brazilian engineers, technicians and pilots trained under the programme. Embraer, Akaer and AEL Sistemas work on structures, systems integration and onboard electronics.

The two-seat variant itself is built only in Sweden, so the Gripen F first flight was always going to happen there. Brazilian engineers nonetheless worked on its structure and on its systems.

Money, amendments and a schedule that slipped to 2032

The contract has been amended twelve times, the Air Force told senators in September 2025. The original plan closed deliveries in 2024, yet the last aircraft is now due only in 2032.

Air Force chief of staff Walcyr Josué de Castilho Araújo told the committee that budgets fell short of the contract. He set out one delivery in 2026, four in 2027 and five in 2028.

The 2026 federal budget carries about R$2.1 billion (US$403.8 million) for the fighter programme. Roughly R$800 million (US$153.8 million) of that sum was blocked under this year’s fiscal squeeze.

Both conversions use the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX selling rate of R$5.2005 to the dollar on 28 August 2026. PTAX is the central bank’s official daily reference rate for the real.

The Air Force extended the life of its Northrop F-5 fleet to cover the gap left by the delays. Those older jets reached 50 years of Brazilian service during 2025.

When Brazil expects to fly the aircraft at home

Saab says the aircraft now enters production acceptance flights, then a step-by-step expansion of its flight envelope. Speed, altitude, G-load and angle of attack limits will be cleared in stages.

Rear cockpit functions and the tactical capabilities specific to the two-seater will be assessed in parallel. The campaign runs from the company’s flight test centre in Sweden.

An Air Force briefing in April 2026 put the arrival of the first two-seater in Brazil in 2028. The Gripen F first flight therefore opens a test phase lasting roughly two years.

Once it arrives, the Air Force plans to move pilots straight from the A-29 Super Tucano to the Gripen. That would remove the need for an intermediate lead-in fighter trainer aeroplane.

A possible second batch of twenty aircraft

Embraer and Saab signed a head of agreement in July 2026 to study building 20 more Gripen fighters. The work would go to Gavião Peixoto, complementing the existing line at Linköping.

The companies stressed that nothing is ordered until the Air Force signs a further contract amendment. Such a deal would take the Brazilian fleet to 56 aircraft.

The Air Force has told Congress that 36 fighters are not enough for a country of continental size. It puts the operational requirement at 66 aircraft.

For now the Gripen F first flight is the programme’s clearest step forward in a difficult budget year. Delivery to Brazil, and any second batch, both remain some way off.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where did the Gripen F first flight take place? It took place on 28 August 2026 at Saab’s airfield in Linköping, Sweden. The aircraft took off at 09:40 local time and flew for 40 minutes. Who was in the cockpit for the flight? Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg flew with Brazilian Air Force test pilot Lieutenant Colonel Abdon de Rezende Vasconcelos. Saab did not publish the aircraft’s registration. How many Gripen fighters has Brazil ordered and received? Brazil contracted 36 aircraft in 2014, 28 single-seat and eight two-seat. Ten were in service by late 2025, plus one more kept for testing.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Sunday, August 30, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro — Sunday opens with warm sun, light rain risk and a beach-ready breeze — ideal for a long shoreline morning.

The city slows down, so pair a free museum run in Centro with an early dinner as locals do.

The business mood is cautious after a hawkish Jackson Hole message; the board carries the exact settle.

It is the day for a slow wander through Rio’s monumental centre, followed by sea air.

Ipanema in the sun, with the Dois Irmãos peaks behind — Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief for Sunday, August 30, 2026. Photo: Christian Haugen, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr.

Monday stays dry and warm. Tuesday thickens with humidity, and Wednesday is hotter with a higher chance of afternoon rain.

Sunset today: 5:41 pm · Water around 22°C with small to moderate waves; green flags at most posts this morning.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CENTRO CULTURAL LOOP A free, air-conditioned art morning where the city began Start at Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil on Rua Primeiro de Março, open 9am to 8pm and free. Walk ten minutes to Museu Nacional de Belas Artes on Avenida Rio Branco, open 10am to 6pm and free. From there, stroll to Paço Imperial on Praça XV, open noon to 6pm with free entry. Take the VLT or Metrô to Cinelândia; the whole loop is walkable and flat. This route gives you three serious art stops in one morning without spending a real.

OUTDOORS — SEA WALL AND SAND The shoreline afternoon that resets a long week After lunch, head to Ipanema or Copacabana for a late beach session. The sun is out, water temperature sits near 22°C, and waves stay small enough for easy swimming. The seafront ciclovia is open; rent a bike near Posto 9 and ride toward Arpoador before sunset.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — SOUTH ZONE Two laptop-friendly rooms for a slow Sunday Coffee Five in Ipanema opens early with good wifi and a calm upstairs table. Curto Café in Centro is a better fit if you stay near the museums; it is open on Sundays with strong espresso and fewer crowds. Both have reliable connections for light work, though Sunday hours can shorten in the late afternoon.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — LAPA NIGHT AIR A grittier, music-first alternative to the beach Skip the sand and cross to Lapa for an early evening walk under the Arcos. Bar Antigamente stays open Sunday with samba circles and cold beer. It is livelier after 7pm; go with a local friend and watch your phone on the street.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Early dinner, Botafogo boardwalk, then home before Monday Reserve a table at Comuna in Botafogo for burgers and craft beer before 8pm. Alternatively, Fogo de Chão in Botafogo serves a full rodízio for a proper Sunday feast. Walk the Botafogo waterfront afterwards; it stays busy and well-lit until late.

ALSO ON TODAY Parque Madureira riverside walk — Parque Madureira, Zona Norte — free, from 8am, easy cycling and running paths Jardim Botânico — Rua Jardim Botânico, 920 — 8am to 5pm, R$40 residents / R$80 foreigners Museu de Arte do Rio — Praça Mauá — 11am to 6pm, R$20, free on Tuesdays Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil — Rua Primeiro de Março, Centro — 9am to 8pm, free Arpoador sunset — Ipanema — around 5:30pm, free, arrive early for the rock

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô lines 1, 2 and 4 run normally on Sunday from 7am to 11pm. Single journey costs R$7.90.

The VLT is running in Centro with reduced Sunday frequency; check the Carioca station board before boarding.

If rain appears in the afternoon, ride-hailing fares may surge near the beach exits.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Try Cais do Oriente in Centro for a refined weekend lunch near the museums. Or grab a quick, honest plate at Bar Luiz on Rua da Carioca for under R$80.

Dinner: Book Comuna in Botafogo for burgers and local craft beer. For a long Brazilian feast, Fogo de Chão in Botafogo serves rodízio until late.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a light layer for air-conditioned museums and a water bottle for the afternoon walk.

Cards and Pix are widely accepted; keep R$60 in small notes for beach vendors and tips.

After dark, stay on the main streets in Lapa and Centro. Avoid the side alleys alone, especially after 9pm.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads meet at Coffee Five in Ipanema on Sunday mornings for a quiet work hour.

Newcomers often join the weekly beach volleyball game at Posto 9 in Ipanema after 4pm — show up with water and introduce yourself.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Flamengo host Botafogo at the Maracanã at 4pm today — a Rio derby that doubles as a title-race test for the visitors’ pursuit of leaders Palmeiras.

Fluminense are on the road at Athletico-PR at 11am. For tickets and last-minute entry rules, check the club channels this morning.

Watching in a bar? The Maracanã area fills early; in the South Zone, Bar do Adão in Botafogo and the waterfront bars are the usual spots.

If you want noise and a screen tonight, head to any bar on Rua Dias Ferreira in Ipanema.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The week ended with global risk assets on the back foot after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh held firm on the 2% inflation target at Jackson Hole.

His message pushed Treasury yields higher and cooled stocks, gold and several Latin American markets.

Local investors still found support in large Brazilian blue chips, leaving the Ibovespa with an eighth straight daily gain.

The coming week turns to US payrolls and any fresh sign of how hawkish the Fed will stay into September.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 30 — Warm and partly cloudy; free Centro museum loop in the morning MON 31 — Dry and 28°C; good day for Jardim Botânico before work TUE 1 — Humid, 29°C; MAR free entry day in Praça Mauá WED 2 — Hotter, 31°C, afternoon rain possible; indoor plans in the afternoon THU 3 — Still warm; check midweek football fixtures if you want a live match

Background: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 29, 2026.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief — Saturday, August 29, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is it safe to visit Centro museums on a Sunday?

Yes, the main museum corridor around Cinelândia, Praça XV and Praça Mauá is busy and policed on Sunday afternoons. Stay on the main streets, avoid empty side alleys, and you will be fine.

Do I need cash or Pix for the beach and small cafés?

Pix is now the default for most small purchases, but beach vendors still prefer cash. Keep R$60 in small notes for water, coconuts and quick snacks.

What is actually open tonight after 7pm?

Restaurants and bars in Botafogo, Ipanema and Leblon stay open late on Sunday. Lapa starts later and feels busier after 8pm, but go with a local if you can.

The city’s cultural circuit is the headline: Museu da Língua Portuguesa is free today, while MASP and Pinacoteca are open but paid on Sundays — their free days are Tuesday and Saturday.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — FREE CULTURE Museum Sunday: Língua Portuguesa free, MASP and Pinacoteca worth the ticket Start at MASP on Avenida Paulista in Bela Vista. It opens at 10am and today is a paid day at R$85, with online booking recommended — free entry is on Tuesdays. The permanent collection of European masters hangs on glass easels, but the Brazilian modernists upstairs are the real reason to go. From Paulista, ride the metro Line 2 from Trianon-Masp to Paraíso, change to Line 1-Blue and get off at Luz. Pinacoteca’s grand brick building is a two-minute walk, opens at 10am and charges R$40 today — free entry is on Saturdays and the second Sunday of each month. Its soaring central hall and Brazilian 19th-century painting collection are unforgettable. Finish at Museu da Língua Portuguesa inside Estação da Luz, a two-minute walk away. Entry is free today — Sundays are its free day — and the interactive exhibits on Brazilian Portuguese feel more like a playground than a museum. It closes at 4:30pm, so aim to arrive by 2pm. All three sit on metro Lines 1 and 2. A single journey is R$5.40. The two paid tickets add about R$125; with metro, coffee and a pastel the day still lands under R$200. You will walk a lot, so wear soft shoes. This trio is the best culture day in the city. It covers Paulista avenue energy, historic Luz architecture and language as living art. You finish by 4pm, leaving time for the park or an early dinner.

OUTDOORS — PARK LIFE Ibirapuera at golden hour, then the lake path Parque Ibirapuera opens at 5am and stays open until midnight. The sweet spot is 4pm to 6pm, when the light turns golden and runners, cyclists and families fill the paths. Entry is free. Rent a shared bike via an app or just walk the loop around the lake. The Japanese pavilion area is quieter than the main entrances. MAC USP inside the park is free and open until 9pm on Sundays. This is the best outdoor reset for a Sunday. Bring water, wear sunscreen and expect crowds near the main gate.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — VILA MADALENA Slow wifi, strong coffee and a Sunday that actually works Coffee Lab on Rua Fradique Coutinho in Pinheiros is the city’s most serious coffee bar. This time of year the cold brew is excellent and the laptop-friendly tables fill up by 11am. Expect to spend R$18 to R$25 on a drink. For a quieter corner, try Sofá Café on Rua Harmonia in Vila Madalena. It has solid wifi, small tables and a calm Sunday crowd. It opens at 9am and is a good base before the street gets busy. Both are walking distance from the Vila Madalena metro station. Bring a charger and expect to share a table if you arrive after midday.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — CENTRO HISTÓRICO Mercadão, Farol Santander and a different São Paulo Skip Paulista and head to Centro instead. Mercado Municipal opens at 6am on Sundays and closes at 4pm. Go early for a mortadella sandwich or pastel de bacalhau upstairs. Entry is free. Then walk ten minutes to Farol Santander on Rua João Brícola. It opens at 9am and costs R$45. The 360-degree viewing deck from the 26th floor is the best skyline view in the city. This is grittier and busier than the west zone. It feels like old São Paulo. Go with a charged phone and keep your bag in front of you.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Samba in Vila Madalena, pizza in Pinheiros Vila Madalena wakes up late on Sundays. Head to Bar Salve Jorge on Rua Aspicuelta after 7pm for cold beer, feijoada and live samba that spills onto the street. Arrive early for a table. Nearby, Posto 6 on Rua Aspicuelta serves excellent petiscos and stays lively until late. It is less crowded than Salve Jorge and has better caipirinhas. For dinner, head to Pinheiros and try Bráz Pizzaria on Rua Grajaú. It opens until 11pm on Sundays and the margherita is around R$70. Book ahead or wait at the bar. The whole area is safe and walkable after dark on a Sunday. Keep your phone in your pocket on the busy bar streets.

ALSO ON TODAY MASP — Avenida Paulista, Bela Vista — 10am-6pm, R$85 today (free Tuesdays), European and Brazilian collections Pinacoteca de São Paulo — Praça da Luz, Luz — 10am-6pm, R$40 today (free Saturdays and second Sunday of the month), grand halls and Brazilian masters Museu da Língua Portuguesa — free — Praça da Luz, Luz — 9am-4:30pm, free today, interactive language exhibits Ibirapuera park walk — Ibirapuera — 5am-midnight, free, lake loop and golden hour light Mercado Municipal — Rua da Cantareira, Centro — 6am-4pm, free entry, mortadella sandwich and pastel stalls Farol Santander viewing deck — Rua João Brícola, Centro — 9am-8pm, R$45, 360° skyline view

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The metro runs a Sunday timetable from around 4:40am to midnight. Single journey is R$5.40. Lines 1-Blue, 2-Green and 4-Yellow connect the main Sunday spots: Paulista, Luz, Pinheiros and Vila Madalena.

There is no rodízio on Sundays, so all license plates can circulate freely all day. Ride apps are plentiful and cheaper on Sunday mornings. Traffic builds after 5pm around Ibirapuera and the bar streets of Vila Madalena.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: At Mercadão, get the famous mortadella sandwich at Hocca Bar or the pastel de bacalhau from a stall upstairs. Budget R$35 to R$50. If you stay near Paulista, try Casa do Porco in Centro — expect a queue and around R$60 for the set lunch.

Dinner: For pizza, Bráz Pizzaria in Pinheiros is the city classic — R$70 a pizza, open until 11pm. For a meatier Sunday dinner, Fogo de Chão in Itaim Bibi does rodízio from around R$150, but book ahead.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a reusable water bottle and sunscreen — the sun is strong through 4pm and museum queues mean standing outside. Most places accept Pix and cards, but keep R$60 in cash for market stalls and street food.

Museu da Língua Portuguesa is free today, so its queue forms early — arrive 15 minutes before opening. MASP and Pinacoteca charge entry on Sundays, which keeps their lines shorter.

In Centro around Mercadão and Farol Santander, keep your phone and wallet in your front pocket and be aware of your surroundings. It is busier on Sundays but still a pickpocket zone.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

For expats and digital nomads, the Sunday morning run club in Ibirapuera starts near Portão 7 at 8am. It is a friendly mixed group and a good way to meet people without a formal event.

Check Internations and Meetup for Sunday board-game meetups in Vila Madalena or English-language samba nights in Pinheiros. The Café des Arts community board in Pinheiros often lists Sunday language exchanges.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

It is a big football Sunday in the city: Corinthians host Santos at Neo Química Arena in Itaquera at 4pm, the Alvinegro derby with Neymar confirmed to start for the visitors.

League leaders Palmeiras visit Mirassol at 6:30pm, while São Paulo FC are not in action today. Tickets for the derby were sold online only, with facial-recognition entry at the arena.

For watching on TV, try O’Malleys in Itaim Bibi or Blue Pub in Pinheiros. Both show Brazilian and European games and have a full Sunday crowd. Heading to Itaquera instead? Take metro Line 3-Red to Corinthians-Itaquera and arrive early.

The Libertadores quarter-finals start on September 8, with Corinthians and Palmeiras both still in the bracket. Plan ahead if you want tickets.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Markets were closed on Saturday and remain shut today, so Friday’s session stands as the week’s close. The mood among professionals is still cautious about US interest rates staying higher for longer.

The story behind the mood: a stronger dollar and firmer US Treasury yields put pressure on Latin American assets on Friday. Brazil’s main equity benchmark bucked the regional trend, which signals continued foreign interest in Brazilian stocks.

Ahead: Monday brings a fresh week of trading and any weekend policy headlines will set the tone. Keep an eye on the US dollar’s trajectory against the real — it shapes import costs and local inflation expectations.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 30 — Sunny, 27°C. Free museums, Ibirapuera walk, samba in Vila Madalena tonight MON 31 — Warm, 28°C, mostly dry. Good day for a Paulista avenue work-from-café session TUE 1 — Still 29°C and dry. Last fully outdoor day before midweek change WED 2 — 26°C with 40% rain chance. Move plans indoors — Pinacoteca or MASP are smarter bets THU 3 — Chance of lingering showers. Check weekend fixtures and plan Saturday football viewing

Background: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 29, 2026.

Background: São Paulo Daily Brief — Saturday, August 29, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Which museums are actually free on a Sunday in São Paulo?

Museu da Língua Portuguesa is free on Sundays and open 9am-4:30pm. MAM, the modern art museum inside Ibirapuera, is also free on Sundays. MASP and Pinacoteca are paid on Sundays: MASP costs R$85 (free on Tuesdays) and Pinacoteca R$40 (free on Saturdays and the second Sunday of the month). MAC USP inside Ibirapuera is always free and open 10am-9pm on Sundays. Farol Santander is not free either — it costs R$45 and opens at 9am.

Is public transport running normally today?

Yes. The metro runs a Sunday timetable from around 4:40am to midnight. A single journey is R$5.40 and you can pay with a contactless card or bilhete único. There is no rodízio on Sundays, so cars with any plate can drive all day. Ride apps are readily available and cheaper before 5pm.

What can I do on a Sunday night if I don’t drink much?

Walk the calm side of Ibirapuera after dark — the main loop is well lit and safe until 10pm. The park officially closes at midnight. For food without a bar scene, go to Pinheiros for pizza at Bráz or an early dinner at any of the restaurants on Rua dos Pinheiros. They stay open to 11pm on Sundays.

World.title: Danish Fund Buys Control of Moroccan Logistics Leader Globex
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Morocco · LOGISTICS & INVESTMENT

Key Facts — Deal Two A.P. Moller Capital funds signed an agreement on 17 August to buy a majority stake in Globex Investissement, a leading Moroccan logistics company. The price and the size of the stake were not disclosed.

— Target Casablanca-based Globex was founded in 1998 as the exclusive FedEx Express licensee in Morocco and employs more than 350 people.

— Continuity Founder and chief executive Omar El Kadiri will stay on, leading the business with his existing management team.

— Hurdle Completion needs merger-control clearance from Morocco’s Competition Council.

The investment arm of the Danish group behind Maersk is buying control of Morocco’s best-known independent logistics network, six months after setting up a dedicated Moroccan fund.

A.P. Moller Capital said on 17 August that two of its funds had signed an agreement to acquire a majority stake in Globex Investissement, a leading Moroccan logistics company. Neither the size of the stake nor the price was disclosed.

The deal is the first big move by a Morocco-only fund the Danish investor set up in February. It lands as the country consolidates its position as North Africa’s main logistics hub.

Container cranes at Tanger Med, the Moroccan port complex that handled more than 11 million containers last year. (Photo: NAC, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What was agreed

The buyers are the Emerging Markets Infrastructure Fund II, known as EMIF II, and the APM Capital Morocco Fund. Together they will take the majority holding and form a partnership with Omar El Kadiri, Globex’s founder and chief executive, who stays in place.

Completion is subject to the usual conditions, including merger-control clearance by the Moroccan Competition Council. Until that lands, the acquisition is agreed but not closed.

Kim Fejfer, the chief executive of A.P. Moller Capital, said the investment aligns directly with the firm’s core sector and geographic focus. He called Morocco a market that is rapidly developing into the leading North African logistics hub, supported by strong economic tailwinds.

What Globex actually does

Globex was founded in Casablanca in 1998 as the exclusive FedEx Express licensee in Morocco. That means it runs the American courier’s brand, pickups and deliveries in the country under licence.

The company now employs more than 350 people and works across express delivery, road freight, freight forwarding, customs brokerage and warehousing. It also holds FedEx and TNT licences in Senegal and Cameroon, and uses the FedEx network to serve more than 220 countries.

The private equity firm Amethis bought a 30.5 per cent stake in 2022 to fund expansion in Morocco and sub-Saharan Africa. A.P. Moller Capital did not say whether Amethis will sell as part of the new transaction.

Who the buyer is

A.P. Moller Capital is a Copenhagen-based institutional fund manager within A.P. Moller Holding, the Møller family holding company that also controls the shipping group A.P. Moller-Maersk. It manages infrastructure funds focused on transportation, logistics and the energy transition in emerging markets.

Its Moroccan arm, APM Capital Morocco S.A., is regulated by the country’s capital-market authority, the AMMC, and led by chief executive Ghislane Guedira. She said the combination of the Danish firm’s sector heritage and Globex’s management team would strengthen the company’s market position.

A fund raised just for this

The APM Capital Morocco Fund was established in February 2026, backed by leading Moroccan institutional investors. Its mandate is transport and logistics, with a pipeline spanning international express, third-party logistics, air cargo handling and cold storage.

The fund raised 1.6 billion dirhams (about US$178 million) in commitments, and EMIF II committed a further 600 million dirhams (about US$65 million) alongside it. That gives the two vehicles 2.2 billion dirhams (about US$243 million) to deploy, at roughly nine dirhams to the dollar.

Why Morocco, why now

The anchor is Tanger Med, the port complex on the Strait of Gibraltar that is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. Its four container terminals handled more than 11.1 million containers in 2025, up 8.4 per cent on the year, and 161 million tonnes of cargo overall.

A second Mediterranean deep-sea port, Nador West Med, is due to start operating in the last quarter of this year. Between them, the ports feed the automotive plants, run by Renault and Stellantis, that have made vehicles Morocco’s biggest export.

Under its new owners, Globex is meant to become a green logistics leader, with solar-powered hubs, an electric fleet and carbon reporting tools. The seller side is moving too: A.P. Moller Capital has separately agreed to sell its 49 per cent of grain-terminal operator Mass Céréales al Maghreb to the investors STOA and Africa50.

What to watch

The first marker is the Competition Council’s clearance, the only named obstacle between signing and completion. The second is whether Amethis stays in the shareholding or exits.

Beyond that, the fund’s own pipeline suggests more Moroccan deals in cold storage and air cargo. For a country selling itself as the logistics doorway between Europe and Africa, Danish money arriving at this scale is itself the story.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is A.P. Moller Capital part of Maersk? Not directly. It is the fund-management arm of A.P. Moller Holding, the family holding company that also controls the Maersk shipping group, so the two are sister businesses under the same owner. How much is the Globex deal worth? The price and the exact stake were not disclosed. The two buying funds hold about US$243 million in committed capital between them. What does Globex do? It is FedEx’s exclusive express licensee in Morocco, and also works in road freight, freight forwarding, customs brokerage and warehousing. It holds FedEx and TNT licences in Senegal and Cameroon as well. What still needs to happen before completion? The deal needs merger-control clearance from Morocco’s Competition Council, plus other customary conditions. Founder Omar El Kadiri stays on as chief executive either way.

World.title: Nigeria Tells Atiku the Land Borders Are Already Open
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

NIGERIA · POLITICS & TRADE

Key Facts —The rebuttal: Nigeria’s presidency says the country’s land borders are already open, dismissing a 2027 campaign pledge by opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar to “open the borders.” —Who said it: Sunday Dare, President Bola Tinubu’s special adviser on media, in a State House statement dated 28 August titled “Atiku and the Borders: Nigerians Deserve Facts, Not Campaign Slogans.” —The record: Most land borders were reopened on 14 March 2024, the statement says, and in February 2026 customs reopened the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors in Kebbi State on Tinubu’s directive. —The jab: Dare called Atiku “unhinged” and argued that an open border is not an uncontrolled border. —The backdrop: The late President Muhammadu Buhari shut Nigeria’s land borders in 2019-2020 to fight smuggling, squeezing trade with Benin, Niger, Cameroon and Chad.

Nigeria’s presidency says the country’s land borders are already open, rejecting a campaign promise by 2027 opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar to reopen them. The unusually sharp rebuttal turns one of Nigeria’s oldest economic grievances into an early election battleground.

What the presidency actually said

“The facts are straightforward: Nigeria’s land borders are already open,” the State House said in a statement issued on Friday, 28 August. It said the government announced the reopening of most of the country’s land borders on 14 March 2024 and has not reversed that position.

The statement, signed by media adviser Sunday Dare, also cited the Kamba border in Kebbi State, which it said President Tinubu opened in February 2026 “with attendant economic and diplomatic gains.” Customs officers formally reopened the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors that month, freeing about 2,000 trucks stranded at the frontier with Benin and Niger.

Then came the attack. “Atiku is unhinged now, and he would say or announce anything to attract and deceive the politically gullible,” Dare wrote, adding: “An open border is not an uncontrolled border.”

The statement leaned on security to make its case. Citing the Global Terrorism Index 2026, it said about 41 per cent of terrorist attacks occur within 50 kilometres of an international border and 64 per cent within 100 kilometres, arguing that troops on Nigeria’s northern corridors reflect border security, not closed borders.

What Atiku promised

Atiku Abubakar, a former vice president who won the African Democratic Congress presidential primary in May, has made border trade a plank of his 2027 campaign. He pledged to reopen any land borders still shut and to ease the importation and movement of goods.

He argues that border closures forced many businesses to shut down and deepened insecurity. He has also promised to develop seaports in Nigeria’s south, where the dominance of Lagos harbours has long been a grievance for coastal states such as Akwa Ibom and Bayelsa.

His claim has a kernel of truth. The presidency itself says only that “most” borders were reopened in 2024, leaving open the question of which crossings remain restricted and why.

How the borders became a campaign issue

In August 2019 the late President Muhammadu Buhari closed Nigeria’s land borders, saying rampant smuggling of rice, fuel and other goods was undercutting local producers. The blockade lasted about 16 months and strained relations with Benin and Niger, whose economies depend heavily on trade with their giant neighbour.

Abuja began unwinding the closure in December 2020, reopening four major posts: Seme on the Benin corridor, Illela and Maigatari toward Niger, and Mfum toward Cameroon. A phased reopening followed, and on 14 March 2024 the Tinubu administration announced that most remaining land borders were open again.

The Kebbi corridors are the newest chapter. Customs area controller Mahmud Matawalle-Ibrahim said the Kamba and Tsamiya posts reopened in February on presidential approval, after talks with Benin to let legitimate cargo move through to Niger’s Tunga Jado border.

Why it matters beyond the campaign

Nigeria’s frontiers with Benin, Niger, Chad and Cameroon carry one of Africa’s densest flows of informal trade, from petrol and rice to livestock and textiles. Seme, west of Lagos, is among the busiest land crossings in West Africa.

Open and predictable borders are also the backbone of Nigeria’s commitments under the African Continental Free Trade Area, the pact meant to create a single market across the continent. Every closure undercuts Abuja’s claim to leadership of that project.

Customs Comptroller-General Bashir Adeniyi has framed the recent reopenings as economic diplomacy: regulated crossings, the service argues, give better oversight and intelligence than closures that push trade into smugglers’ hands.

What is still unverified

Neither side has published a definitive list of which crossings remain restricted. Traders’ groups have long reported that some posts operate with de facto limits even after formal reopening, and the presidency’s “most borders” phrasing does not settle that.

The terrorism statistics are quoted from the presidency’s own statement and were not independently checked against the Global Terrorism Index 2026 report. Atiku’s camp had not responded to the “unhinged” remark at the time of writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Nigeria’s land borders open right now? The presidency says yes, pointing to a 14 March 2024 decision reopening most land borders and the February 2026 reopening of the Kamba and Tsamiya corridors in Kebbi State. Opposition candidate Atiku Abubakar says some crossings remain shut, and neither side has published a full list. What did Atiku Abubakar promise about the borders? The ADC presidential candidate pledged to reopen any land borders still closed and ease the movement of goods if elected in 2027. He says past closures killed businesses and worsened insecurity, and he has also promised to develop seaports outside Lagos. When did Nigeria close its land borders? President Muhammadu Buhari closed them in August 2019 to fight smuggling. Reopening began in December 2020 at four posts, including Seme and Mfum, and the Tinubu administration announced that most borders were open again on 14 March 2024. What is the Kamba border? Kamba is a crossing in Kebbi State, northwest Nigeria, linking the country to Benin and, via the Tsamiya corridor, to Niger. Customs reopened it in February 2026 on President Tinubu’s directive, releasing about 2,000 stranded trucks.

World.title: Turkish Arms Ship Freed Off Somalia as Rescue Accounts Clash
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Somalia · MARITIME SECURITY

Key Facts — Seizure Eight armed men seized the Cameroon-flagged MV LUTUF on 17 August, about 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district.

— Crew The ten people aboard were six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards.

— Release Somalia’s defense ministry said a joint Somali-Turkish operation freed the ship on 29 August and killed 14 alleged pirates. Puntland’s security ministry says the pirates left after a ransom was paid.

— Context Before the release, the International Maritime Organization said six merchant ships and more than 90 seafarers were being held in the region.

A cargo ship carrying Turkish military equipment is free after twelve days off Somalia’s Puntland coast, but the two governments involved tell sharply different stories about how.

Somalia’s defense ministry said on 29 August that Somali and Turkish forces had freed the MV LUTUF, the Cameroon-flagged cargo ship held by pirates off the Puntland coast since 17 August. It said the operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four of their boats.

Puntland, the semi-autonomous region where the ship was held, immediately rejected that account. Its security ministry said no military operation took place and that the pirates left voluntarily after being paid.

A skiff carrying pirates leaves a hijacked merchant ship off Somalia during an earlier seizure, under naval observation. (Photo: US Navy, Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jason R. Zalasky, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Mogadishu says happened

The federal defense ministry said the vessel and its crew were freed in a joint operation by the Somali army and the Turkish navy that lasted ten days. It said the remaining pirates fled the vessel, allowing the forces to take control of the ship.

The operation was conducted under a defense cooperation agreement between Somalia and Turkey aimed at strengthening maritime security, protecting Somalia’s coastline and combating piracy, the ministry said. Turkey is one of Somalia’s closest security partners and trains thousands of Somali soldiers.

The ministry gave no details about casualties among its own forces or the well-being of the crew. Abdullahi Warsame, a local elder from the Jiifle community in the Godob Jiiraan district where the vessel was held, told the Associated Press that the vessel and its crew had been freed.

The hijacking itself

The LUTUF was seized on Monday 17 August, about 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district, a Somali official told the Associated Press. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, the Royal Navy’s shipping-alert desk, said eight armed individuals boarded the vessel and took control of it.

The ship, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was sailing from Turkey toward Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. Its cargo was weapons, communications and satellite equipment bound for TURKSOM, the Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu that is Ankara’s largest overseas base.

The ten-member crew comprised six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards. Neither the Indian nor the Turkish authorities made any public statement while the ship was held.

The eight pirates were believed to belong to the same group that seized the merchant vessel Sward on 26 April. They steered the LUTUF toward the coast near Garmaal, in Puntland’s Dangoroyo district on the Nugaal shore.

Puntland tells a different story

Puntland’s Ministry of Security rejected the military-rescue account outright. It said the pirates freed the LUTUF voluntarily after receiving the ransom they had demanded.

The ministry said the payment was facilitated by members of the federal government, who it said had been in phone contact with the pirates since the day of the hijacking. Local media and journalists in Puntland put the ransom at US$2.5 million; earlier unconfirmed reports of the pirates’ demand had cited about US$2 million.

Puntland’s government condemned any ransom payment, warning that it risks emboldening pirates and undermining efforts to combat piracy along Somalia’s coast. Turkish authorities have not commented publicly on either version of the release.

The strike that killed four men

On 18 August, a day after the hijacking, a small boat delivered khat, a stimulant widely chewed in Somalia, to the held vessel. After the boat returned to shore, an airstrike hit the area, killing four men and wounding two.

The Associated Press could not establish who carried out the strike or whether the dead had any connection to the pirates. Turkish naval vessels, helicopters and drones had been reported monitoring the area, but Ankara has never publicly confirmed a strike on Somali territory.

Puntland says the dead were fishermen, and its president, Saeed Abdullahi Deni, accused Ankara of killing civilians in strikes on 18 and 20 August. Garmaal held burials for the men, and former foreign minister Abdisaed Muse Ali called the killings a brutal act of aggression by Turkey.

A piracy season like the old days

The LUTUF was the fifth merchant ship seized off Somalia since April, and not the last. Three days after it was taken, six armed men boarded the tanker Seamull about 136 nautical miles east of Mukalla in Yemen and diverted it toward Somalia.

That prompted the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations shipping agency, to warn that six vessels were being held in the region: the Honour 25, taken on 21 April; the Sward, on 26 April; the Eureka, on 2 May; the Asana, on 17 July; the LUTUF; and the Seamull. Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said more than 90 seafarers were captive and demanded their immediate release.

The resurgence has coincided with heavier traffic along the Somali coast. Security threats in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz have pushed carriers to reroute through the western Indian Ocean, putting more ships within reach of pirate groups operating from the shore.

What to watch now

The first open question is the crew. Ten men, most of them Indian, spent twelve days in pirate hands, and no government has yet confirmed their condition or where the LUTUF will be taken.

The second is money. If a ransom was paid, as Puntland insists, negotiators will have handed the region’s pirate networks fresh funding at the very moment the world’s navies are stretched between the Gulf of Aden and the Gulf.

Five of the six ships on the maritime agency’s list, and their crews, remain in pirate hands tonight. The LUTUF’s release, however it was bought, is the exception in this season, not the rule.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where exactly was the LUTUF hijacked? About 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district on 17 August. The pirates then moved the ship to the Nugaal coast near Garmaal, where it was held until 29 August. Was a ransom paid for the ship? That is disputed. Somalia’s defense ministry says a joint Somali-Turkish military operation freed the vessel, while Puntland’s security ministry and local media say a ransom of about US$2.5 million was paid. Turkey has not commented on either account. Who are the crew, and are they safe? Ten people: six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards. A local elder said the crew was freed with the ship, but no government has officially confirmed their condition. Is piracy off Somalia getting worse? Yes. Six merchant vessels were seized between April and August, and the International Maritime Organization counts more than 90 seafarers held hostage, the worst spell of Somali piracy in about a decade.

World.title: Mundubile Surrenders to Zambian Police After Two Weeks in Hiding
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

ZAMBIA · POST-ELECTION CRISIS

Key Facts —The surrender: Brian Mundubile, runner-up in Zambia’s 13 August presidential election, surrendered to police on Thursday after about two weeks in hiding, much of it under United Nations protection in Lusaka. —The allegations: Police are questioning him and running mate Makebi Zulu over “alarming activities” they say could threaten national security. Some Zambian outlets report detectives recorded formal statements linked to possible treason allegations; no charge had been announced as of the latest reports on Friday. —The election: The electoral commission declared President Hakainde Hichilema re-elected with about 61 percent of the vote. Mundubile won roughly 38 percent and disputes the result. —The context: A post-election security raid in Lusaka left a former minister dead and 11 people under arrest, and the country’s top courts were closed on the final day to challenge the result.

Zambia’s main opposition presidential candidate, Brian Mundubile, surrendered to police on Thursday after about two weeks in hiding, ending a standoff that began with a disputed election and saw him take refuge under United Nations protection. He faces questioning over what police call threats to national security, and no formal charge had been announced as of Friday.

From UN refuge to police custody

Mundubile and his running mate, lawyer Makebi Zulu, were handed over to police on Thursday under an agreement between the UN Secretary-General’s representative in Zambia and President Hichilema, Channel Africa reported. Under the terms of that agreement, the state pledged the two men would be treated according to the rule of law.

Police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi confirmed the pair were being interrogated with their lawyers present, the Lusaka-based News Diggers reported. Police said they would issue a full statement once the interviews were complete.

The two men had sought protection from the United Nations in Lusaka on 17 August, four days after the election. When police issued a public summons on 21 August, they said they knew where the men were and assured the organisation that no harm would come to them.

A disputed election

The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared Hichilema the winner on 18 August with 2,965,326 votes, about 61 percent of the roughly five million cast. Mundubile finished second of 14 candidates with 1,856,217 votes, roughly 38 percent.

The commission suspended counting on 14 August, citing attacks and threats against election staff, and resumed the following day. During the suspension Mundubile said his campaign’s parallel vote tabulation showed him ahead; his Tonse Alliance later insisted he had not declared himself the winner.

Two reports by independent observers found indications that Hichilema’s official tally was inflated, but concluded he would have won anyway, Reuters reported. Hichilema denies any fraud, and European Union observers said the vote was largely peaceful while criticising late legal changes and an uneven playing field.

Mundubile is a former provincial minister under the late president Edgar Lungu and leads the opposition Tonse Alliance. He contested the presidency on the ticket of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), a smaller partner in the alliance.

The raid that set off the crisis

On the night after the election, security forces raided a property in Lusaka’s Kabulonga area where Mundubile was present and arrested 11 people. Police accused the group of possessing materials for an armed insurrection.

Former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead in an exchange of gunfire during the operation. Mundubile denied any plot and said the raid was an attempt on his life.

The government has not brought charges or publicly produced evidence to support the insurrection claims, drawing condemnation from international organisations, Reuters noted. Days after the raid, Mundubile went into hiding.

What Mundubile faces now

Police say they want to establish links between the two men and “various alarming activities” with the potential to threaten national security, some of them allegedly conducted on premises owned by or linked to the pair. After hours of interrogation, the Zambian outlet Wansom reported that detectives recorded warn-and-caution statements — a formal step before possible charges under Zambian criminal procedure — in connection with treason allegations; that account had not been officially confirmed.

Mundubile has previously dismissed the allegations as fabricated. It is his second brush with the law this year: in March he was arrested and charged with aiding hate speech under cyber security laws over a Facebook page, and released on bond.

His legal options on the election itself narrowed this week. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court were closed on Monday, the final day to petition the result, in what authorities called a security measure — a step the Law Association of Zambia warned could undermine the constitutional right to challenge an election. A separate petition brought by former association president Linda Kasonde and two other applicants has since been filed.

Why it matters beyond Zambia

Zambia, Africa’s second-largest copper producer, has long been regarded as one of the continent’s more stable democracies. Hichilema won power in a landslide in 2021 and campaigned this year on an economic recovery that followed a 2020 debt default.

Analysts say the post-election crackdown is out of character and risks tarnishing that reputation. “This is completely out of the bounds of the ordinary for Zambia,” Nicole Beardsworth, a politics lecturer at the University of the Witwatersrand, told Reuters.

Frequently asked questions

Who is Brian Mundubile? He leads the opposition Tonse Alliance and ran for president on the NRPUP ticket. A former minister under the late Edgar Lungu, he finished second in the 13 August election. Has Mundubile been charged? No formal charge had been announced as of the latest reports on Friday. He is being questioned over alleged threats to national security, and some Zambian outlets report possible treason allegations, which officials have not confirmed. Who won Zambia’s election? The electoral commission declared President Hakainde Hichilema re-elected on 18 August with about 61 percent of the vote, against roughly 38 percent for Mundubile. The opposition disputes the result. Why was the United Nations involved? Mundubile and his running mate sought UN protection in Lusaka on 17 August. The UN Secretary-General’s representative brokered the terms under which they were handed to police on 27 August, with a state pledge of due process. Can the election result still be challenged? The official deadline to petition closed on 24 August, when the top courts were shut for what authorities called security reasons. A separate petition by lawyer Linda Kasonde and two co-applicants has been filed, but the court route for the opposition is uncertain.

World.title: The Lifeguards Who Transformed Playa Dominical in Costa Rica
World.content:
Playa Dominical has a well earned reputation as one of Costa Rica’s premier surfing spots. Its powerful and consistent beach break draws riders from all over the world. It regularly hosts stops for the official Costa Rican Surf Federation National Surf Circuit (Circuito Nacional de Surf) and also has its own highly competitive local tourneys.

It is also one of Costa Rica’s most dangerous beaches, with violently crashing waves, hazardous rips, and a topography underfoot that goes quickly from shallow to deep. The Rio Baru empties into the sea at the north end of the beach, adding to the turbulent mix. While experienced surfers navigate the challenging conditions, the ocean is not forgiving to those who venture in unprepared.

In the first half of the 1990s, Dominical averaged a startling twenty drownings per year. An untrained samaritan attempting to rescue a swimmer caught in the merciless rip sometimes resulted in a double tragedy.

As Dominical’s popularity grew throughout the 1990s, a small group of foreign residents – all California natives immersed in the surfing culture– decided to take action. The solution was evident: There was a clear need for trained lifeguards to stand watch and be ready to rescue swimmers unable to return to shore.

A search was made and in December, 1996, a veteran beach lifeguard arrived from the states, and the first professional lifeguard program in Costa Rica began. A team of eight longtime local Dominical area residents was trained and began manning shifts from the newly constructed lifeguard tower.

For the next five years, the program was kept afloat mainly through private donations. Beginning in 2002, an annual July 4th fundraiser was held to raise money for paying salaries of the workers and maintaining the necessary equipment. The beachfront Roca Verde Hotel hosted the event for many years and the community came together for a day of revelry and came through time after time with sufficient money to keep the lifeguard program afloat.

And with good reason: The number of annual preventable drownings in the areas patrolled was now zero. In the thirty years since the seeds of the idea were planted, the program has been active for all but a couple– there was a year with no captain, which led to some disorder, and then covid. For the first twenty years there was zero help from any branch of the government.

All of the necessary steps were taken to obtain assistance. A corporation was formed, paperwork was completed, and despite the obvious service that was being provided, it took several years for a response. Then briefly, between 2017-2022 there was help from the local municipality, which paid the salaries and caja for two full time lifeguards.

In 2024, with help from the muni suspended, it was time to seek out new sources. With the generous backing of a recent arrival to the area, the officially named Guardavidas Costa Ballena are now on full time watch. A new expanded and roofed guard building houses the workers. A second tower is up further down the beach.

Awareness has been raised. In 2025, over 200 people from throughout Costa Rica gathered at a hotel in Escazu. All were connected with various up and coming beach lifeguard programs.

In a country that sees between 150-200 drownings annually, many on beaches with challenging conditions, the fact that there have been no preventable drownings along the patrolled area for 29 years in Dominical is testament to the importance of having trained lifeguards on our beaches.

The ideal would be a Guardvidas Costa Ballena type organization patrolling every major beach up and down both coasts. The workstaff would be trained locals, paid a salary just as are the police and firefighters. The reality is far from the ideal: The bureaucracy crawls along indifferently, and the further you are from San Jose, the less help you should expect.

The example of Dominical is not to wait for the government to step in. The community stepped up, private donors made investments that benefit the area, and the trained lifeguards continue keeping the sheet clean with no preventable drownings in almost thirty years

World.title: Ship Pays Record Amount to Cross Panama Canal Amid Drought Restrictions
World.content:
A ship paid a record $5.3 million to cross the Panama Canal sooner, just days before a reduction in vessel traffic takes effect due to drought caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon. The canal, which handles 5% of global maritime trade, will reduce the number of ships allowed to pass through each day from 36 to 34 beginning September 3. Twelve days later, the daily limit will fall to 32 to conserve the fresh water needed for operations.

The interoceanic waterway operates using rainwater stored in the artificial Gatún and Alhajuela lakes, where water levels have fallen because of the adverse effects of El Niño. Incoming canal administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta confirmed on Thursday, in response to a question from AFP, that a ship had paid $5.3 million to cross the route.

“It is the largest amount” ever paid to transit the canal, she said, without providing details about the vessel. Bloomberg reported that South Korean company SK Gas Ltd. paid the amount for the G. Spirit to cross on September 1. A local team located the vessel a few kilometers from the canal’s Pacific entrance.

“We have had three auctions like this, with somewhat high bids, recently,” added Espino de Marotta, who will formally take office on September 7. Nine out of every 10 canal crossings, whose main users are the United States and China, are scheduled through reservations. The remaining slots, or transit times changed because of last-minute contingencies, are auctioned.

Information about the payments made by shipping companies is confidential. On Friday, the Panama Canal announced temporary changes to its Transit Reservation System for large Neopanamax vessels to “increase flexibility and promote equitable access to available slots.”

The changes will take effect on August 30 for reservation dates beginning September 13. In April, a vessel paid as much as $4 million because of the urgent need to transport hydrocarbons amid increased demand caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. With fewer transits, “there are fewer opportunities to secure a reservation,” meaning the slots “have greater value,” Espino de Marotta said. She added that the price is “set by the market” and the vessel’s “need.”

The Panama Canal Authority, an autonomous government agency, reported that the average auction price between October 2025 and February 2026 was approximately $55,000. Former canal administrator Jorge Quijano said on Friday that payments “could be” even higher because more than 120 ships are waiting to cross the canal.

According to Quijano, some of those vessels do not have reservations and could seek a slot through an auction to deliver their cargo on time and avoid multimillion-dollar penalties from customers. The canal primarily connects the East Coast of the United States with China, South Korea and Japan.

World.title: U.S. President Trump Announces Major Venezuela Oil Deal
World.content:
United States President Donald Trump announced on Friday an agreement guaranteeing the United States majority control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. Described by Trump as the “largest oil deal in history,” it will bring Venezuela nearly $100 billion in private investment, according to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves. The United States has exerted intense pressure on the country since overthrowing and capturing Nicolás Maduro in January. His vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, assumed power on an interim basis and, under pressure from Washington, pushed through reforms in the oil and mining sectors that opened the door to foreign investment.

According to the Republican president, the agreement will allow his country to more than double its crude oil reserves. Rodríguez confirmed the agreement with Washington on Telegram and described it as “historic.” She said the deal covers the development of “17 strategic fields” and will generate “more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the state.”

The agreement “will have a significant impact on the rebirth of our nation,” Rodríguez added. “I am deeply grateful to the president of the United States of America, Donald Trump, as well as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. government, for their willingness to develop this agreement,” she said.

Expanding transition

The agreement was negotiated by Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in partnership with “private companies,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “This transaction will greatly strengthen the already expanding relationship between Venezuela and the United States!” he added.

Rubio said the agreement demonstrates how “President Trump’s bold foreign policy is delivering victories” for the United States, this time by securing “stable reserves and low-cost oil” in the hemisphere. He said it would also lower domestic gasoline prices in the United States. “For the Venezuelan people, this agreement will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, support thousands of well-paying jobs and help rebuild Venezuela’s economy,” the top U.S. diplomat said.

Jorge Piñon, a researcher at the University of Texas at Austin’s Energy Institute, said the agreement was unconventional and that questions remained about how the assets would be transferred. “We do not know how the transfer would be carried out,” he said. “Is it a sale? Is it a transfer of title? Does the transfer happen only once the reserves have actually been produced?”

Venezuelan crude oil production reached 1.2 million barrels per day at the end of July, according to official sources, an increase of 29.8% since January. Venezuela produced as much as 3 million barrels per day at the end of the last century, but a lack of investment and U.S. sanctions reduced its capacity.

Relief at the gas pump

With his approval ratings falling, Trump insisted that the agreement would lower gasoline prices for Americans, a sensitive issue ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections following the start of the war against Iran. The conflict, which has now lasted six months, has disrupted the global oil supply.

News website Axios reported on Thursday that the two countries were discussing about a dozen productive oil fields containing 90 billion barrels of proven reserves, approximately one-third of Venezuela’s total proven reserves. According to Axios, the agreement would more than double U.S. oil reserves at a time when the country’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level in 40 years.

Trump is urging U.S. companies to invest in Venezuela, although they remain cautious because of deteriorating infrastructure and the Chávez movement’s history of expropriating assets belonging to foreign investors. John Kilduff, an energy expert at Again Capital, said the biggest concern for companies operating in Venezuela is “the security and protection of their investment.”

Chevron, the only U.S. oil company still operating in Venezuela when Maduro was overthrown, said in July that it had increased its daily crude production to 280,000 barrels and planned to raise output by 50% by the end of 2028. Meanwhile, the wells covered by the agreement announced on Friday will take between five and 10 years to reach “100% operation,” Oswaldo Felizzola, an oil expert and professor at Venezuela’s Institute of Advanced Management Studies, said.

World.title: El Salvador’s Fireball Festival Lights Up Nejapa
World.content:
If you are in El Salvador this weekend and want to see something you will not find anywhere else, head north from San Salvador on Monday night. The district of Nejapa, in San Salvador Oeste, holds the 104th edition of its fireball battle on 31 August. Two teams of residents take up positions at opposite ends of the main street and hurl burning balls of cloth at each other for about two hours while thousands of people watch from the sides.

The municipal government has built a two-day program around it, running 30 and 31 August, with music, food, parades and cultural events leading into the battle itself. The 30th is also marked locally as Día de la Juventud. Everything about it is free.

The balls are made months ahead and Cotton rags are bound with wire into rough spheres and then submerged in barrels of gasoline for weeks so the fuel soaks all the way through. Organizers have prepared upwards of 3,000 in recent years. Once lit, the flames run higher than a meter (3.3 feet).

The players, known as boleros, paint their faces, soak their clothing, and wear gloves and long sleeves. Burns still happen. That is part of why people come. Two accounts of the tradition’s origin circulate in Nejapa, and residents will tell you both. One holds that it commemorates the 1658 eruption of the El Playón volcano, which destroyed the original settlement and forced the population to move.

The other traces it to 1917, when the San Salvador volcano erupted and the town was spared, which locals attributed to the intervention of their patron saint, San Jerónimo Doctor. In either version, the saint threw fire to turn the lava away. The festival in its current form dates to 1922. The Ministry of Culture declared it a Bien Cultural in 2019.

If you go, a few things are worth knowing.

Do not wear synthetic fabric. It melts onto skin. Long trousers and closed shoes are the right call, and shorts and skirts are specifically discouraged by organizers because a stray ball against bare leg causes a serious burn. Stay out of the playing zone, and do not pick up a ball and throw it. Balls do go astray into the crowd, and spectators who join in are the ones most likely to hurt someone.

Leave infants and small children at home and this is not a judgment call the crowd will help you with once you are inside it. Arrive well before dark. Parking fills, the main street closes, and the walk in from where you leave a vehicle gets longer as the evening goes on. Local families set up food stalls through the afternoon, so coming early is no hardship.

Nejapa sits roughly 25 kilometers (16 miles) north of San Salvador. Note that this route is not affected by the weekend closure of the Panamericana at Los Chorros, which is west of the capital.

For a country that spent decades being described to outsiders in a single register, Nejapa on the last night of August is a useful corrective. It is loud, it is genuinely dangerous, and it has been happening every year for more than a century because a town decided its survival was worth remembering out loud.

World.title: Costa Rica Delays Yellow Fever Vaccine Rules Until October
World.content:
Costa Rica has delayed new yellow fever vaccination rules for travelers to eight countries, giving you another month to get vaccinated before the requirements take effect. The Health Ministry announced yesterday that the new rules will now begin on October 1, 2026, instead of August 31.

The change applies to Costa Rican citizens and legal residents traveling to Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela, Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana. Starting October 1, travelers heading to any of those destinations will need to have received the yellow fever vaccine at least 10 days before leaving Costa Rica. They will also need a valid International Certificate of Vaccination against Yellow Fever.

Health officials said the extra month is intended to help people who already booked trips but have not had enough time to get vaccinated and complete the required paperwork. The delay does not apply to every destination. Costa Rica’s existing yellow fever vaccine requirements remain in effect for people traveling to Colombia, Brazil and Peru, as well as African countries considered at risk for the disease.

Those heading to those destinations should continue following the current rules and the Health Ministry recommends arranging the vaccine well ahead of a trip because it must be given at least 10 days before departure for the certificate to meet the requirement. Travelers can get their vaccination certificate digitally through the Health Ministry’s online office, the EDUS health app and the government’s Pura Vida Móvil app.

Yellow fever is a viral disease spread by infected mosquitoes. It is found mainly in tropical areas of South America and Africa and can cause fever, headaches and other symptoms. Severe cases can be life-threatening. Costa Rica has tightened its yellow fever travel rules in recent years as health officials respond to cases and outbreaks elsewhere in the region. Costa Rica went decades without a locally reported case, although an imported case was confirmed in October 2025 involving a traveler who had visited Peru.

Anyone planning a trip from Costa Rica to one of the eight newly added destinations on or after October 1 should check their vaccination status now rather than waiting until shortly before departure. The Health Ministry also recommends checking the latest requirements before traveling, since health rules can change depending on conditions in destination countries.

World.title: Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday
World.content:
Belize stays hot and mostly dry this Sunday

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Warm and relatively dry conditions prevail over Belize today, according to the National Meteorological Service.

Expect sunny skies with a few cloudy intervals through the day and partly cloudy skies tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a low chance of a few more over southern Toledo tonight.

Inland temperatures will reach 95 degrees Fahrenheit before dropping to 74 overnight. The coast reaches 90 with a low of 82, while the hills stay at 82 and fall to 68.

At sea, easterly winds will blow at 5 to 15 knots with a light chop and waves of 2 to 4 feet.

Monday and Monday night will continue mainly fair and warm with isolated shower activity.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Sunrise was at 5:38am and sunset comes at 6:07pm.

The forecast was issued at 6am by forecaster Derrick Rudon.

World.title: You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic
World.content:
You will be dead much longer than you will be tired, the Sunday arithmetic

By Horace Palacio:

A line has been circulating this week, dressed in the name of Alexander the Great.

You will be dead much longer than you will be tired.

Did Alexander actually say it? Honesty first, as always in this column. No ancient historian records the sentence, and it carries the fingerprints of the internet, which loves to lend its best lines to famous corpses. But for once, the internet mailed the quote to the correct address. Because whether or not the words are his, no life in recorded history argues them harder.

Consider the record. A young man inherits a small kingdom at twenty. By thirty two he has marched an army more than twenty thousand miles, from Greece to the edge of India, never once losing a battle, founding cities from Egypt to Afghanistan that carry his name to this day. He fought at the front, not the rear. At one siege in India an arrow went through his chest into his lung, and the man got up and kept campaigning. Plutarch records that Alexander said it was sleep that reminded him he was mortal. Tiredness, to him, was weather. You do not negotiate with weather. You march through it.

Now sit with the sentence itself, because it is really a piece of arithmetic, and arithmetic is this column’s love language.

How long will you be tired? Tonight, perhaps. This season, maybe. Tiredness is a visitor. It arrives, it sits heavily, and it always, always leaves, usually by morning, sometimes by Monday, occasionally by next year.

How long will you be dead? Forever. Not a long time. Forever. Every year that has ever passed and every year that will ever come, stacked end to end, and then eternity after that. Death is not a visitor. Death is the address.

So the sentence is simply asking you to compare the two durations before you make any permanent decision based on the temporary one. And yet, look around Belize, and listen to the national anthem we actually sing daily. Mi tired.

Let me be careful here, because this column has spent a year honoring Belizean tiredness, and I will not insult it now. The mother working the hotel shift and the market stall, whose month is longer than her money, she is not the target of this sermon. She is its proof. She wakes exhausted every single morning and rises anyway. She has been living Alexander’s arithmetic her whole life without a meme to tell her so. Salute her.

No, the sentence aims at something else entirely. It aims at the dreams we execute with fatigue as the weapon. The business never registered, because mi tired. The course abandoned at module three. The field never planted. The application never sent. The apology never made, the book never opened, the savings circle never started. Ask the honest question, Belize. How many of our unlived lives were cancelled not by failure, not by enemies, not by lack of talent, but by a feeling that would have passed by Thursday?

We keep signing permanent resignations with temporary ink.

Now, the double edge, because this column never sells half a story, and Alexander’s own life carries the correction inside it.

Two facts about the undefeated general. First, the only force that ever beat him was tiredness itself, just not his own.
