World.title: Relief and sorrow in Iceland after EU membership talks referendum fails
World.content:
A mix of relief and dejection spread across Iceland on Sunday after the country narrowly voted "No" to resuming talks with the European Union on potential membership.

 

Many Icelanders had gathered in the capital Reykjavík to follow the results as they came in overnight, with both supporters and opponents of accession negotiations celebrating as the count progressed.

In Saturday's vote, 52.8% rejected resuming EU entry talks, while 47.2% voted "Yes," according to public broadcaster RÚV.

Speaking from Reykjavík after the result was called, Skuli Olafsson Skuli, a pastor, said he was "a little bit relieved."

"It has been quite aggressive, this discussion," he said. "But now I hope the opposing parties will find a way to make this community here in Iceland a little bit better just by using our own methods and, of course, those relations we have with Europe, America, and Asia."

Anna Maria Bogadottir, an artist, said the outcome of the vote had left her "in a kind of denial."

"It's hard to grasp that it's a no," she added.

Iceland's centre-left prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, has pledged to "respect" the result while also praising the high voter turnout.

"It's obvious that close to half of the country wanted to continue these negotiations, but over half of the population did not. We will respect that result," Frostadóttir told a press conference on Sunday.

"The fact that we got people to the table on a matter like this is extremely important for us," she continued. "It gives us a stronger mandate to make a decision on this matter."

Writing on X, former Icelandic President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson - who had backed the "No" campaign - said the "nation has spoken."

A supporter wearing a European Union flag attends an election-night gathering in Reykjavik, Iceland, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The result of the referendum has also been hailed by right-wing figures from across the UK and France.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage - who was a key supporter of Brexit - congratulated Iceland on "voting to keep their independence."

France's Marine Le Pen added: "At a time when some are pushing for greater federalism and the transfer of sovereignty to the European Commission, this vote serves as a reminder that another Europe is possible – a Europe of free, sovereign nations cooperating voluntarily on matters of common interest."

For its part, the European Commission offered a short statement on the result, saying it "takes note of the outcome" and that it "respects the choice of the Icelandic people."

Iceland first applied for EU membership in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, with the Commission issuing a favourable opinion in February 2010. A new Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.

World.title: 'A close partner': EU offers muted reaction after Iceland rebuffs accession talks
World.content:
The European Commission has issued a muted reaction after Iceland rejected the reopening of accession negotiations with the bloc in a hotly contested referendum, a decision that risks dampening the momentum on enlargement.

 

The vote came down to the wire: 52.8% chose "no" and 47.2% chose "yes".

"The European Commission takes note of the outcome of Iceland's referendum," a Commission spokesperson said in a brief statement.

"The Commission respects the choice of the Icelandic people. Iceland remains a close partner of the European Union."

Meanwhile, European Council President António Costa exchanged messages with Iceland's Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir during which "both leaders expressed their desire to continue to strengthen the relationship between the EU and Iceland", according to Costa's spokesperson.

"President Costa stressed that the EU fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people in today's referendum. Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," the spokesperson said.

Frostadóttir had previously said she would abandon the matter of EU membership entirely for the remainder of her term if voters rejected the proposal.

"47% of the population was interested in it," Frostadóttir said on Sunday. "I think it is important that we go into the coming months and weeks and respect that point of view."

Officials and diplomats in Brussels had seen in Iceland a five-star candidate that could have proven enlargement sceptics wrong. The Nordic country was all but guaranteed to become a frontrunner, given its extensive degree of integration with the bloc.

In the lead-up to the vote, the Commission, which oversees accession, had kept a low profile but signalled its intention to find "creative" solutions with Iceland to address what would have been the two most contentious issues: fisheries and agriculture.

Though Iceland enjoys broad access to the single market, the arrangement excludes the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

Those two chapters were left untouched the last time that Reykjavík and Brussels engaged in accession talks, a process put on hold in 2013.

It remains to be seen how large an impact the Icelandic referendum will have on the bloc's enlargement drive, which, after years of stagnation, jumped to the top of the political agenda in the aftermath of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Montenegro is the current frontrunner, having provisionally closed 18 of the 33 accession chapters. The country aspires to become the 28th member state in 2028, an ambition that has inspired the "28 by 28" slogan.

Even if Brussels refuses to commit to artificial deadlines, it recognises the importance of delivering on the promise of enlargement before candidates run out of patience. Coupling Montenegro with Iceland was considered a potential avenue.

The Commission is preparing reforms to bring tangible benefits to candidates, such as access to certain EU programmes, before they become full-time members.

World.title: Guinea-Bissau votes in referendum to rewrite constitution and boost presidential powers
World.content:
Voting got off to a slow start in some areas when the polling stations opened at 08:00 CET. According to media correspondents, security was stepped up at strategic points in the capital, with members of the National Guard and the police deployed at key locations.

 

This referendum is taking place against a backdrop of political instability and is being challenged by the opposition, not only because it has already been approved and published in the Official Gazette of the Republic -before the people had been ‘heard’- but also because it was drafted by the military junta, that is, by a transitional government without prior consultation.

"No one was consulted, neither political parties nor civil-society organisations, let alone traditional and religious leaders, and so on. So everything was done in secret," said the head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, Bubacar Turé, last week, speaking to Euronews.

Turé also stressed that campaigners for a "no" vote in the referendum were not authorised to campaign. "This is not an environment of freedom," he added, which is another reason why the opposition has called for a boycott of today’s vote.

Some analysts say the military government lacks legitimacy to change the constitution, which has fuelled discontent among citizens.

"The fundamental question is: who drafted this constitution, and on whose behalf? To protect which interests or institutions? Who stands to gain from this constitution?" said Guinea-Bissau political analyst Paulino Quadé, speaking to the Associated Press.

A military government seized power in November 2025 following disputed elections in which both the former president, Umaro Sissoco Embaló, and the opposition candidate, Fernando Dias, claimed victory.

After the military junta took power, it appointed General Horta N'Tam as transitional president under a temporary constitutional charter that bars him from standing in elections.

Election officials wait for voters to cast their ballots during a referendum on granting new presidential powers AP Photo/Darcicio Barbosa

If it goes ahead, the new constitution drafted by the self-styled National Transitional Council will give the president more powers and reduce parliamentary representation, among other changes.

The military junta currently in power unanimously approved a constitutional amendment to shift the country from a parliamentary to a presidential system, and the public is now being asked to endorse it. The new text proposes scrapping the previous system, under which the prime minister came from the parliamentary majority, leading to complex power-sharing arrangements. It would also allow the head of state to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet members, as well as to dissolve parliament.

Measures the opposition contests, arguing that they downgrade political parties and the popular will.

"This constitution significantly weakens the prime minister and the government, subordinates the National People’s Assembly and the political parties, and undermines, or even ignores, the popular will expressed at the ballot box, bringing all the inherent risks of division and political and social tensions," said Muniro Conté, spokesperson for the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), to the Associated Press.

The military authorities argue that a smaller parliament, reduced from 102 to 65 seats, would allow for easier and more substantive debates, while the new presidential powers would underscore the president’s higher authority over the prime minister, which they say has been a source of political instability in the country.

Coup after coup

FILE - The Transitional President of Guinea-Bissau, General Horta Inta-A-Na Man, centre, and the President of Senegal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye P Photo/Abubacar Queta

Since winning independence from Portugal in 1973, West Africa’s only Portuguese-speaking country has been rocked by several coups and attempted coups. Indeed, last year’s coup in Guinea-Bissau deepened West Africa’s democratic crisis, adding to the growing number of countries in the region under military rule.

In November 2025, the army seized power a few days after the presidential elections, toppling then president Umaro Sissoco Embaló and suspending the electoral process as the vote count neared its end and it was becoming clear who the new president-elect would be.

Several African leaders described the situation as a "staged" power grab after the military allowed the former president to hold a press conference to announce that he was being removed from office and that he was allowed to leave the country in seemingly favourable circumstances. The most sceptical observers say Embaló handed power to the military after realising he was losing the election.

During the 2023 legislative elections, Embaló himself dissolved parliament, which was dominated by the opposition, in response to what he described as an attempted coup, and then ruled by decree until he was deposed by the army.

This referendum follows a series of similar moves in other African countries, including Zimbabwe and Chad, which have amended their constitutions in recent years to extend presidential terms, remove age limits or strengthen executive powers.

With around 2.2 million inhabitants, Guinea-Bissau has suffered five coups and a series of attempted coups since 1974. The country has the highest ratio of natural wealth per capita, according to the World Bank, yet more than half the population lives in poverty.

Of the more than 2 million inhabitants, around 915,000 are eligible to vote today.

Sunday’s voting ends at 17:00 GMT, and the first provisional results are expected on Tuesday.

World.title: Inside Kourou: how a satellite is readied to watch Europe's skies and prevent natural disasters
World.content:
After two flights and more than 7,000 kilometres from Paris, we have witnessed first-hand a launch that has put Europe at the forefront of global space technology: the placing in orbit of a state-of-the-art satellite that speeds up mapping of the Earth’s surface to monitor disasters and help prevent floods and fires from continuing to devastate countries across the Old Continent.

 

The heart of the Ariane 6 launch system is not on the pad, but in a windowless control room several kilometres away. That is where we are received by the deputy launch director, Frédéric, whose surname we are withholding to protect him from cyberattacks, and several engineers who walk us through the details of the milestone. The rocket that is about to place the new European weather satellite in orbit was built on a very specific premise: to be cheaper and more versatile than its predecessor, Ariane 5, in a far more competitive international environment than a decade ago.

The launcher: a rocket designed not to waste time in Kourou

The key, the engineers explain, lies in where each task is carried out. The Ariane 6 core stage is manufactured and fully tested in France; the upper stage in Germany. Both arrive in Guiana already "ready to fly", with no need for any further functional tests once they are unloaded from the Canopée. Transport is handled by the dedicated cargo ship Canopée, the same one with the large sails that made the shipping line famous, which also picks up parts in Bordeaux and Rotterdam before completing the route to South America.

The solid-fuel boosters that assist at lift-off, by contrast, are manufactured in French Guiana itself, at the Regulus and Europropulsion plants. "It is much more practical and convenient to manufacture the boosters here than to ship that type of propellant from Europe," the engineers sum up. Once all the pieces are on the ground, the ArianeGroup team needs only between seven and nine days to assemble the launcher’s central core and have it ready to fly.

"It is not like pulling up at a petrol station, filling the tank and driving off. Filling the launcher takes two hours, and then another hour and a half of thermal stabilisation, because the liquid oxygen is at about -150°C and the liquid hydrogen at -250°C," Frédéric tells us.

The MTG-I2 satellite, launched on board an Ariane 6 rocket from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana on 27 August 2026. ESA

The MTG-I2 flight also featured two rare technical characteristics. It was the first time an Ariane 6 had flown to a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO), the most distant orbit reached by the rocket so far, in its A62 configuration with two side boosters. And, for the first time since the maiden flight, the mission had a launch window of two hours and 30 minutes instead of a fixed lift-off instant, giving the team some leeway to deal with unexpected issues.

The rocket’s upper stage, powered by the Vinci engine, can also be re-ignited in mid-flight thanks to a helium pressurisation system, which settles the propellant at the bottom of the tank before each re-ignition: a capability Ariane 5 did not have and which Ariane 6 is debuting on this type of mission.

The build: robots assembling a rocket horizontally

The rocket is assembled horizontally, not vertically. Guided vehicles move the lower and upper stages into a common position, where the two pieces are joined with a tolerance of barely a millimetre. "It is not a fully automatic process, it is assisted: there are many steps that the staff have to check and validate before triggering the next automatic sequence," the experts stress.

From the moment the two stages arrive in the facility, it takes around ten days until the central core is ready to be moved to the pad. The facility has two parallel assembly lines, which makes it possible to start putting together the next rocket as soon as the previous one heads out to the launch platform. The goal of the programme is to reach a cadence of nine to ten launches a year from 2027.

The satellite: the most sensitive passenger ever to fly on an Ariane 6

A few metres away, in the encapsulation building, the air is filtered, temperature-controlled and its humidity finely regulated. It is the last room where technicians have direct physical access to the satellite before it is sealed inside the rocket’s fairing. For MTG-I2, an optical meteorological observation instrument that is extremely sensitive to contamination, that cleanliness is not a minor detail: any particle can degrade the quality of its future images.

The process even includes a system of light traps for insects and birds: when the container with the satellite arrives at night and the gigantic doors of the building open to let it in, any animal that slips inside could jeopardise the cleanliness of the payload. "We cannot just open the container and let it out with a bird inside, obviously," explains one of the managers of the facility, who has spent almost a year coordinating this final stretch of the campaign with the spacecraft team.

Technical data for the Ariane 6 that launched MTG-I2 in August 2026 from French Guiana. Ariane Space

The Júpiter control room: the chain of command for the countdown

Eleven hours before lift-off, the final timeline begins and the centre of gravity shifts to the Júpiter control room at CNES, the French National Centre for Space Studies. A large operational screen shows the status of all systems in green, the planned trajectory and the countdown clocks.

Bruno Erin (left), Arianespace mission director, and Maxime André (right), CNES operations director. Euronews

In the centre sits Maxime André, the launch operations director, responsible for coordinating safety across the entire launch range (people, assets, environment) and, together with the quality team and the measurements officer who monitors telemetry, radar and tracking, providing the final voice and eyes that give the go-ahead.

Right up to the last minute, the mission team remains in contact with the satellite’s own control centre, located some four kilometres from the Júpiter room, to confirm that everything remains nominal and pass that confirmation up, step by step, to the operations director.

Lightning veto: the weather that can stop a launch

A few metres from the launch complex, a small team is watching the sky as closely as the engineers watch the rocket. François Laforge, meteorological analyst at the spaceport’s station, keeps his eye on two parameters above all others: lightning and wind. "Rain or temperature are not so important; what really matters are thunderstorms and wind, both at the surface and at altitude."

Rain or temperature are not so important; what really matters are thunderstorms and wind, both at the surface and at altitude François Laforge, analista meteorológico del CNES

The criteria are strict: no storm within a ten-kilometre radius around the base, either during preparations or during lift-off itself; and no cloud above 6,500 metres in that same radius, because as the rocket passes through such a high cloud it can generate static electricity capable of triggering lightning. To monitor this, the team combines radars that measure cloud height with a triangulation system of three antennas that pinpoint every electrical discharge in real time.

Weather balloons with radiosondes, launched several times during the countdown, measure the wind profile at altitude, data that Leonard Bouchaillot, flight safety engineer, uses together with the rest of the team to ensure safe conditions so that the pre-calculated "launch corridor" – the zone where, for safety, a possible flight termination of the rocket is simulated – remains valid.

This, he explains, is a requirement set out in French space law to guarantee public safety. The final weather check comes barely ten minutes before lift-off. Once in the air, the risk changes in nature: the rocket passes the speed of sound in under 50 seconds and 50 kilometres in altitude in under two minutes, so wind very quickly ceases to be a real threat. The real risk, they insist, lies on the ground.

A 6-billion-euro programme with benefits topping 61 billion

James Champion, head of the MTG project at the European Space Agency (ESA), set out the 16 years of work on the Meteosat satellite programme. It has meant almost two decades anticipating technology that did not yet exist but had to be factored in when placing MTG-I2 in orbit.

The cost of the programme in today’s economic conditions has been around 6 billion euros, while its benefits exceed 61 billion, once infrastructure is taken into account, not to mention the number of lives that will be saved thanks to satellite data helping, for example, to trigger evacuation plans. This family of satellites will be key to forecasting and preventing adverse weather events.

The science: a watchful hawk’s eye over Europe every 2.5 minutes

With the satellite just hours away from being placed in orbit, Cristian Bank, director of programme preparation and development at Eumetsat, sets the launch in its real context: that of a continent increasingly hit by extreme weather events. "In the past five years we have seen losses of 10 billion a year in damage in Europe and thousands of deaths. Fortunately, the number of fatalities is falling as our forecasts and warnings improve, but the damage to infrastructure remains. We need to be more resilient," he warns.

MTG-I2 is the third part of a complementary trio: the first satellite, launched in 2022, offers a hemispheric view – Europe, Africa, the Atlantic as far as the Indian Ocean – feeding global weather models; the second, launched in 2025 and almost operational, measures the atmosphere in depth (humidity, temperature, wind, pressure); and the third, whose launch we have just witnessed, will focus on Europe and in particular the Mediterranean basin, which is heavily affected by adverse weather events, updating its data every two and a half minutes.

Related Valencia flood survivors still seeking justice a year after disaster struck the region

"That frequency is crucial for local weather forecasting in Europe and the Mediterranean, but also for civil protection: firefighters detecting forest fires, droughts, or Mediterranean tornadoes, which are becoming more frequent and more violent.

Bank estimates that the new satellite will need around half a year of commissioning before it can be integrated and calibrated with its two siblings. From then on, probably around April 2027, the three will operate as a single system.

The technical specifications: 500 million pixels every ten minutes

Graeme Mason, head of meteorological programmes at ESA, laid out the figures that make MTG-I2 one of the most advanced observation instruments ever placed in orbit. While the first satellite in the family scans the entire visible Earth disc every ten minutes at a resolution of 500 metres – around 500 million pixels per full sweep, distributed across 16 channels – MTG-I2 will focus solely on the upper quadrant centred on Europe, repeating the scan every 150 seconds.

Its second instrument, the lightning detector, operates in a very narrow band of the spectrum, the oxygen emission line at 777 nanometres, taking 1,000 samples per second. To resolve features 500 metres across from an orbit 36,000 kilometres above the Earth, the satellite needs extreme stability across its three axes.

Technical data for MTG-I2, the third-generation Meteosat that will map Europe to monitor natural disasters. ESA/ArianeSpace

This programme is an example of the strength of the European aerospace industry: with more than 17 European countries and 70 companies involved; over 200 subcontracts; and more than 2,200 people working on the project.

"This image generator is the best geostationary 'imager' in the world. The lightning detector is the best 'lightning imager' in the world, a technology that is ahead even of that of the United States. In ten years, ESA expects to send the next family of satellites to continue leading the way in monitoring and analysing the climate and its impacts.

Europe is a world leader in Earth observation, and in meteorological science in particular Graeme Mason, ESA

Between the Ariane 6 control room, the satellite encapsulation facility and the weather station that tracks every cloud over Kourou, the launch of MTG-I2 has in fact been the sum of dozens of technical decisions taken by teams that rarely share the spotlight with the lift-off itself.

With this satellite in orbit, Europe completes the first operational trio of its third-generation meteorological constellation, a system that is set to support climate monitoring of the continent at least until well into the 2040s.

World.title: Spain announces €165m emergency package for Ceuta as migrant returns continue
World.content:
Spain's government plans to allocate €165 million to Ceuta's recovery, an emergency package of measures that will be approved this Tuesday by the Council of Ministers, one month after the mass arrival of migrants in the autonomous city.

 

The sum will be added to the medium-term recovery plan worth €180 million, according to local media, in a move previously announced by First Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.

The new package aims to revive the local economy and strengthen public services after a crisis that has disrupted activity in the autonomous city and shaped the start of the new political year. Of the total, €80 million will be channelled into Ceuta's economy over the next four months, and another €70 million is earmarked for 2027.

In all, €150 million will go into direct economic support over the next year and a half. Of that, €35 million will be devoted to direct aid for small and medium-sized enterprises and the self-employed, while another €15 million will be used to boost trade and tourism, sectors that were particularly hard hit in August.

The Council of Ministers also plans to allocate 15 million to strengthen education, healthcare and the justice system in Ceuta — three of the areas that have been at the centre of public demands in recent weeks.

One month on from the crisis

The migration situation continues to shape the city's recovery. One month after the events of 30 and 31 July, around 5,000 of the roughly 72,000 people who entered irregularly remain in Ceuta, while efforts continue to open new reception facilities and speed up return procedures.

In that context, the Minister for Territorial Policy and Democratic Memory, Ángel Víctor Torres, who heads the single command created by the government of Pedro Sánchez to deal with the crisis, has pledged that all migrants who entered the country irregularly will be returned to Morocco.

"Our intention is that all of them are returned, everyone who entered between the 30th and 31st, in accordance with the law," Torres said in remarks broadcast by RTVE, referring to the "approximately" migrants who, he said, "remain on the streets" of Ceuta.

The government considers the emergency package separate from the 180 million euro plan, which is structural in nature and currently being negotiated with business organisations, trade unions and representatives of different sectors of the city.

World.title: NASA launches first telescope named after female scientist
World.content:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after NASA's first Chief of Astronomy, will observe black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

NASA has launched a powerful new telescope designed to explore distant planets, exploding stars and black holes while surveying the universe on an unprecedented scale.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after one of the first women to hold a senior leadership position at NASA, was launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday.

The telescope is expected to reach its destination, approximately 1.6 million kilometers (about one million miles) from Earth, in approximately one month's time.

The mission has a total budget of more than $4 billion (€3.45 billion). The first images are expected back on Earth in early 2027.

What will the Roman telescope do?

Astronomers will use "Roman" to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena, including black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.

"It's going to find thousands of supernovae, tens of thousands of planets, billions of galaxies and tens of billions of stars," said NASA science mission director Nicky Fox. "It's going to be able to do things that we've never been able to do before with its massive field of view."

Roman operates in a similar way to the Hubble Space Telescope, which was launched in 1990 and is now showing signs of age while operating with reduced capabilities.

Scientists expect Roman to generate more than 500 terabytes of data every year [FILE: November 2025] Image: Jolearra Tshiteya/NASA/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, Roman is designed to survey the sky far more quickly and will be capable of completing in just one month observations which would have taken Hubble a century.

Scientists expect Roman to generate more than 500 terabytes of data every year. By way of comparison, Hubble has collected approximately 400 terabytes of data in over three decades in space.

"Roman's vast reach will allow us to find the weird, the rare and the unusual," senior project scientist Julie McEnery said on Saturday. "We'll redefine what it means to find a needle in a haystack."

How the Webb telescope captures breathtaking images To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who was Nancy Grace Roman?

The James Webb Space Telescope, named after former NASA administrator James Webb, was launched in late 2021 to complement Hubble. Webb observes the universe at different wavelengths, complementing the observations that will be made by Hubble and Roman.

Launching nearly a year ahead of schedule and within budget, Roman is NASA's first space telescope to be named after a woman. Nancy Grace Roman served as NASA's first Chief of Astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and retired NASA scientist Ed Weiler said the honor was long overdue.

"This is very, very fitting," he said. "I think Nancy would be very proud."

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right
World.content:
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has embarked on a confrontational course toward the churches. Representatives of the Catholic and Protestant churches are responding with a mix of anxiety and resolve.

Flags flutter in the wind outside Magdeburg's Catholic cathedral. "Love thy neighbor, dialogue, human dignity, solidarity. VOTE CONSCIOUSLY!", they proclaim. Just a few minutes' walk away, a sign on the building of the Protestant Cathedral Congregation reads: "DIVERSITY IS DIVINE." Other Protestant churches across the region display banners reading "Heart Instead of Hate."

For many months now, warnings about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is particularly strong in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, have been part of everyday church life. During a sermon at a pilgrimage event in September 2025, Magdeburg Bishop Gerhard Feige remarked almost in passing that pilgrims of hope do not cast their votes on a whim, "into the blue." He was interrupted by prolonged applause — blue is the AfD's party color.

The AfD holds a commanding lead in the polls ahead of the state election on September 6. The prospect of a government led by the party alone appears increasingly plausible. At the same time, Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Churches speak out against AfD

In Saxony-Anhalt, 10% of the population is Protestant and 3% is Catholic; only a few thousand people belong to the Muslim or Jewish faiths.

More than 85% of the state's 2.1 million residents have no religious affiliation, compared with a national average of 47%. Nevertheless, the churches play an important role as defenders of democracy — and that, apparently, is precisely what troubles the AfD.

With its so-called government program, adopted at a state party conference in April, the party launched a broadside against both the Protestant and Catholic churches. The program calls for an end to all state payments to the two churches and for the abolition of church tax collection by public authorities, a service for which the churches themselves pay.

Bishop Gerhard Feige has said he could never have imagined that so many people could once again be so easily led astray by the far right Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

In cases of so-called church asylum, where refugees seek shelter on church premises for fear of renewed persecution in their countries of origin, the AfD is calling for churches to be held financially accountable on a "permanent" basis.

The Protestant Academy of Saxony-Anhalt should also no longer receive any state funding whatsoever. The reason, according to the AfD, is its "political agitation in line with the established parties: climate dogma, gender ideology, and the rainbow cult." The academy is said to advocate "unchecked mass immigration." Yet in scarcely any German federal state is the proportion of foreign nationals as low as it is in Saxony-Anhalt.

From estrangement to open confrontation

The sharpness of the criticism goes far beyond anything typically heard from other regional branches of the Alternative for Germany or from the party's national leadership. Long gone are the days when representatives of the then-emerging party complained about not being invited to church congresses or Catholic conventions.

In February 2024, the plenary assembly of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference unanimously adopted a declaration entitled "Ethnic Nationalism and Christianity are Incompatible." In it, the bishops identified an ethnonationalist mindset within the AfD and spoke of a "genuine right-wing extremism." The document was prompted by the state elections scheduled to take place later that year in the eastern German states of Thuringia, Saxony, and Brandenburg. Now, in September 2026, elections are due to follow in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

At present, the confrontation between the AfD and the churches is nowhere more intense than in Saxony-Anhalt.

Germany's churches get creative about new ways to worship To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Bishop Feige, the AfD's current direction is "without question" an expression of ethnonationalism. "Until now, Saxony-Anhalt's motto has been 'Thinking Modern'. The AfD wants to replace it with 'Thinking German'," he told DW. "The AfD's election posters speak a very clear language: 'Save your country', 'Take your country back', 'Deport from day one!' What else could that be but ethnonationalism?"

The 74-year-old said he "could never have imagined that so many people today could once again be so easily led astray, or that arsonists, pied pipers and respectable-looking agitators could emerge, and that so many would fall for them."

As an example, Feige cited the so-called flag assembly that the AfD wants to reintroduce in the state's schools: the raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem. "This existed during the Nazi era and was later adopted by the GDR," he said, referring to the former East Germany. "And now it is supposed to return? I find that inconceivable."

Bishop Friedrich Kramer said Christian messages should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party Image: Martin Schutt/dpa/picture alliance

Both major Christian churches emphasize they are speaking out not against a particular party, but in defense of a Christian view of humanity. Whether the issue is climate protection and the safeguarding of creation or the treatment of strangers, the churches' interventions are "primarily not political messages, but Christian ones, and should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party," Friedrich Kramer, bishop of the Protestant Church in central Germany, recently told the online magazine Die Eule.

Religious freedom, according to the AfD

Jews and Jewish life, incidentally, are never mentioned in the government program. By contrast, Islam appears repeatedly. According to the AfD, it will "restore religious freedom to appropriate limits." Islam is described as a "religion alien to our culture." Freedom of religion, the party argues, does not oblige Germans to "fulfill every demand of the Islamic lobby."

Representatives of the state's Jewish association, which includes the synagogue of the Jewish community of Halle targeted in a 2019 right-wing extremist attack, as well as representatives of the largest mosque congregation in the state, declined to comment when asked.

Notably, the AfD's platform speaks of a "Christian mission" that, in its view, the churches supported by church tax, which it labels the "church-tax churches," no longer fulfill. This evokes the support that US President Donald Trump receives from influential evangelical and conservative Christian groups in the United States. In Saxony-Anhalt, however, there is only a limited presence of comparable religious milieus.

Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why bishops are sounding the alarm

"A government involving the AfD would have devastating consequences," Kramer said. That is why, he added, cultural institutions and civil society organizations are joining forces to warn against the AfD.

His Catholic counterpart, Feige, likewise cautioned against "downplaying" the prospect of an AfD-led government. During the election campaign, he said, the party is presenting itself "with messianic ideas" and promoting slogans such as "Everything will be fine" or "Anything is possible."

Because the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, "comes across as highly polished and enthusiastic," some people ask what could possibly be "right-wing extremist or dangerous" about him. "But behind him stand forces that give cause for concern," said Feige. "If an AfD single-party government comes to power here, it will be a pilot project. Then Saxony-Anhalt will become a gateway to national politics."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides — but it could backfire
World.content:
The EU wants to lift a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air, allowing drones to be used for greater precision. But experts warn the plan could lead to even more pesticides being used in agriculture.

In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed.

The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package , which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030.

Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light.

Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides

"I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely.

How toxic is the industry behind pesticides? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain."

"At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection.

Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash

Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved.

When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism . Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it.

To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment.

The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release .

Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment

European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years.

Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans.

Bayer wins in US court, but at what cost to public health? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence.

The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important.

Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said.

Agriculture can work without pesticides

Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved.

But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012.

Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author.

Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically.

The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security.

What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change."

World.title: Germany news: Politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
World.content:
08/30/2026 August 30, 2026 German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

Germany's centrist parties reject any cooperation with the AfD [FILE: June 30, 2026] Image: Paul-Philipp Braun/IMAGO

High-ranking German politicians have advocated for proceedings to ban the most radical regional branches of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, called for bans to be initiated swiftly in a joint guest op-ed in the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

"We once again strongly urge that proceedings to ban the party be initiated as soon as possible, with a particular focus on the AfD's clearly ethno-nationalist state branches in Thuringia, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Brandenburg," Pistorius and Özdemir said.

Their comments come just days before the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where an AfD victory could result in a far-right party leading a German state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.

Pistorius and Özdemir argue that it is important to distinguish between different factions within the AfD.

The two politicians say that the party's more radical, ethnically based wing rejects the constitutional principle. In their view, this wing should be subject to legal scrutiny.

They refer to this faction of the AfD as "völkisch" — a German adjective derived from das Volk, meaning "the people." The völkisch movement was an ethno-nationalist movement and precursor to Nazism. Today, the AfD is often accused of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.

However, Green Party lawmaker Irene Mihalic warned against a selective ban.

"I see a risk that the idea might eventually take hold that there is an unconstitutional part of the AfD and a constitutional one," she told the Handelsblatt newspaper. "In my view, it is now clear that the entire AfD is at odds with our democratic constitution."

World.title: Guinea-Bissau votes to reshape presidency
World.content:
The West African nation's military government wants to amend the constitution to give more powers to the president. The junta, which seized power last year, says it will hold elections in December.

Guinea-Bissau voted on Sunday in a referendum on whether to give the president new powers as the country prepares to transition from military to democratic rule.

The tiny West African nation of around 2.2 million people has been under army rule since last November following a disputed election.

What will the referendum decide?

Guinea-Bissau's junta has unanimously approved a constitutional amendment to switch the country from what it frames as a parliamentary to a presidential system.

This means abandoning the old system where the prime minister came from the parliamentary majority.

The amendment would allow the president to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and dissolve parliament.

If passed, the new constitution will cut the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65.

The junta says the change seeks to stabilize institutions before new presidential and parliamentary elections, scheduled for December 6, which are meant to hand power back to civilians.

Opposition groups, however, have urged the public to boycott the vote, saying it will allow the junta leader to cement power and calling it a "source of political instability at all levels."

Guinea-Bissau is due to hold parliamentary and presidential elections in December Image: REUTERS

When are the results due?

Polls close at 1700 GMT on Sunday, with the first provisional results due from Tuesday.

One of the world's poorest countries, Guinea-Bissau has experienced five coups and a series of attempted coups since 1974.

A military government seized power in November following a disputed election in which former President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory.

After legislative elections in 2023, Embalo himself dissolved the opposition-dominated parliament in response to what he described as an attempted coup.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Ferry carrying over 260 people capsizes off Cyprus
World.content:
Several people have died after a passenger ⁠boat carrying more than 260 people capsized off ‌northern Cyprus, Turkish media has reported. ‌

A passenger ferry capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, shortly after leaving port, the local government said.

At least seven people have died, Turkish state media reported, citing Unal Ustel, prime minister of the self-proclaimed Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC).

Ustel said some 237 people had been rescued, while 23 people were missing.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974, with the northern part under the administration of the TRNC, which is recognized internationally only by Turkey.

Numerous vessels and helicopters were used in rescue operation Image: Jewel Samad/AFP

Passenger boat heading from northern Cyprus to Turkey

Turkish media reported that a ferry carrying more than 260 passengers was traveling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in southern Mersin province when it sank.

Erhan Arikli, the TRNC's transport minister, told Turkish and Cypriot media that there were 267 people on board — 259 passengers and eight crew members.

"All necessary preparations are being made for a swift response from rescue and health services," the TRNC's Health Ministry said in a statement.

Search-and-rescue operations ongoing

In a post on X, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said: "We are closely following the unfortunate incident that has occurred and providing all possible support to the search-and-rescue efforts."

Turkey's state-run TRT news channel reported that the ferry began taking on water 7.5 kilometers (4 nautical miles) from the coast.

Edited by: Natalie Muller, Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
World.content:
A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.

Voters in Iceland have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.

The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.

The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.

Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote, 82% of whom did so.

Nearly 53% of Iceland's voters reject EU membership To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iceland PM: 'Not a setback'

Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who backed the "yes" campaign, said she did not see her fellow citizens' vote as a defeat but as a fair democratic result.

"I don't see this as a setback. I see this as a victory for democracy," she said. "We had over 80% of the country participate in a matter like this."

She confirmed that her government was "not going forward with the accession talks this term" but that it would continue ⁠to strengthen ⁠its relationship ​with the ​European Economic ​Area.

"I don’t feel that there is bitterness," she said. "I know tempers run high for some people, but I have now spent time with a large group of people from all over the country and people are quite open to different outcomes."

Meanwhile, EU chief Antonio Costa told Frostadottir the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" of the island's voters not to resume EU membership talks, according to a spokesperson.

"Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," said the spokesperson for the European Council president.

Iceland votes no to EU. What happens now? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iceland opposition: 'This isn't the time'

The count through the night had the island nation on edge as the "Yes" campaign took an early lead, attributable largely to votes in the capital, Reykjavik, before results swung in favor of the opposition.

By dawn, only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in rural areas of the country where opposition was greater.

"This isn't the time to go," one "No" voter, Daniel Bjarkason, told the Associated Press.

"Maybe in 10, 15, 20 years or more, we can take another look. But, for now, we're too divided and that's not a good look. Because it should be 70-30 'Yes' if we're going to [join the EU]."

Neck-and-neck vote after long debate

Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming a member of the bloc.

The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.

Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a referendum next year but brought the vote forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fishing industry pulled weight

The decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.

The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.

The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

World.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
World.content:
Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between the two countries?

A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.

For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."

Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.

Kastellorizo caught up in Greece-Turkey dispute (09.2020) To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.

Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.

During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis (right, seen here with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Athens in July 2022), has worked to build closer ties with Saudi Arabia Image: dDimtiris Papamitsos/Greek Prime Minister's Office/AP/dpa/picture alliance

Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.

An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.
