World.title: DELF 2026: Hong Kong Advances AI Integration Across Arts and Entertainment
World.content:
HONG KONG – The Hong Kong SAR government is moving from AI strategy planning to active execution focusing on infrastructure expansion and application-driven development. This was announced by Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry, Professor Sun Dong, at the Digital Entertainment Leadership Forum (DELF 2026) on Aug. 28.

“The committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy is established to empower industrial transformation through AI, with an initial focus on health technologies and embodied AI, extending to transportation, cultural and creative industries, and more. The Hong Kong AI Research and Development Institute will also come into operation later this year to translate upstream research into real-world applications,” said Professor Dong in his opening remarks.

Key initiatives also include a risk-based ethical AI framework, AI adoption in 100 public procedures and a growth in computing power at Hong Kong’s IT hub Cyberport.

“AI is transforming the digital entertainment industry, turning imagination into unprecedented experience,” emphasized Professor Dong. “And technology only serves its purpose when everyone can participate in it. That is why we launched the $50 million AI for All Inclusive Program – Cyberport, the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks, and the Hong Kong Productivity Council will roll out awareness-raising programs and practical training targeting at different sectors of the community to promote AI awareness and enhance professional skills as well as competitiveness through AI.”

The creative industry has already observed the impact of these changes, according to Terry Lam, Dean of the School of Film and Television at The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts.

“In the old days, if you went to any university in Hong Kong, they would not talk about the creative industry. Now, even if you go to the most famous or high-ranking university in Hong Kong, in an engineering course or scientific course, they will still have a sub-topic called the creative industry,” he said.

Terry Lam also expressed strong interest in collaborating with arts institutions across Central Asia noting substantial opportunities for cross-cultural exchange.

This vision aligns with growing ties between Hong Kong and Eurasia. This June, Cyberport agreed on cooperation with Central Asian’s largest innovation clusters Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan during a visit of Hong Kong business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, led by Chief Executive John Lee. The partnership focuses on technology transfer, supporting tech companies in areas such as AI, fintech, smart city solutions and Web 3, and facilitating overseas expansion and global market access for innovation and technology companies from both regions.

Held under the theme “Dreamtic Circus,” the three-day forum featured four themed experience zones: digital entertainment, culture and arts, smart living and business, and robotics and drones. Major showcases were the immersive interactive art exhibition titled “Gudo: Another World,” Harbour dreams VR/XR simulator guided by AI panda An An flying over Hong Kong sights and an eVTOL, the city’s first passenger drone test flight.

The event also hosted AI interactive workshops, film screenings, drone performances and competitions.

World.title: China Consolidates Position as Kazakhstan’s Top Trading Partner
World.content:
ASTANA – China is strengthening its position as Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner, overtaking Russia in the country’s foreign trade structure.

In January-June, China accounted for 23.2% of Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover, compared with 18.4% for Russia. Bilateral trade with China reached $16.65 billion, while trade with Russia stood at $13.22 billion, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The shift matters not only for trade volumes but also for the structure of bilateral trade.

According to an analysis by Tengenomika published on Aug. 27, Kazakhstan imported around $9.14 billion worth of goods from China in the first half of this year, compared with approximately $9.74 billion from Russia. However, the composition differs considerably. China is increasingly supplying machinery, equipment, electrical goods and other investment products, while Russia remains a broader source of fuel, food and industrial inputs.

The export structure is also different. Kazakhstan exported around $7.51 billion to China, compared with nearly $3.49 billion to Russia. Exports to China are dominated by ores and concentrates, copper, oil and other raw materials, while exports to Russia are more diversified and include metals, chemicals, machinery and equipment.

China’s growing role is particularly significant as Kazakhstan enters a new investment cycle. The government forecasts that goods imports will rise to $88.4 billion by 2029, while exports are projected at $88.5 billion.

Tengenomika highlights that the shift represents more than a change in Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner.

“China is increasingly becoming a supplier of the machinery, equipment and components needed for new production and infrastructure, while Russia continues to play a major role in supplying the goods and inputs needed by Kazakhstan’s economy today,” Tengenomika said in its analysis.

This emerging division of roles highlights how Kazakhstan’s trade ties with the two countries are evolving, with China playing a growing role in investment-driven demand and Russia retaining a broad position across the domestic supply chain.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Global Ties, Economic Outlook, Abai’s Legacy and More
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Singapore-Kazakhstan relations, political and economic developments, energy expansion, cultural cooperation with Vietnam and more.

Singapore keen to build on goodwill, deepen ties with Kazakhstan: SM Lee

Singapore wants to build on the goodwill it enjoys in Kazakhstan and deepen ties in areas ranging from business to connectivity, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said as he wrapped up his first visit to the Central Asian country, reported The Straits Times on Aug. 28.

Lee said on Aug. 27 that Singapore’s relationship with Kazakhstan was “an account well worth cultivating”, with Singapore companies showing growing interest in the country and trade and investments increasing significantly in recent years

“We enjoy a lot of goodwill,” he told Singapore media in a doorstop interview at the St. Regis Astana Hotel, noting that Kazakhstan remembers warmly founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew’s first visit in September 1991, three months before the country became an independent republic.

The Goethe of the Steppe: How Kazakhstan’s national philosopher shapes the bridge to the global economy

News Mark released an article on Aug. 10 exploring how Abai Kunanbayev’s philosophy, literary legacy and emphasis on education, honest work and openness to other cultures can help international investors understand Kazakhstan’s modern business culture and economic ambitions.

“Anyone wanting to invest in Central Asia’s dynamic market today cannot ignore one name: Abai Kunanbayev. What Johann Wolfgang von Goethe is to Germans, Abai (1845-1904) is to Kazakhs. He is not only the undisputed national poet, but also the ethical foundation of a country rapidly transforming from a former nomadic state into a global economic player. For international decision-makers, his work offers the key to understanding the mentality, business culture, and economic ambitions of modern Kazakhstan,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan after Kurultai elections: Expanding opportunities for co-operation with the European Union

EU Reporter published an article on Aug. 25 about parliamentary elections on Aug. 23 that completed the formation of Kazakhstan’s new legislature – the Kurultai – the central element of the country’s renewed political system following constitutional reform. Seven political parties took part in the vote. Turnout stood at 74%.

“The first convocation of the Kurultai has cemented the completion of the institutional transition and marked the country’s entry into a new political cycle.

The Aug. 23 elections have concluded the phase of institutional renewal in Kazakhstan and opened the period of practical implementation of reforms. For the European Union, this means a more predictable foundation for cooperation with Kazakhstan in the key spheres of energy, raw materials, and transport infrastructure. Kazakhstan enters a new political cycle with an updated institutional system, reinforcing its position as a strategic partner of the EU in Eurasia,” reads the article.

Astana Finance Days 2026 to bring global investors and financial leaders to Kazakhstan

More than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries are expected to gather in Kazakhstan’s capital on Sept. 9-10 for the ninth Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 forum, hosted by the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC), reads an EU Reporter article on Aug. 24.

The forum will bring together investors, representatives of the financial and technology sectors, regulators, government and quasi-state institutions, and international businesses.

Since its launch in 2018, Astana Finance Days has developed into one of the region’s major financial forums, providing a platform for discussions on capital markets, investment and financial cooperation. The 2026 program will focus on capital markets and investment products, regulation and market confidence, institutional innovation, financing the real economy, and regional and cross-border capital cooperation.

After ending power shortages, Kazakhstan can become electricity exporter

An EU Reporter article published on Aug. 25 covered Kazakhstan’s planned expansion of electricity generation in 2026-2027, the growing role of gas and renewable energy, and the government’s goal of moving from an electricity deficit to a surplus while building a reserve for the national grid.

“The expected 1.3 billion kilowatt-hour surplus by the end of 2027 marks an important shift in the government’s projections. The objective is no longer limited to covering immediate electricity consumption but also includes creating a reserve that could strengthen the reliability of the national grid. However, installed generation capacity and actual electricity output are not identical. The amount of electricity ultimately available to the system will depend on factors including the operating performance of new plants, fuel supply, grid infrastructure and, in the case of wind and solar projects, weather conditions,” reads the article.

Vietnam, Kazakhstan boost experience sharing in cultural industry development

Vietnam Pictorial released an article on Aug. 27 about Vietnam and Kazakhstan strengthening cooperation in cultural industries, tourism, education and other sectors while using cultural exchange as a tool to deepen bilateral ties and diversify economic relations.

During the meeting with Aida Balayeva, deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information of Kazakhstan, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Pham Thi Thanh Tra called for stronger people-to-people exchanges, local cooperation and tourism, noting that nearly 200,000 Kazakh tourists visited Vietnam in 2025 following the visa exemption policy for ordinary passport holders, according to the article.

Kazakhstan’s expanded Korea: A cultural legacy

The Chosun Daily published an article on Aug. 26 about Kazakhstan’s large Koryoin community and how Korea’s historical diaspora, cultural influence and growing popularity among Kazakh youth connect the two countries across generations.

“The ties between Kazakhstan and Korea date back much further than these cultural interactions. In 1937, the Stalinist regime forcibly relocated approximately 170,000 Koryoin from the Primorsky Krai region to Central Asia, citing fears they could become Japanese spies. Many of those transported by cargo trains settled in Kazakhstan, where around 120,000 of their descendants still live today. Kazakhstan is the country with the second-largest Koryoin population in the world, following Uzbekistan,” reads the article.

World.title: Experts Say Kazakhstan’s New Kurultai Leadership Reflects Diversity, Faces Heavy Legislative Agenda
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s new unicameral legislature, the Kurultai, elected its leadership and heads of eight standing committees during the first session of its first convocation on Aug. 28. Experts say the newly elected leadership reflects political and gender diversity and will face a significant legislative workload from the outset.

Aibek Dadebai, chairman of the Adilet party and former head of the Presidential Administration, was elected Kurultai Chairman. He thanked President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev for nominating him and deputies for supporting his candidacy, describing the position as a “great honor and responsibility.”

Adilet deputy and former Senator Nurlan Beknazarov, who represented Shymkent in the Senate from 2018 to 2026 and most recently chaired its Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, and Ak Zhol party chairwoman and former Mazhilis Deputy Chair Daniya Yesspayeva were elected Deputy Chairs. Former Commissioner for Children’s Rights Dinara Zakiyeva, who served as a Mazhilis deputy from the Amanat party from 2021 to 2023, became the third Deputy Chair.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership reflects broad political and gender representation.

“In other words, the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership is diverse with respect to both party affiliation and gender,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Zhandos Aktayev, chairman of the Esti Bol Qory public foundation and Doctor of Law, said the new legislature would face a substantial workload from the outset.

“Although the Kurultai is a new institution, it will inherit legislation left unfinished by the previous Parliament, giving deputies an immediate and substantial workload,” Aktayev said.

Deputies also elected the chairs of the Kurultai’s eight standing committees. Serik Yegizbayev of the Auyl party was elected to head the Committee on Agrarian Affairs. Askhat Aimagambetov will chair the Committee on Social and Cultural Development, Unzila Shapak the Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, Olga Perepechina the Committee on Finance and Budget, Amirbek Ospanbekov the Committee on Regional and Infrastructure Development, Marat Kozhayev the Committee on International Relations, Defense and Security, Darkhan Akhmediyev the Committee on Digitalization, Innovation and Science, and Natalia Godunova the Committee on Economic Policy, Energy and Industry.

The standing committees will review draft legislation before the full chamber considers it, making them central to the Kurultai’s legislative work.

Seven of the eight committees are headed by deputies from Adilet, the majority party. The new legislature has eight standing committees, compared with seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate.

All 145 deputies took an oath to the people of Kazakhstan during the inaugural session, marking the formal start of the new legislature under the constitutional framework that took effect on July 1.

Speaking after his election, Dadebai said the scale of reforms requires “well-balanced decisions, professionalism and dedicated work,” adding that the Kurultai should contribute to the country’s modernization and constructive public dialogue.

“A lot of work lies ahead. I am confident that we will go through this responsible path together,” he said.

World.title: Saturday March in Tbilisi: growing emigration. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Abkhaz blogger who spoke of ‘shared future’: Who was late Daur Buava?
World.content:
Abkhaz blogger found dead in Georgia

Young Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava has been found dead in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi. According to neighbours, they raised the alarm after Buava had not been seen for several days. Emergency services called to his rented flat found his body inside.

The cause of his death has not yet been established, and an initial examination of the body found no signs of violence. Georgia’s Interior Ministry has opened an investigation under the article covering “incitement to suicide”.

Who was Daur Buava?

Daur Buava, 32, was an Abkhaz blogger who attracted public attention for his open and unconventional views on Georgian-Abkhaz relations. On social media, particularly TikTok, he regularly posted videos advocating peaceful coexistence, dialogue and the rebuilding of trust between Georgians and Abkhaz.

Buava was born in Abkhazia in 1994. The Georgian-Abkhaz war had ended a year before he was born, meaning his understanding of the conflict was largely shaped by what he had been told by those around him. In 2021, Buava travelled to Tbilisi in an attempt to examine that version of events for himself.

“Later, I realised that it was the truth as seen by only one side. I learned the other side’s truth here,” he told Georgian media outlet Netgazeti that same year.

Within months, Buava had become one of the most recognisable Abkhaz bloggers on TikTok. His videos focused primarily on relations between Georgians and Abkhaz, the war, peace and Abkhazia’s future. He had tens of thousands of followers, including young people in Abkhazia.

Buava’s public activities were not confined to social media. He gradually became one of the few Abkhaz voices openly advocating dialogue with Georgians. It was this position that made him a target of persecution in Abkhazia.

Meeting the “enemy”

Buava said that before travelling to Tbilisi, his views of Georgia had been based largely on the information he received in Abkhazia.

One of the reasons he decided to visit Georgia was a TikTok livestream in which Georgians and Abkhaz called each other enemies and exchanged insults. For Buava, this became another reason to see for himself the place he had been taught since childhood to regard as hostile.

He said that in both societies there was a small group of people fuelling hatred, while most people wanted to communicate with one another.

Daur Buava

Persecution in Abkhazia

Buava’s activities did not receive unequivocal support in Abkhazia from the outset. In late 2021, he said that many people criticised his presence and activities in Tbilisi, although he also received messages of support from Abkhazia. Over time, however, criticism was followed by threats.

According to Buava, his supporters also faced pressure. He said that people who posted positive comments during his livestreams were identified and, in some cases, people even went to their homes. Buava also said that several of his supporters had been beaten.

In June 2022, Abkhazia’s de facto security service opened a criminal case against Buava on charges of “high treason”.

The agency said that videos posted by Buava on TikTok contained appeals that undermined Abkhazia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, state security and defence capabilities”. It also accused him of promoting the idea of Abkhazia existing as an autonomous republic within Georgia.

The case against Buava was opened in absentia. He remained in Tbilisi and no longer planned to return to Abkhazia.

‘Amra’ and idea of shared future

In Tbilisi, Buava and his Georgian friend Mikheil Kvatashidze founded the Amra youth movement. The name means “Sun” in Abkhaz. The organisation aimed to create opportunities for young Georgians and Abkhaz to communicate with one another.

In December 2022, Buava obtained Georgian citizenship, which he said was granted under a simplified procedure. This became another source of criticism against him within Abkhaz society.

In 2023, Buava was invited to the European Parliament, where he spoke about relations between young Georgians and Abkhaz, the free exchange of information and overcoming the conflict.

“We must move forward and build a shared future,” he said.

At the European Parliament, Buava also addressed Russia’s role. In his view, Moscow had contributed to the escalation of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict and was continuing to obstruct dialogue between Georgians and Abkhaz.

That same year, Buava opposed the adoption of the so-called “apartments law” in Abkhazia, saying he did not want Russians to buy property and settle in Abkhazia in large numbers. He regarded the main threat to Abkhazia as not the restoration of relations with Georgians, but the loss of its own demographic and cultural identity.

World.title: Georgian president pardons nine activists, one may face deportation to Russia
World.content:
Georgian president pardons nine activists

On the occasion of the Orthodox feast of Mariamoba (the Dormition of the Mother of God), Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned 226 prisoners. They included nine people detained during various protests. Georgian civil society groups and several organisations consider them political prisoners.

According to pro-government media, those pardoned include Denis Kulanin, a Russian citizen who, according to his lawyer, faces possible deportation.

World.title: Moscow posters: Are radical nationalists acting independently of Kremlin in Azerbaijan row?
World.content:
Protest at Azerbaijani embassy in Russia

On 27 August, at a time when independent political protests have become rare in Russia, a group of radical nationalists staged a protest outside Azerbaijan‘s diplomatic mission in Moscow. Participants put up three posters, filmed the action and posted the video on the group’s Telegram channel, which has tens of thousands of subscribers.

Azərbaycanın Rusiya səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında naməlum şəxslər tərəfindən Azərbaycan əleyhinə təxribatın videosu pic.twitter.com/3CkEXuYacp — Unikal.az (@UnikalOrgPortal) August 27, 2026

Although the protest was small, it raises a question: can radical nationalists in Russia, where public expressions of opposition are tightly restricted, intervene in relations between Baku and Moscow without the Kremlin’s knowledge?

There is no clear answer so far. The issue is not whether the Kremlin learned about the protest after the event, but what boundaries the authorities set for the activities of such groups.

There is no evidence that the protest was organised at the request of the Russian authorities. However, the fact that the same group has now targeted Azerbaijan for a second time, coupled with the authorities’ differing treatment of public expressions of political views, raises questions about whether such groups may receive preferential treatment.

What accusations appeared on the three posters?

According to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, the posters were placed not outside the main embassy building but in front of its guest house. The protest was covered by the Telegram channel Direct Action Z, which describes itself as an information resource of Eduard Limonov’s Other Russia party.

The posters accused Azerbaijan’s State Security Service of torture and President Ilham Aliyev of covering it up. They also carried the slogans “Russian blood is on your hands” and “Hands off Russian citizens”.

In a statement, the organisers portrayed the detention of eight Russian nationals in Azerbaijan, criminal proceedings against Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev, Baku’s position on Ukraine and the deaths of Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh in 2023 as manifestations of a single “anti-Russian policy”. They also accused the Azerbaijani diaspora of running “shadow businesses”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry described the incident as an “unacceptable provocation” and said it could be a continuation of what it alleges is a campaign against Azerbaijan by a number of Russian media outlets. Baku called on Moscow to investigate the incident and ensure the security of its diplomatic mission.

Azərbaycan Respublikasının Rusiya Federasiyasındakı Səfirliyinin qonaq evi qarşısında təxribatla bağlı açıqlama



⬇️⬇️⬇️https://t.co/YPLnFLJ4Mx



Statement on the provocation in front of the Guest House of the Embassy of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Russian Federation… pic.twitter.com/D9TwDicyqr — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 27, 2026

Same group staged protest exactly one year ago

One detail that makes it difficult to dismiss the incident as a random street protest is the date. On 27 August 2025, three members of the same movement staged a protest outside the Azerbaijani consulate in St Petersburg. They were detained by police.

The accusations made at the time differed from those voiced now. The protesters opposed Baku’s alliance with Ankara, its support for Ukraine and Azerbaijan’s competition with Russia on the energy market. In the following months, individual pickets were also held outside the consulate under the slogan “Russophobia is a disease”.

The fact that the second protest took place exactly a year later gives the impression that it may be a continuation of the earlier campaign. However, the organisers did not say whether the date had been chosen deliberately.

Close to Kremlin or opposed to it?

The Other Russia of E. V. Limonov is an unregistered political organisation founded by former members of the National Bolshevik Party, which a Russian court designated as extremist and banned in 2007. Its ideology combines Russian nationalism, “Soviet nostalgia” and imperialist ideas.

Its members support Russia’s war against Ukraine, and some have fought on the Russian side. The movement’s Interbrigades unit has operated in Donbas since 2014. In this respect, the group’s foreign policy rhetoric does not contradict the Kremlin’s broader line.

However, this does not mean the organisation is directly controlled by the Kremlin. National Bolshevik activists have also protested against the Central Bank, Roskomnadzor and other state bodies. In October 2025, four members of the movement were detained during a protest outside the Central Bank. In February 2026, activists from the organisation placed a lock on the door of Roskomnadzor’s Moscow office before leaving the scene.

On 18 August, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that statements by Knyazev, Uralov and Chadayev did not reflect Moscow’s position towards Azerbaijan. In their latest statement on Azerbaijan, the National Bolsheviks, in turn, accused the Foreign Ministry of failing to defend the three men. The group claimed that the state was putting the interests of “foreign entities” above those of Russian citizens.

In other words, the protest was directed not only against Baku but also against Moscow’s own policy, which the organisers regard as “not tough enough”.

Question of preferential treatment

National Bolshevik activists themselves are also periodically detained and given administrative jail terms. It would therefore be an oversimplification to portray them as an untouchable group carrying out the Kremlin’s orders.

On the other hand, it is clear that political protests in Russia are not treated equally. According to the latest available data from OVD-Info, more than 20,000 detentions for expressing anti-war views were recorded between February 2022 and July 2025. At the same time, groups that support the war in Ukraine but call on the authorities to take a tougher line have been able to hold public events, raise donations and operate actively on social media.

The Counter Extremism Project, which researches extremist movements, describes the relationship between the Kremlin and the National Bolsheviks as an “uneasy alliance”: the group criticises the authorities and its members are periodically detained, but its activities in Ukraine and pro-war campaigning are generally treated with considerably greater tolerance.

This pattern does not prove that the protest outside Azerbaijan’s diplomatic mission was organised at the state’s behest. However, it once again raises the question of which protests the authorities immediately suppress and which they allow to proceed without intervention.

Defending rights or exerting ethnic pressure?

The situation of the Russian nationals detained in Azerbaijan continues to raise questions that remain unanswered. In footage released after their detention, some appeared to have visible signs of violence on their faces. There have also been reports that the psychological condition of convicted Russian national Dmitry Fedorov has deteriorated and that he has stopped recognising his relatives.

However, the National Bolsheviks’ statement goes beyond defending the rights of individual detainees. It combines human rights concerns with rhetoric about “Russian blood”, criticism of Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine and accusations directed at the Azerbaijani diaspora as a whole.

World.title: Why is Russian tourist boom in Abkhazia giving way to falling demand? Video from Pitsunda
World.content:
Russian tourists in Abkhazia

Pitsunda is perhaps the most popular tourist destination in Abkhazia. The town receives around 20–25% of all incoming tourist traffic, thanks to the high-rise Pitsunda Resort complex and its private accommodation sector.

The overwhelming majority of tourists visiting Abkhazia come from Russia, meaning the success or failure of the tourist season largely depends on the situation there.

Even before international sanctions were imposed on Russia following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, Abkhazia received around 1.2–1.5 million tourists per season, with Pitsunda already operating at the limits of its ageing accommodation capacity.

At the time, Abkhazia was marketed as a budget alternative to neighbouring Russia’s Sochi. Infrastructure problems — including water and electricity shortages and ageing utility networks — existed even then, but were viewed more tolerantly because of the low cost of holidays.

After the start of the war in Ukraine, Abkhazia saw an unprecedented influx of Russian tourists. A record 1.88 million people visited in 2025.

Demand increased as many countries introduced restrictions affecting Russian citizens.

But since the start of the 2026 season, demand for holidays in Abkhazia has fallen noticeably, by 15–20%.

Experts cite several main reasons:

Increased competition. Inflation has pushed prices in Abkhazia to levels comparable with holidays in Turkey, Egypt and cheaper European destinations.

Legal and logistical barriers. In particular, border-crossing rules for children under 14 are creating significant difficulties.

● Infrastructure problems, including electricity and water outages at the height of the tourist season.

● Price dumping by major Russian tour operators, which is driving small local businesses out of the market.

● The threat to Pitsunda’s relict pine grove from uncontrolled construction.

● A general mismatch between the quality of service provided and the prices being charged.

What Abkhazia’s tourism market looks like

The private sector and guest houses account for 65–70% of the market, including small hotels, flats in apartment blocks and private homes in the villages of Ldzaa and Alahadzy. Most tourists choose these types of accommodation.

Large hotels, boarding houses and Soviet-era resorts, including the high-rise buildings of the Pitsunda Resort complex, as well as sanatoriums and newer mid-sized hotels, account for 30–35% of the market. However, they attract the lion’s share of the most lucrative tourists — those who book organised tours and package holidays.

Positive developments over the past couple of years include the partial modernisation of old Soviet-era resort buildings, the opening of modern boutique hotels in Ldzaa and the digitalisation of services, with a shift towards online booking and cashless payments.

Private accommodation sector reluctant to pay taxes

The main economic problem is that an estimated 60–70% of private accommodation providers have operated in the shadow economy for years, without paying full taxes into the local budget.

In recent years, the authorities have sought to tighten oversight by introducing a patent-based tax system for the self-employed and mandatory classification of accommodation providers. However, these measures have been slow to take hold.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Opinion: Mdinaradze resignation ‘prelude to Kobakhidze’s downfall’
World.content:
Opinion on Mdinaradze’s resignation

According to political analyst Gia Khukhashvili, Georgian Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze’sdeparture from politics is not simply the end of one politician’s career, but part of a process whose ultimate target is Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Khukhashvili likened Kobakhidze’s current position to that of “a child left home alone”.

Earlier, Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze said he was stepping down from his post and leaving politics altogether. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to spend more time with his family.

Gia Khukhashvili: “This is a logical continuation of the processes already under way. Mdinaradze himself is of little interest. The main question here concerns Kobakhidze. Whose prime minister is he now?! The only subordinate he had was Mdinaradze. There is no one else in the government under his authority.

Kobakhidze is now like a child left home alone: he can do foolish things, but no one will let him do anything meaningful. Accordingly, Mdinaradze’s resignation is a prelude to Kobakhidze’s ultimate downfall, a kind of preview, and nothing more. Mdinaradze himself was of no real significance; the true target of his resignation is Kobakhidze.

Kobakhidze had already been lined up to be pushed out for quite some time. I use that term because this is characteristic of [ruling party founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili. Kobakhidze has now been left ‘home alone’, because the government is purely technocratic. No one in the government answers to him or has listened to him for a long time. It is a technocratic government with no political component left.

I am not predicting that this will happen tomorrow or the day after, because Bidzina Ivanishvili naturally needs to saddle Kobakhidze with the blame for the problems that have accumulated recently and send him on his way carrying that baggage. Ivanishvili has to gain something from his departure, after all. When he decides to do that is another matter. But there can be no doubt that Kobakhidze has been left ‘home alone’: one only has to look at the composition of the government to see that

As for Mamuka Mdinaradze, after leaving the State Security Service, he effectively held only nominal positions and was left in limbo. In reality, his entire career ‘odyssey’ was part of the process of isolating Kobakhidze. We have now reached a point where Kobakhidze has no real control over anything, and Mdinaradze was the only person left in the government he could talk to.

So Kobakhidze is a child left home alone who still has matches in his hands, but I doubt anyone will let him start a fire. Mdinaradze’s resignation means nothing in itself; it is merely a prelude to Kobakhidze being pushed out.”

World.title: Abkhaz experts discuss fuel crisis, Georgian debate on Georgian-Abkhaz conflict resolution. VIDEO
World.content:
The fuel crisis in Abkhazia

Editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda Inal Khashig and political analyst Astamur Tania discuss recent developments:

The fuel crisis in Abkhazia and unexpected petrol supplies from Tbilisi;

Georgian opposition politician Nika Gvaramia ’s statements that Abkhazia may want to rejoin Georgia once Georgia becomes part of the EU;

’s statements that Abkhazia may want to rejoin Georgia once Georgia becomes part of the EU; A campaign launched in Turkiye calling for measures to end Abkhazia’s isolation.

Main arguments:

Fuel crisis in Abkhazia and commercial contacts with Tbilisi: The experts see this as a positive step towards de-escalation and building a climate of trust. They call for pragmatism and openness to unconventional economic solutions amid broader instability.

The experts see this as a positive step towards de-escalation and building a climate of trust. They call for pragmatism and openness to unconventional economic solutions amid broader instability. Nika Gvaramia’s statements on ways to resolve the conflict and Georgian domestic politics: The experts say violence was committed by both sides during the war. In their view, Georgian society still has a taboo around discussing abuses committed by its own armed forces during the Abkhaz war, although acknowledging them is necessary to understand the causes of the tragedy.

The experts say violence was committed by both sides during the war. In their view, Georgian society still has a taboo around discussing abuses committed by its own armed forces during the Abkhaz war, although acknowledging them is necessary to understand the causes of the tragedy. Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation launched in Turkiye: The experts believe ending Abkhazia’s isolation is in the region’s long-term interests and does not contradict Georgia’s interests, despite Tbilisi’s continued efforts to create obstacles.

Full text of the discussion

Inal Khashig: Hello! On the air is “Chegemskaya Pravda.”

The past week was very event-filled. Strictly speaking, that is what we will be discussing. Many events occurred there, both in foreign and domestic policy. And today, our regular political expert, Astamur Tania, is visiting us. Astamur, good day!

Astamur Tania: Good day!

Inal Khashig: Yes, the problem with gasoline, with fuel, which has gripped Abkhazia and not only Abkhazia – Russia is reeling from a gasoline shortage as well. And today I refueled at 110 rubles per liter.

Astamur Tania: You can be congratulated.

Inal Khashig: Yes, two or three weeks ago this would have seemed, probably, like something unnatural.

Astamur Tania: Maybe you’ll save the gasoline and sell it in a week for 150.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but that’s how it turned out. I refueled and I’m happy. It turns out one doesn’t need much for happiness. And in this context, of course, there is a lot of all kinds of talk regarding this shortage. A certain portion of the shortage was compensated through deliveries from Georgia.

This is no humanitarian aid; it is pure business, but nevertheless, a heap of all kinds of talk. By the way, I took a look with my own eyes at who said what officially. The Abkhaz government acknowledged the shortage and said that it would not obstruct it. In Georgia, the authorities said that the Georgian government has nothing to do with it; it is pure business. Nevertheless, in Georgia itself…

Astamur Tania: They also said that they would not obstruct it.

Inal Khashig: They won’t obstruct it, yes.

A portion of our society is chronically opposed to any contacts with Georgia in this regard. On the other hand, as for me… Well, you know, not all contacts are the same. When your entire economy is at a standstill due to a lack of gasoline at the height of the resort season, and you have the opportunity to buy, to acquire this gasoline in Georgia, then it seems to me that here one needs to set what is more important—certain conventionalities, or the fact that a lack of gasoline primarily hits the security of the country. It seems to me that this is the most important thing.

On the other hand, in Georgia itself, there is also a scandal. That is, there are also people unhappy there with the fact that gasoline is being sold to Abkhazia. And there it is being presented under the sauce that this gasoline goes directly to Russian military bases. That is, such nonsense as well, but which many willingly believe. Nevertheless, such is the situation. And based on what is happening with oil refineries in Russia, the end of this crisis is not visible in the near term at all.

How do you generally view this entire situation with this fuel, with all these deliveries from Georgia, and so on?

Astamur Tania: Over many years, you and I have spoken with enviable regularity about the need to search for and expand contacts in areas representing mutual interest. In particular, we spoke about the development of border trade, about the legalization of trade relations. So it would be strange if I were now to say that I am against these deliveries.

If we speak about the political component of our relations, despite this, we have quite fruitful relations in the field of energy. And why hide it, there are very many Georgian agricultural products on our market. It can be said that an expansion of the product range has occurred.

Despite the fact that both Abkhaz and Georgian representatives of their respective authorities state that they are not obstructing it and that it is linked to humanitarian and other issues, even here it was openly acknowledged that this gasoline comes from Georgia. They even came up with the term “gasoline from alternative sources.” It makes it seem as though we border Russia to the west and alternative sources to the east. A political science term for local application could already be coined: “Abkhaz-Alternative negotiations took place…”

Joking aside, I think this is ultimately a positive step. When you and I discussed this, we were aiming precisely at the point that a de-escalation of our relations is necessary. There is a lot of propaganda and hate speech involved in all of this, yet steps like these help build a climate of trust—that much cannot be denied.

It is another matter entirely whether this will remain a one-off occurrence or project into something broader, leading to significant decisions in other areas. Time will tell.

Naturally, we see that the reaction on the Abkhaz side is also mixed. However, our main political figures refrained from using this situation to issue statements condemning the Abkhazian leadership. We know that voices within opposition circles have also repeatedly stressed the need for a negotiation process with Georgia. In that sense, a certain consensus exists. The situation in Georgia, of course, is quite different, as internal political tensions there are much sharper.

Inal Khashig: They’re jailing people there.

Astamur Tania: Yes. In general, if we look back—even if we trace things back to the origins of the armed conflict—I believe domestic political circumstances were among the main drivers that triggered it.

The illegitimate State Council regime in power at the time held onto authority almost purely through force. In suppressing the supporters of the ousted president, Gamsakhurdia, they conducted bloody raids into Western Georgia. Their position was extremely precarious, so they shifted the center of escalation to Abkhazia to address their internal political objectives.

They ultimately lost control over Abkhazia, but it must be acknowledged that Shevardnadze’s regime managed to retain power back then. That was the price.

Today, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict continues to be used primarily for domestic political ends.

We saw how former president Saakashvili, currently imprisoned, suddenly re-energized. It appears this entire wave was initiated by him. He provoked it, drawing on his substantial base of supporters, effectively giving the green light to inflame the crisis surrounding gasoline deliveries to Abkhazia.

I view this entire affair as a maneuver in an internal political struggle.

How much restraint and patience the current authorities will display remains to be seen. As for the opposition spectrum, it is naturally heterogeneous.

Even if we imagine a scenario where a power shift takes place in Georgia, it would be naive to expect liberals to take charge. Judging by the prevailing tone in the media space, there is a serious threat that populist-chauvinists could come to power—figures with whom it would be far more difficult for us, and indeed for Georgian society, to deal. That risk is by no means zero.

The real concern is that we risk once again becoming a tool for aggressive domestic political propaganda, and we must keep that in mind.

There is another aspect that directly concerns us: we must diversify all risks related to fuel supplies and secure multiple sources. If the Georgian side were to become the sole supplier of fuel, that position would quickly turn into a lever of economic coercion.

Our approach must remain highly flexible and rely on diverse sources—from Georgia, from Russia, and from other avenues we have yet to explore.

Inal Khashig: As before. There was Romania, Bulgaria.

Astamur Tania: Yes. All these possibilities need to be explored.

In general, we need to get used to the idea that, unfortunately, the stable period—stable in an economic sense, in terms of deliveries, financial inflows, and so on—is, in my opinion, behind us. Our authorities and political circles must be prepared for extraordinary steps and new, unexpected challenges.

We simply need to understand that we are living in such a time, and it is not getting any better.

In this sense, it seems to me that these emerging contacts with the Georgian side still need to be brought into the realm of political detente as well. I believe there is someone to talk to in Georgia.

The tragedy is simply that Georgian legislation on occupied territories prohibits Georgia itself from conducting negotiations with Abkhazia. As a result, our relations are reduced to exchanging mutual claims in the public sphere.

Even regarding this decision on gasoline—localized as it is—if such a situation had occurred during the existence of the Coordination Council prior to 2008, I don’t think it would have caused such upheavals. The two sides would have sat down, agreed, signed a protocol, and affixed the signatures of international representatives, as the UN and others did. It would have been a bilateral agreement, and no questions would have arisen from either side.

Therefore, I say once again: we need to think about how to revive a full-fledged negotiation format where two sides exist. Otherwise, we will encounter these issues continuously and will have to solve them manually.

Inal Khashig: The topic of Georgia has been quite prominent in recent days. I don’t know whether it is connected to another anniversary of the start of the war, the events of August 8, or something else, but nevertheless, while this discussion around the conflict isn’t the primary headline in Georgia, it remains on everyone’s lips.

Former State Minister of Georgia Gia Baramidze gave an interview to a Georgian YouTube channel. In it, he stated that during the war he participated on the Georgian side of the commission for the exchange of prisoners, refugees, and the search for missing persons—working alongside Paata Zakareishvili. Beslan Kobakhia represented our side. To clarify his role back then: he stated that during the war, the Georgians could not execute prisoner exchanges with the Abkhazians because they had no leverage or prisoner pool left, as they were actually executing Abkhazian captives.

Naturally, a scandal erupted in Georgia, leading to a very telling reaction from the Georgian authorities: they opened a criminal case against Baramidze under the charge of high treason—not under slander, mind you, but high treason.

Astamur Tania: Because he was an official who possessed relevant information. And he presented this information, which was classified, in an open format. All of this is being hidden.

Inal Khashig: But on the other hand, this means that they do acknowledge it after all. I see another opportunity here. The war and what happened during it—how it started, how it developed, how it ended, and so on—constantly becomes a tool tailored to the political climate within Georgian society, serving both domestic political agendas and external audiences.

If you remember, it originally started as a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict. Now, however, they deny that it is a Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, choosing instead to view it strictly as a conflict with Russia, with the Abkhaz framed as mere bystanders.

This admission might actually serve as a starting point for them to confront the root causes of the war internally and finally acknowledge what they ultimately did.

If we look at the facts, I can name a dozen Abkhaz right now who were taken prisoner and executed. For example, in August, at the very beginning of the war, Oleg Ashba was captured and shot. The same happened to the Akirtava brothers, Sasha Mirzoyan, Amichba, and many others who were taken prisoner and ostentatiously executed right at the funerals of Georgian soldiers. These facts are well-attested. On our side, thank God, all of this is fully documented: there is the White Book, and the Prosecutor General’s Office formally recorded these cases at the time.

If people in Georgian society truly want to understand what happened and how, it costs nothing to present these documents. The names, surnames, dates of capture, and execution details are all fully recorded. I think this could serve as a genuine starting point in searching for a resolution to the conflict. Obviously, the overall issue is vast, but concrete steps are necessary. If they want to understand why the war started and how it unfolded, this is where they ought to begin—especially now that there is a public admission from a former high-ranking Georgian official who directly handled missing persons and prisoner exchanges. Let them investigate it; I believe it is vital.

There is another interview currently sparking active debate in Georgian society—an interview with Nika Gvaramia, the former Prosecutor General and an opposition leader who recently served time and is now free. By the way, he is originally from Sukhumi. He pointed out that Georgian society spends far too much time clinging to memories, dwelling on what Abkhazia used to be, grieving its loss, and so on. He argues that they need to abandon this mindset and focus instead on the future—discussing what lies ahead rather than constantly digging through the past.

I think this is a very important message. How he visualizes it in practice and how it will unfold remains another question. Nonetheless, he asserts that the Abkhaz must be shown progress toward the European Union, demonstrating that they would feel secure and comfortable within it.

I believe any real initial steps must begin with trust, right? If trust is the goal, then we inevitably return to that ill-fated Law on Occupied Territories that restricts us in every way. That law would likely need to be repealed if you want to achieve results on the other side…

Astamur Tania: Well, at the same time, he sharply criticized the idea of fuel deliveries to the territory of Abkhazia.

Inal Khashig: There is no cohesive approach.

Astamur Tania: In my view, all of this belongs mostly to domestic political discourse. Abkhazia is simply being used there to heighten emotional intensity. That applies to Gvaramia’s statement, and I would emphasize once more that no one should draw far-reaching conclusions based on a single remark. We need to watch how public sentiment evolves.

As for Baramidze’s statements, there is nothing new for us here. Parties in any armed conflict live within a standard narrative—at least one generated for public consumption and propaganda—where only noble knights like Ivanhoe or Wilfred of Ivanhoe fought on your side, while the other side was made up of savages. In reality, to chart a path toward understanding this problem—despite all the complexities of our pre-war political relations with the Georgians (which, by the way, were barely evident at the everyday level, but certainly present politically due to differing national projects)—the primary responsibility always rests with the side that made the moral choice to resort to violence.

If a side made that moral choice, one must expect that military abuses of the kind Baramidze described would stem primarily from them. They did not dispatch regular units into Abkhazia without a track record; these were people whose hands were already stained with blood. They had just brutally suppressed the Zviadists in Samegrelo, gaining extensive experience in illegal detentions, arrests, and crackdowns. They were well-practiced in these methods, and naturally, such behavior came seamlessly to them.

For the residents of Abkhazia, it was an absolute shock—not only for the Abkhaz, but for local Georgians as well. They could not believe their own countrymen were capable of such actions, given the notorious criminal background of the leaders driving the entire process and the figures actively carrying it out.

Of course, as a conflict expands and intensifies, violations inevitably occur on all sides. It would be naive to imagine that the Abkhaz are the kind of people to turn the other cheek in such a situation; it is a completely different reality, and that must be understood.

Crimes were committed on both sides, but the fundamental responsibility for initiating the process rests with the party that started it.

As for their methods… why stick our heads in the sand? Those methods are well known, not just from what happened in Abkhazia, but from what took place within Georgia proper.

It is clear that due to current domestic political issues in Georgia, they prefer to sweep this topic under the rug. I see virtually no public discussion about what transpired in Western Georgia on the eve of the Georgian-Abkhazian conflict. A taboo has been placed on that topic for obvious reasons—nobody wants to reopen those raw wounds when society already faces so many problems. Nevertheless, it must be taken into account.

Sooner or later, history always resurfaces in its darker manifestations if we attempt to study it in a sanitized form. We must know this history in its entirety. As for that… I suppose that is everything I wanted to say on the matter. Yes.

We are operating against a very heavy historical backdrop, yet there are occasional glimmers showing that people are attempting to look at the problem from a different angle. This is even happening within government circles.

Take, for example, the statements made by Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze. We certainly do not expect him to tell us how wonderful we are or that they intend to recognize Abkhazia’s independence, but he did mention the restoration of confidence-building measures. That is a very important step. Occasionally, articles appear offering a relatively objective look at the history of our relations since ancient times. Furthermore, some Georgian writers are even addressing the notorious pseudo-scientific theory of Ingorokva, which has poisoned the minds of multiple generations. Granted, such pieces are rare amid the vast sea of opposing literature, but they do appear.

In that sense, there are small glimmers of hope that genuine realization will come.

We also need to draw conclusions regarding our own policies—for instance, concerning the Gali district. That is something we will inevitably need to address.

However, given the current lack of trust, any step forward is easily misinterpreted as granting unfair advantages to the other side. For that reason, I do not believe in grand, immediate solutions, nor do I think it is productive to debate overarching political questions right now. Instead, targeted measures—focusing on transport, communication, humanitarian concerns, and the movement of people and goods across the border—are precisely what would help establish the foundational conditions needed for genuine dialogue.

Inal Khashig: Let’s move on to another topic: the de-isolation of Abkhazia. In Turkey, a campaign to de-isolate Abkhazia is gaining momentum. On the one hand, it includes the recognition of Abkhaz passports as valid travel documents; on the other, it seeks to restore direct communication—specifically maritime links—between Turkey and Abkhazia that existed immediately after the war. For a time, those connections operated, people could travel, and passenger boats ran. Although that was later cut off, a campaign to revive it is unfolding now.

At first, this was an initiative driven by private individuals within the Abkhazian and Adyghe civil sector. It then expanded to the point where eight political parties represented in the Turkish parliament formed a united front, declaring that Abkhazia must be de-isolated. Initially, our Confederation of Abkhaz Communities in Turkey (Abkhazfed) reacted with a certain degree of possessiveness, arguing that the movement had no right to take the lead and that Abkhazfed should have authored the idea. It was a completely unnecessary friction. However, after Abkhazian society here voiced strong support and our Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement, a course correction took place. Representatives from both the initiative group and Abkhazfed met and reached a consensus that a consolidated movement for de-isolation is essential.

How do you view this prospect overall? On the one hand, these eight political parties belong to the opposition, spanning a varied spectrum from left to right. How viable is this initiative, and to what extent might it simply be an element of internal Turkish political maneuvering to capture votes—specifically from the Abkhaz and Adyghe diaspora, who by various estimates number up to four million—ahead of upcoming parliamentary and early presidential elections?

In your view, is this driven purely by domestic politics, or is there a real opportunity here to translate this into a broader movement originating from the civil sector and picked up by the opposition? Could Ankara actually take concrete steps such as de-isolating Abkhazia, recognizing Abkhaz passports, and reopening maritime transport?

Astamur Tania: Naturally, I supported this initiative—as did you and many others. It would be foolish not to support it. Indeed, many on our side did.

At the same time, we must recognize that over the last few decades, there has been an obvious degradation in our expert and public outreach across all fronts, including the Turkish direction.

I carefully read what Elchin Adzinba wrote. Fortunately, we have experts of such high caliber who understand the inner workings of Turkish politics. We must take his insights into account in our work, as there are bound to be hidden undercurrents. But in politics, nothing is ever entirely positive or entirely negative; it is a constant struggle. He called for expanding the circle of people with whom we engage because decisions on such a significant issue—whether made behind the scenes or officially voiced—are ultimately crafted in government corridors. This strategy ensures the effort does not look like a mere pawn in Turkey’s internal political competition. He specifically warned about this, and we must keep it in mind.

Returning to the reaction of our own society: it often resembles a sparkler. Something reactive happens, everyone flares up instantly, and then all at once it goes out, gets forgotten, and passes. In six months, no one will even remember it. That is the tragedy.

We still have public organizations and specialized institutions that operate on state funding. Previously, we periodically held conferences, including on legal issues, where our situation was discussed from the perspective of international law—specifically how our rights are restricted regarding freedom of movement, education, and other matters.

In international politics, only that which exists in the information space actually exists. If we say nothing ourselves—well, thank God Turkish Abkhazians stepped up to raise this topic. But the initial momentum ought to stem from here, as they do not face direct isolation problems themselves; they hold passports that allow free movement worldwide. Yet no initiative originated from our side.

As a proposal, we could hold a scientific conference—one with real public resonance. Rather than merely recounting history, it should analyze how this tightening of constraints came about, which norms of international law it violates, and what consequences it brings. Even if we set aside the Georgian side’s internal political confrontation, the de-isolation of Abkhazia does not contradict their interests either.

Obstacles are always created from that side. For instance, after the armed conflict, we conducted negotiations and signed documents on the non-use of force, peacekeeping forces, and refugee return procedures. Then they claimed it did not suit them because the return was too slow. Now they make empty claims about 300,000 refugees, even though that many people never lived in Abkhazia to begin with. Meanwhile, we returned about 50,000 refugees to the Gal district—which apparently was still not enough for their narrative.

Later, we held negotiations on confederate relations and union structures—using various terminologies from 1997 to 1998, up until the May events. Domestic political circumstances intervened again. In the end, who won? Neither the refugees nor Georgian society. The exact same logic applies to this issue.

Honestly, I would consider it rational if the Georgian side did not obstruct Abkhazia’s de-isolation, as it could easily be included in a package of measures to build mutual trust.

As for Ankara, everyone understands that if the Georgian side stated it had no objections, the matter would be resolved much more easily. Otherwise, it is difficult to predict how long it will take or whether it will yield concrete results.

However, the fact that both our society and our diaspora are actively engaged around this vital issue is a result in itself. Regardless of whether our passports are ultimately recognized in Turkey, it demonstrates that society is thinking about its prospects and modeling its future. It shows a living society.

And this is not our only challenge; we have plenty of other problems. Sometimes one recalls how dynamic things were in the 1990s and early 2000s—the proactive responses, the strong stances taken by different individuals and organizations. Now, it feels like a stagnant swamp, with only the occasional outburst. You cannot achieve results in such a state. We must work on all fronts and in all directions. Some efforts will succeed, others won’t—but it can be said with certainty that if you do nothing, nothing will happen.

Life recently forced us to deal with pressing issues like fuel supplies. We will face many more such challenges, and we will have to manage them. If you claim to be an independent state, you have to act like one. Independence is not just a collection of legislative acts and political declarations; it requires active work to fill those structures with real substance. It is a creative process.

If a nation lacks that creative drive, it begins to fade and dull. Unfortunately, we are observing this trend. You and I spoke about the Abkhaz language earlier—it is good that there is activity, though whether it will yield results remains to be seen. But above all, society must show signs of life. Nobody will look out for us if we don’t stand up for ourselves. That is what I wanted to say.

Inal Khashig: In any case, during our turbulent times—and not only in turbulent times, but in any period, whether peaceful or turbulent—there must be clear plans for the future. Moreover, there should be multiple options across all directions, including a Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C, along with continuous modeling of potential scenarios.

I am basing this once again on the recent gasoline crisis, when under Aslan Bzhania, a sudden decision was made to hand the entire fuel market over to a single pair of hands. One ought to have considered the consequences beforehand and anticipated how all of this would play out—not just focusing on how beautiful and well-maintained our gas stations would look, but realizing that the primary problem arises when there is no gasoline at those stations in the first place. That situation highlights a lack of deep analysis and the absence of a pragmatic, truly calculated strategy.

Astamur Tania: Well, you understand that we aren’t experts in all fields of government, right?

Inal Khashig: No, of course not.

Astamur Tania: On gasoline, I’m definitely not an expert, nor on these monopolies. One simply needs to involve the expert community where we do not understand. Give public resonance to the problem. I see many things being done, but they lack competent public coverage.

Inal Khashig: Astamur, say you have money, right? No level-headed businessman will tell you that all your money needs to be placed in one specific bank. He spreads it across different banks.

What I’m getting at is that when we have no oil of our own—oil might be lying around somewhere, but there is neither refining, nor extraction, nothing—and we buy this gasoline… When you buy this gasoline, there must be different sources.

Astamur Tania: Now you and I are going in circles. I agree with you, which is why we spoke about diversification.

Inal Khashig: On that note, we will actually conclude our conversation: with the fact that Astamur agrees.

Astamur Tania: To each his own sore point. As for me, I don’t drive.

Inal Khashig: I drive. It somehow turned out that not only I, but probably the majority of Abkhazian drivers go to sleep in the evening with the thought of where to refuel tomorrow, where to find this gasoline. And in the morning they wake up with the same thought. And I think that for the state, this should be the very last problem in reality—when for its citizens, their main thought consists of how to get gasoline. In short, so that we don’t have such problems, I will wrap up. Astamur, thank you very much.

Astamur Tania: Thank you. All the best.

Inal Khashig: Let there be light. Goodbye.
