World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: SCO expands economic agenda as Central Asia gains global weight
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is becoming an increasingly important platform for Central Asian countries as they seek to expand regional connectivity, attract investment and strengthen cooperation in transport, energy, finance and digitalization. With the SCO summit approaching in Bishkek, the organization's growing economic agenda is gaining particular relevance for the region, whose economies are undergoing rapid expansion and deeper integration with major markets.

In recent years, SCO cooperation with its Central Asian members has increasingly focused on practical economic priorities alongside security issues. Discussions on transport corridors, energy cooperation, financial mechanisms and digital infrastructure have gained momentum, while individual countries have simultaneously expanded economic partnerships with China, Russia, Azerbaijan and other external partners.

This trend reflects a broader transformation in Central Asia's economic position. The region is strengthening its role in Eurasian trade and transit while attracting investment into energy, industry, infrastructure and technology. Against this backdrop, the SCO has the potential to provide an additional framework for coordinating cross-border projects and facilitating economic cooperation among its members.

Against this backdrop, the Bishkek summit is expected to further develop the SCO's economic agenda, with particular attention to transport connectivity, energy cooperation, investment and financial mechanisms.

Finance could become a new pillar of SCO cooperation

One of the most significant developments is the continuing work on an SCO Development Bank.

SCO Deputy Secretary-General Sohail Khan said in May that consultations on the institution had begun and that the proposed bank could become a key mechanism for financing joint projects and strengthening the organization's financial architecture.

The issue remained on the agenda at the July meeting of SCO foreign ministers in Cholpon-Ata, where member states noted progress in consultations on the bank, particularly in relation to joint investment, infrastructure and transport and logistics projects.

For Central Asian economies, the potential significance is substantial.

The region is entering a period of intensive infrastructure development, requiring large amounts of capital for railways, roads, energy generation, electricity transmission, industrial facilities and digital infrastructure. An SCO financial institution, if established and adequately capitalized, could provide an additional source of long-term financing for projects involving several member states.

The proposed institution could also complement existing financing channels rather than replace them. Central Asian governments already work with the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, European financial institutions, Chinese policy banks and national development institutions.

This makes the SCO Development Bank potentially more useful as an additional instrument for cross-border projects than as a substitute for existing international financial institutions.

The same logic applies to discussions on increasing the use of national currencies in mutual settlements. Greater use of local currencies could gradually reduce transaction costs and exposure to fluctuations in third-country currencies, although the scale of such a shift will depend on the development of financial markets and mechanisms for converting and settling those currencies.

Transport connectivity offers the most immediate opportunity

Transport is arguably the area where SCO cooperation could produce the most visible benefits for Central Asia.

At a meeting of SCO transport ministers in Bishkek in April, members discussed the development of transport corridors, digital solutions and measures to improve connectivity.

For Central Asian countries, the objective is broader than simply increasing transit volumes. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are seeking to reduce logistical costs, diversify export routes and strengthen connections with China, Russia, the Caspian Sea, South Asia and Europe.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is particularly relevant in this context. Once developed, the project could strengthen China's connection with Central Asia while providing Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan with an additional east-west transport route.

At the western end of this emerging network lies the Caspian Sea and the Middle Corridor.

During Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov's July meeting with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Japarov highlighted Azerbaijan's role as a key link in the Middle Corridor connecting Central Asia with European markets. This illustrates an important point: Central Asian connectivity is not developing along a single axis. The region is simultaneously strengthening links with China to the east and the Caspian, South Caucasus and Europe to the west.

"Your role in the development of ties between Central Asia and the South Caucasus is of particular importance. Azerbaijan's participation in the Consultative Meetings of the Heads of State of Central Asia opens up new opportunities for expanding cooperation in the trade, economic, transport, and energy spheres," Japarov said.

The SCO could contribute to the integration of existing transport initiatives by promoting greater coordination across the region. Harmonizing customs procedures, digital documentation, logistics operations, border-crossing processes and transportation standards could improve the efficiency of individual infrastructure projects and strengthen their contribution to regional connectivity.

Energy cooperation could link the region's complementary resources

Energy is another area where SCO cooperation could have a long-term impact.

At the June meeting of SCO energy ministers in Bishkek, member states discussed energy security, energy efficiency, infrastructure protection, the energy transition and renewable energy. They also continued discussions on the possible creation of an SCO Energy Consortium.

The idea is particularly relevant to Central Asia because the region's energy resources are complementary.

Among the SCO's Central Asian members, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have substantial oil and gas resources, while Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan possess significant hydropower potential. At the same time, solar and wind capacity is expanding across the region as electricity demand rises. Turkmenistan, although not an SCO member, is also an important part of the region's wider energy landscape, particularly through its extensive natural gas cooperation with China.

Recent China-Central Asia projects demonstrate the scale of investment already entering the sector.

Tajikistan has discussed with Chinese companies the implementation of the 160-megawatt Ayni and 100-MW Yavan hydropower projects, as well as a 200-MW solar power plant. Turkmenistan continues to deepen its energy partnership with China. In April, Turkmengas and China National Petroleum Corporation signed an agreement on the fourth phase of development of the Galkynysh gas field, a project valued at about $5.1 billion.

These projects are bilateral rather than SCO projects. However, they demonstrate the broader economic environment in which the organization is attempting to expand energy cooperation.

If an SCO Energy Consortium eventually moves beyond consultations and develops concrete projects, its potential value could lie in coordinating investment, infrastructure and energy flows across countries with different but complementary resources.

Digitalization is emerging as a new area of cooperation

The recent engagement between Uzbekistan and the SCO Business Council suggests that the organization's economic agenda is also moving beyond traditional infrastructure. At an August 13 meeting, the sides discussed potential investment in Uzbek IT startups as well as cooperation in digital infrastructure, data centers and research and development.

The discussions included electronic mapping, government information platforms, transportation and healthcare information systems, while participants also examined integrated projects combining computing capacity, energy supply and operational infrastructure. The development is significant because Central Asia's next phase of economic growth will increasingly depend on productivity and technological capabilities rather than infrastructure alone.

Kazakhstan is pursuing a similar strategy. During his July visit to Shanghai, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a Kazakhstan-China Digital Bridge initiative and emphasized the importance of developing domestic human capital, digital infrastructure and institutional capacity.

The trend suggests that the economic relationship between China and Central Asia is evolving from infrastructure and commodities toward technology, industrial localization and digital services. For the SCO, this creates an opportunity to expand its economic agenda into artificial intelligence, data infrastructure, research and development and technology investment.

China's growing role raises the value of multilateral coordination

China's expanding economic role in Central Asia is an important factor behind the region's growing interest in connectivity and investment mechanisms.

China was Uzbekistan's largest trading partner in January-May 2026, with bilateral trade reaching $7.7 billion. Trade with Kyrgyzstan reached $2.09 billion during the same period, accounting for 33.4% of Kyrgyzstan's total foreign trade.

Tajikistan's trade with China reached $1.4 billion in the first five months of the year, while China remains a major market for Turkmenistan's gas exports.

Kazakhstan is also deepening its economic relationship with Beijing. During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's July visit to Shanghai, the two sides signed more than 70 commercial agreements worth over $15 billion, while new projects in industrial production and renewable energy were subsequently announced.

These developments demonstrate that China's economic presence in Central Asia is already extensive. The role of the SCO, therefore, is unlikely to be about creating China's economic presence in the region. Instead, it could provide a broader multilateral framework through which Central Asian countries seek to maximize the benefits of their economic relationships with major powers. This is particularly important because Central Asian states continue to pursue multi-vector economic policies.

They maintain extensive relations with China and Russia while simultaneously developing partnerships with the European Union, Türkiye, the Gulf states, South Korea, India and countries in the South Caucasus. The SCO is consequently more likely to function as one component of this architecture than as an exclusive economic bloc.

Central Asia could benefit from a more practical SCO

The interests of the region's Central Asian members largely converge around several objectives: attracting investment, improving transport infrastructure, strengthening energy security, expanding trade and developing new sources of economic growth.

The SCO can potentially contribute to each of these areas.

For Kazakhstan, improved transport connectivity can strengthen its position as a major Eurasian transit hub.

For Uzbekistan, expanded investment and regional connectivity can support industrialization, exports and the development of its technology sector.

For Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, better transport and energy connectivity can help unlock their geographic and hydropower potential.

For Turkmenistan, deeper energy cooperation provides opportunities to strengthen its role as a major regional energy supplier.

At the same time, regional cooperation can create benefits that individual bilateral agreements cannot always provide.

A railway crossing several countries, for example, requires coordination between customs authorities, logistics companies, infrastructure operators and governments. Similarly, regional electricity projects require compatible infrastructure and coordinated energy policies. This is where multilateral mechanisms could provide practical value.

Bishkek will test whether the SCO can move from declarations to implementation

The success of the September summit will ultimately depend on the extent to which existing initiatives advance toward implementation and produce tangible economic and institutional outcomes.

Four areas will be particularly important.

First, members could provide greater clarity on the future of the SCO Development Bank and its institutional structure.

Second, the proposed SCO Energy Consortium could receive additional political support or move toward concrete areas of cooperation.

Third, transport discussions could produce practical measures aimed at reducing logistical and customs barriers.

Fourth, the growing emphasis on digitalization could become a more established part of the organization's economic agenda.

None of these developments would immediately transform the SCO into an integrated economic bloc. The organization includes countries with substantially different economic structures and geopolitical interests, making deep institutional integration difficult. The more realistic scenario is the gradual expansion of project-based cooperation. Countries do not need to share identical foreign-policy priorities to cooperate on a railway, an energy project, a financial mechanism or digital infrastructure. This flexibility could ultimately become one of the SCO's greatest advantages.

The outlook: a platform rather than an economic bloc

For Central Asia, the SCO's future economic relevance will depend on whether it can complement — rather than duplicate — the growing number of regional and international cooperation formats.

The region is already becoming part of an increasingly complex economic network connecting China, Russia, the Caspian Sea, South Asia, the Middle East and Europe. The China-Central Asia mechanism, the Middle Corridor, the Eurasian Economic Union, international financial institutions and bilateral partnerships all play different roles in this architecture.

The SCO can complement these mechanisms by providing an additional platform for coordinating cooperation across a broad group of countries. Its future role could increasingly focus on facilitating practical collaboration in areas such as transport, energy, finance and digitalization.

If the Development Bank becomes operational, energy cooperation acquires an institutional framework, and transport and digital initiatives produce measurable improvements, the SCO could become considerably more relevant to Central Asia's economic development. The Bishkek summit therefore represents less a turning point in the region's external relations than a test of the SCO's ability to become more practical.

For Central Asia, the real measure of success will be whether the organization can convert its growing economic agenda into capital, infrastructure, connectivity and technology. If it does, the SCO could emerge not as a replacement for the region's other partnerships, but as another important layer of Central Asia's increasingly interconnected and multi-vector economic architecture.

World.title: Weekly review of oil prices in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. The average prices of Azeri Light CIF, Azeri Light FOB Ceyhan, Dated Brent, and Urals crude oil decreased last week (August 24-28).

According to Trend's calculations based on data from the oil market source, the price of Azeri Light CIF crude, produced at the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli field in Azerbaijan, dropped by $2.28, or 2.4%, compared to the previous week (August 17-21), to $92.75 per barrel. Data shows that the maximum price for this grade of crude oil during the week (August 24-28) was $95.13 per barrel, and the minimum was $91.51.

The average price of Azeri Light crude oil on a FOB basis at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $89.39 per barrel, which is $2.13, or 2.3%, less than the previous week (August 17-21). During the week (August 24-28), the maximum price was $91.62 per barrel, and the minimum was $88.11.

The price of Urals crude oil fell by $1.78, or 2.6%, compared to the previous week (August 17-21), standing at $65.70 per barrel. During the week (August 24-28), the maximum price was $68.41, and the minimum was $64.32.

The Dated Brent crude oil price averaged $89.80, down by $3.15, or 3.4%, compared to the previous week (August 17-21). During the week (August 24-28), the maximum price was $92.60 per barrel, and the minimum was $88.53.

World.title: SCO supports Kyrgyzstan’s multi-vector foreign policy course – expert (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 30. Participation in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) supports Kyrgyzstan’s multi-vector foreign policy by bringing together key Eurasian states, including China, Russia, India and the Central Asian countries, Temirlan Razbaev, chief expert at the Analytics and Coordination Department of the National Institute for Strategic Initiatives under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic, told Trend.

"The SCO supports Kyrgyzstan’s multi-vector approach, as China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran, Belarus and the four Central Asian states - Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan - are represented in one format. This allows Bishkek to discuss security, trade and infrastructure issues simultaneously with key Eurasian centers of power. A concrete institutional result for Kyrgyzstan is the establishment in Bishkek of the SCO Center for Combating Transnational Organized Crime," he said.

According to him, the chronology regarding Azerbaijan is important: Baku has been an SCO dialogue partner since 2015 and participated in the SCO Plus meeting in Tianjin in 2025.

"On July 31, 2026, Kyrgyzstan and Azerbaijan signed a Treaty on Allied Relations and a package of documents covering road transport, cargo transportation and shipping, energy cooperation for 2026–2028, cybersecurity, the financial market and precious metals. It would be incorrect to say that these agreements emerged solely because of the SCO - they are the result of bilateral rapprochement. However, the SCO complements bilateral mechanisms with a common political platform and strengthens Kyrgyzstan’s positioning as a link between Central Asia and the South Caucasus," he added.

Responding to a question about the main expectations for the upcoming SCO summit, given that Kyrgyzstan is hosting the meeting this year and that considerable attention is focused on it, he said the main expectation is to translate political agreements into implementation mechanisms.

"The meeting of the Council of Heads of State is scheduled for September 1, 2026, while high-level events in the SCO Plus format will take place on August 31 and September 1. On July 24, foreign ministers approved the draft Bishkek Declaration marking the 25th anniversary of the SCO, thematic statements and other decisions as a basis for further work. Therefore, the final package of documents cannot yet be considered approved.

I would assess the outcome based on three criteria: modernization of the SCO’s legal framework and mechanisms; practical implementation of the Development Strategy through 2035 and the 2025 agreements on new security structures; and project-based decisions in transport, digital trade, energy and investment," he added.

Temirlan Razbaev noted that three interconnected areas are priorities for Kyrgyzstan.

"The first is security. In Tianjin in 2025, agreements were signed on the SCO Anti-Drug Center and the SCO Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats. The latter is expected to include a structure in Bishkek for combating transnational organized crime. This gives Kyrgyzstan not only a political but also an institutional role in the SCO’s overall security system.

The second area is trade and transport. From January through March 2026, China accounted for 31.1 percent of Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade turnover, while Russia accounted for 27.1 percent; together, they represented 58.2 percent. Therefore, even technical solutions related to customs procedures and logistics have a direct economic impact on the country. The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway project is valued at $4.7 billion. The Kyrgyz section is more than 304 kilometers long and includes 50 bridges and 29 tunnels with a combined length of about 120 kilometers, meaning that almost 40 percent of the section will consist of bridges and tunnels.

The third area is energy, climate and the digital economy. These sectors are included both among the official priorities of Kyrgyzstan’s SCO chairmanship and in the documents of the Tianjin SCO Summit," he added.

He noted that Azerbaijan’s interest emerges at the next stage: new transport flows could be linked through the transport networks of Central Asia and the Caspian Sea with the Middle Corridor. However, this will not happen automatically – it will require through tariffs, coordinated schedules, digital documents and faster border-crossing procedures.

The SCO was established in 2001 and initially comprised China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Over the past 25 years, its membership has expanded to 10 countries. The 26th SCO summit will be held in Bishkek on August 31-September 1, 2026, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship. The meeting will focus on the organization’s further development, strengthening economic and transport cooperation, and security cooperation. Following the summit, the leaders are expected to consider a number of documents related to the development of the SCO’s financial and economic mechanisms, including initiatives to expand settlements in national currencies and establish new cooperation institutions.

World.title: Hundreds lost in Nepal mourned in vigils across Australia
World.content:
As search efforts enter the fifth day in Nepal and rescue teams continue to comb through mud and debris for signs of life, hundreds gather across Australia for vigils honouring the flood-stricken region and the 42 Australians still unaccounted for.

Almost 9,500 kilometres away from the ongoing rescue operations in Nepal, crowds gathered at King George Square in Brisbane for a candlelight vigil organised by city's Nepali community.

A candlelight vigil, organised by NAQ, attracted hundreds in Brisbane. (ABC News: Lottie Twyford)

TreasurerJim Chalmers addressed the hundreds gathered to share a message of support for the Nepali community.

"We appreciate the Nepalese community every day, but on days like today we are there for you," he said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) committed a further 12 response personnel after eight arrived in Kathmandu this morning.

The Australian government has also pledged a further $3 million to the recovery efforts.

Mr Chalmers said some of the country's "finest" had gone to the "majestic" Himalayan site to provide assistance.

"Australia sends some of its finest people, we send millions of dollars in aid, but most of all I know that every single Australian at this very difficult time sends our love," he said.

The Nepalese Association of Queensland (NAQ) says it has been a difficult time, with many hundreds dead and thousands missing.

It has thanked the wider community for their prayers and support as they wait for news of their loved ones.

Crowds gathered at King George Square in Brisbane. (ABC News: Lottie Twyford)

NAQ president Tikaram Sarma found out today one his cousins was among the missing.

"We still have hope. We can find many people," he said.

"[But] it's a difficult rescue mission."

He urged anyone who could to donate to fundraising efforts.

Brisbane mourned those lost in the Nepal-Tibet floods with a candlelight vigil. (ABC News: Lottie Twyford)

In Darwin, about 100 people gathered on the steps of the Northern Territory parliament on Sunday evening, to light candles in memory of those killed or missing in the flooding disaster in Nepal and Tibet.

Crowds gathered at the Northern Territory parliament in Darwin to light candles for those missing and killed. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Trilochan Sapkota from the Northern Territory's Non-Resident Nepali Association said in a speech that the tragedy in Nepal had reached far beyond its borders, and that each candle represented a life lost, and the hope that those still missing would be found.

Each candle represented a life lost, and the hope that those still missing would be found. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Student Simran Kandel said many local events and festivals had been cancelled in the wake of the disaster, and encouraged donations to the Nepali Prime Minister's disaster relief fund.

"Even though there are thousands of people missing, we're hoping that they arrive safely back home, and that's why we collect here today to send our blessings to those people," she said.

World.title: At least 8 killed with more missing after boat capsizes off northern Cyprus
World.content:
At least eight people have died and 23 are missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off North Cyprus, leaving survivors clinging to its overturned hull.

Ünal Üstel, prime minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, told Turkish state broadcaster TRT that 237 people have so far been rescued.

A search is underway for another 23 people, he said, and it will continue until all victims are found.

The privately owned ferry, the Filo Jet, left the port of Kyrenia at 12:30pm local time (7:30pm AEST) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, authorities said.

It was heading for the port of Tasucu in the Mersin province of Turkey in the eastern Mediterranean.

Filo Jet, a vessel that capsized off the coast of North Cyprus on Sunday, in Tasucu, Turkey, captured in 2024. (Reuters: Altay Alan)

Mr Üstel said the ferry faced adverse weather conditions and began taking on water just 15 minutes after departure. A call for help was issued shortly after, he said.

Police detained eight people — including the ferry captain — as part of an investigation into "every aspect" of the sinking, he added.

However, Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman said weather conditions "were not bad" and urged against speculating about the cause of the accident.

Türkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the rescue "continued uninterrupted", offering his "condolences and best wishes for a speedy recovery to our nation and to the Turkish Cypriot people".

He said Türkiye had launched "extensive" search-and-rescue efforts "in-cooperation" with the northern Cyprus authorities.

23 people still missing

The disaster occurred just off the coast of Kyrenia, a popular holiday resort for both locals and tourists.

The ferry involved, a catamaran, was one of several shuttle sea services that link North Cyprus with Turkey daily.

The boat was carrying around 270 people, according to media reports. (Reuters: Stringer)

Mr Erhurman said the vessel went down in waters 500 metres deep, encumbering search efforts.

"We are deeply saddened by this," he told CNN Turk in a live broadcast.

Video footage showed people in red life jackets sitting or standing on top of the overturned vessel as authorities scrambled for coastguard and private vessels to assist in bringing them to shore.

"We have still not been able to reach 23 people. Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them," Mr Erhurman said.

"If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well."

Major rescue operation underway

The day prior, Cyprus was battered by fierce storms, with one person dying after his sailboat crashed onto rocks in rough seas in the island's south-east.

Asked about the cause of the capsize, Mr Erhurman noted the storm on Saturday, but said the weather was considered suitable for travel.

"There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... we are extremely saddened.

"Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort," he said, speaking from the crisis centre set up in the area.

"Our sole priority right now is human life. All institutions of our state, our security forces, our health teams and our search and rescue elements are on the ground in full coordination," he told reporters after chairing a crisis management committee.

The Turkish Cypriot Interior Ministry said the passenger ferry was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew, and it began taking on water about four nautical miles off Kyrenia while sailing from Kyrenia to Tasucu in Turkey.

Four Turkish Cypriot coast guard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, the ministry statement said.

ABC/AP/Reuters

World.title: Manhunt underway for rave shooter in Switzerland
World.content:
A manhunt is underway in Switzerland following a deadly shooting at a rave in the early hours of Sunday morning, local time.

Police in the northern Swiss canton of Aargau wrote on X that a 22-year-old woman died of injuries at the scene.

Four men and one woman, between 24 and 27 years old, were taken to the hospital with injuries ranging from minor to severe.

A 22-year-old woman was killed and a suspect is at large after shooting at a rave in Switzerland. (AP: Michael Buholzer)

All of the victims are residents of Switzerland, police said. They did not release their names in line with Swiss privacy rules.

Emergency services have cordoned off the area with a major police operation involving police in Freiburg, in neighbouring Germany.

"The manhunt is continuing nonstop at full speed," police spokesperson Bernhard Graser told reporters.

"In terms of its nature, this incident is certainly unique in recent years," Mr Graser said.

" We don't yet know the full extent of it, but based purely on the circumstances, it is something truly extraordinary. That's why there's such a large police presence. "

He said police had no information yet about possible motives.

Asked whether a terrorist attack was a possibility, Mr Graser said that "the fact that the rave was already winding down suggests that's not the case. A fight could also be a possibility."

Public shootings are rare in the alpine country despite relatively widespread gun ownership.

Residents were advised to stay away from the area cordoned of and heavily populated by emergency services.

Police are investigating possible motives amid an ongoing manhunt for a person involved in a deadly shooting at a rave. (AP: Michael Buholzer)

Swiss daily Blick reported that visitors of the rave initially mistook the shots for fireworks until somebody shouted "everyone down".

The newspaper wrote that the shooting took place right after the rave ended. Police later took all remaining visitors to a nearby gym, Blick reported.

Police called on possible witnesses who have video or photos of the incident to share them with police.

Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is 46km west of Zurich. It is about 30km south of the German border.

AP

World.title: 'There's only one Tony Mundine': Legendary boxer dies aged 75
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name of a person who has died.

Australian boxer Tony Mundine has died aged 75.

One of the country's most accomplished Indigenous fighters, Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally in four weight divisions.

He held the Australian titles at middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight.

His death was confirmed by his son, former world champion boxer Anthony Mundine.

"I don't know what to say, I'm broken," Anthony Mundine wrote on Instagram.

"Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul," he wrote.

"I'm on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.

"Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength, gonna miss you Tonza, there's only one Tony Mundine."

Tony Mundine was born in Baryulgil , New South Wales, where he took part in a number of tent boxing shows as a teenager.

His career peaked with a world title challenge in October 1974 against Argentina's Carlos Monzon.

Despite losing via a seventh-round knockout, Tony Mundine said he had fulfilled a childhood dream.

"I was just a little chocolate boy from Baryulgil, and here I was travelling the world, you know," he said.

Tributes from the boxing world flowed in for Mundine after the news of his death.

Former Australian professional boxer Danny Green paid tribute to Mundine, saying he was a "gentleman I had a tonne of respect for."

"Grew up watching him on TV ringsidem drew a great deal of inspiration from watching him, one of my late father's favourite fighters," Green wrote.

Australian professional boxer Billy Dib said Mundine was "widely recognised as one of Australia's greatest fighters".

"Uncle Tony was a beautiful human being and a genuinely good man who always showed me love and respect."

Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984.

He was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1986 for his services to sport and Aboriginal youth.

He is survived by his son Anthony, his grandson — professional boxer Rahim Mundine — and his cousin — businessman and Indigenous rights advocate Warren Mundine.

ABC

World.title: Iceland rejects EU-accession talks in close-fought referendum
World.content:
Iceland has voted to stay out of the European Union, referendum results show, as Icelanders reject a government push to reopen membership talks and side with those who said Iceland's fishing waters were too important to risk.

The Arctic island of 400,000 people has debated whether to join the EU for well over a decade and had initially been narrowly expected to back holding membership talks, but opinion polls this month showed views had changed.

Iceland referendum on EU Iceland is a nation divided as its people decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

In Saturday's referendum, 52.8 per cent of ballots cast were against the government's proposal to hold negotiations with Brussels, 47.2 per cent were in favour, and 82.5 per cent of eligible voters took part, public broadcaster RUV and other Icelandic media reported.

The vote count through the night had the nation on edge as the “Yes” vote took an early lead before eventually swinging in favour of the opposition.

By dawn, a margin of only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in areas of the country where opposition was greater.

Supporters of the Yes campaign celebrate after Reykjavik results put their side into a narrow lead early into the election-night. (AP Photo: Marco Di Marco)

The government framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented the referendum as a "now or never" moment. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said a "no" would end the debate for as long as her centre-left coalition was in power.

The government is set to hold a press conference at 1pm local time on Sunday.

Decades of membership debate

In Brussels, some officials had voiced hopes a vote to join from Iceland could ease scepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.

Europe weighs how to deal with Trump's Greenland threats America's rattled European allies are debating how to stand up to Donald Trump after he escalated his threats to take over Greenland and pledged to punish its supporters with tariffs.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said he wants to do a deal to acquire another Arctic island, Greenland.

More broadly, geopolitical turmoil, including war in the Middle East, has stoked inflation and increased the vulnerability of smaller economies.

Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country's small, exposed economy.

A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.

Interest rates and cost of living

Debates inside Iceland have focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living rather than on security.

Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates that have made mortgages expensive.

Supporters of a "yes" vote have said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief.

Iceland's central bank interest rate is 8 per cent, compared with 2.25 per cent at the European Central Bank.

"It would not solve Iceland's structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy," said chief economist Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson at Viska, one of Iceland's largest labour unions.

Opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, who led the "no" campaign, said the economic case is overstated.

Leaders of the No campaign react as early results from rural Iceland put the No side ahead. (AP Photo: Marco Di Marco)

"These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve," she said.

Voter Ragnhildur Skarphedinsdottir, 70, said Iceland was managing well on its own and that she was voting "no".

"By staying independent as we are, we look brightly to the future," she said before casting her ballot in Reykjavik.

Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns, among other factors.

Some Icelandic officials have said Iceland would therefore retain control of its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades.

Ms Hafsteinsdottir disputes that.

"I know that the European Union will come up with some promises of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good," she said.

Reuters/AP

World.title: One Nation could revive NSW trade posts scrapped in 'jobs for the boys' saga
World.content:
One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman has said he would consider bringing back overseas trade commissioners if elected next year.

Mr Newman, 54, the party's candidate for Cessnock, was the state's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024.

The Minns government scrapped the roles when it came to power following a "jobs for the boys" scandal involving former deputy premier John Barilaro's appointment to the New York position.

Mr Newman (left) was NSW's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024. (ABC News)

The veteran investment banker, a critic of the state's "bloated" bureaucracy, told the ABC it was a mistake to get rid of the trade posts.

"I commend the Minns government, to be honest, for living up to an election promise. I'll give them that," Mr Newman said.

"But I think what they did was capture what was a scandal and turn it into perhaps a poorer decision.

"If I'd still been the senior trade and investment commissioner during Minns's term to date, he would have been harangued by me constantly to have gone into Japan, Korea, India.

"You can't be the hermit kingdom."

'Too many public servants'

During his announcement as leader on Friday, Mr Newman pledged cuts to the state's public service, which he said was the largest in the southern hemisphere.

"There is so much money and waste that is inside the public service," he said on Friday.

"Having worked inside, I saw firsthand how your money is being misallocated and misspent."

'Like Florida and Texas': One Nation's plans for NSW Former NSW investment commissioner Mike Newman will lead the party to the 2027 state election.

But in an interview with the ABC on Saturday, Mr Newman said the trade commissioners were valuable, and he would seek to reinstate the roles.

"If One Nation has the opportunity to lead, I would definitely look at doing something similar to that, but as I said I want to bring experienced people from the private sector," Mr Newman said.

The trade commissioners were paid a salary of about $487,000 plus allowances, according to a parliamentary committee report in 2023.

The committee reported that the six posts cost taxpayers $12.7 million in 2021-22.

Asked whether bringing back the jobs would increase the size of the bureaucracy, Mr Newman said he wanted to hire people that want to serve their state.

"When I talk about the bloated bureaucracy, I'm saying there are too many public servants, especially amongst those in the senior executive class, who basically see this as a self-serving situation.

" Put it this way, I could have done five times as much business [as trade commissioner] on one-fifth the number of staff. "

Mr Newman says he has seen firsthand how "money is being misallocated and misspent" in the public sector. (ABC News: Bridget Murphy)

Tomorrow, Premier Chris Minns begins a four-day visit to India to "attract investment", his first overseas trip as the state's leader, and one Mr Newman said he should have made much earlier.

On Saturday, Mr Minns said he was "pretty impressed" by Mr Newman's candour.

"He seems like he's going to say what's at the top of his head. I think it's going to be very difficult for Pauline [Hanson] to muzzle him," Mr Minns said.

"I think he's going to say whatever he wants to say. I think that's a good part of politics, I welcome him to the debate."

World.title: Rider dies after 'critical incident' during motorcycle racing event
World.content:
A rider has died after a "critical incident" at a motorcycling racing event south-east of Adelaide.

SA Police said emergency services were called to a private racetrack at a motorsport event at Elwomple following reports of a crash just before 11AM on Sunday.

"Sadly one person has died and a report will be prepared for the coroner," a police spokesperson said.

In a statement, Motorcycling South Australia and The Bend said a "critical incident occurred" during a motorcycle racing event.

The Bend is a motorsport park about 100 kilometres south-east of Adelaide.

"The rider was treated by paramedics and died at the scene," the statement said.

The statement also thanked officials, paramedics and first responders.

"We extend our deepest condolences to the rider's family, friends and the wider motorsport community.

"We ask that the privacy of the rider's family, friends and all those affected be respected at this difficult time."

Motorcycling Australia said it was working with the "relevant authorities" following the incident.

World.title: 'I was a wreck': Popyrin bares his soul before US Open bid
World.content:
Alexei Popyrin hit rock bottom when he feared he wouldn't enjoy even his own wedding next month.

From the giddy high of taking down Novak Djokovic at the 2024 US Open, Popyrin needed a wildcard into this year's New York grand slam after slumping to as low as number 139 in the rankings last month.

He knew then he needed professional help.

The fallen Australian tennis star turned to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach and credits Emma Murray for helping him find contentment again. To a point.

"It's not easy," Popyrin said in a raw interview ahead of his first-round Open date with former semi-finalist turned 2026 qualifier Grigor Dimitrov.

"A lot of that is what was eating at me, thinking about things, searching for that feeling of being at the career-high rankings, of playing at that level, and it becomes a kind of an unhealthy obsession.

"It becomes a really negative and bad balance between you and tennis and it's what was really not helping me and it was the main culprit in what has been happening over the last few months.

Emma Murray is now working with Alexei Popyrin as he tries to rise in the rankings. (Getty Images: Kym Illman)

"I needed to change that and I needed to change just the whole way I look at tennis as a whole, and it's still a work in progress and it's not going to be a quick fix over one or two weeks."

Popyrin took his first mental-health break after Wimbledon last year before needing another reset following a straight-sets first-round loss at the All England Club six weeks ago to Jiri Lehecka.

"After Wimbledon, I was a wreck," said the former French Open junior champion.

"I used to — well, I still do — every time I lose, I think I don't deserve to have fun. After, I think I don't deserve to be happy.

Popyrin's birthday win Alexei Popyrin has won for the 12th time in 13 matches at the Canadian Masters, giving himself a 27th birthday present by reached the last 32 for the third year in a row.

"I was worried that I wouldn't enjoy my wedding because of my tennis, and when I had that thought for the first time I was like, 'OK, something is really, really wrong and I've really got to take some time and figure things out.'"

The 27-year-old one-time world number 19 has been working with Murray for only a short time, but already the high-performance emotional regulator is making progress.

"I'm trying to not associate my results with how I feel as a person," Popyrin said.

"I'm trying to look at it in a way that it's just a journey that I'm on. Where I am is where I am and what I have to do is just continue trusting the process that I'm on.

"I've stuck with the same team and I haven't changed anything. I believe in the guys. I believe in myself. I believe that everything is just mental for me.

"And if I'm able to make those changes up in my head, then I'm able to not only get to where I am, but I believe I can go further.

"I've got to kind of start from scratch, which is never easy. It's something I have done before, but it's even harder for me to do that because of where I have been and what I have done and what I have achieved.

"But it's important for me if I want to continue playing tennis that I get through this, and the way I get through this is continuing on the trajectory that I have been the last month."

AAP

World.title: Decades on from backpacking, I nervously returned to a ‘challenging’ destination
World.content:
InspirationAsia Decades on from backpacking, I nervously returned to a ‘challenging’ destination Patricia Sheahan August 31, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The noodle soup I sit down to eat in a Shanghai restaurant is one of the best I’ve ever had. Full of fresh herbs and tender spicy lamb, it also represents a personal triumph of sorts. You see, I am flying solo in this city of nearly 30 million and, frankly, a bit nervous. The last time I travelled alone to what I regard as “a challenging destination” was as a backpacker 40 years ago. I’m out of practice at being out of my comfort zone. Paying for stuff was the first mental hurdle. I buy a bottle of water using Alipay, China’s “super app” (that does a zillion other things than just pay for goods and services) in a 7-Eleven, and it all works easily. A nearby eatery displays huge, colourful photos of its fare. I point at that delicious lamb soup and, before you can say “open sesame”, I’ve Alipayed it with my phone. Anxiety melts away. Like Sydney’s Vivid light show every night of the year: the Shanghai skyline. Getty Images My time alone soon ends as I join an Intrepid, eight-day “Highlights of China” tour. I’m en route to Europe, breaking my journey with the brisk tour that acquaints me with one of the world’s cultural, historical and political behemoths. Our group of 15 comes from almost every Anglophone country. Aboard bullet trains and buses, we will cover some serious territory in this vast country, from Shanghai travelling north-west to Xi’an and finally heading further north to Beijing.



Gavin Lee, our guide, is a local who polished his English-language skills with a stint in Africa. He seems nonplussed as the group vents about troublesome e-sims and apps. 



Leaving one of China’s most modern cities, we board a G-Series train that takes us 1500 kilometres to the ancient city of Xi’an in China’s north-western province of Shaanxi. After passing through a stringent security check at Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station (in China even bags are screened for a subway trip), it’s a comfortable five-hour, 40-minute journey, at up to 350 km/h and with full meals available on board. Far from Shanghai’s glittering cosmopolitan feel, this city – once the starting point for the Silk Road – feels more dusty and interesting. Xi’an is fortified by an ancient wall on which people stroll or cycle and is home to the AD 652 Buddhist Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and a busy, touristy Muslim quarter. The Terracotta Army attracts a crowd, but remains a must-see. iStock A stallholder in Xian’s Muslim Quarter sells pomegranate juice. iStock Thousands flock here mainly because it is the gateway to visit the famed Terracotta Army, thousands of life-size figures buried with China’s first emperor, Qinshihuang to protect him in the afterlife. The trip to the Terracotta Army begins by bus from our hotel in the centre of Xi’an. It is, rightly, one of China’s tourism highlights, but a visit can be a struggle and utter purgatory if you hate crowds.



Sheer visitor numbers – capped at 65,000 daily – mean lots of standing on tippy toes, the odd unintentional elbow to the head and patience while waiting to see the awesome two-football-fields-sized Pit One, in which the most spectacular warrior figures, many in the process of being repaired, stand. Three other, slightly smaller, pits contain, among other figures, horses and kneeling crossbow-men. Despite the hectic atmosphere, it’s a must-see. The next night, before the four-hour train journey to Beijing, I break from the group – most of them visit a Tang Dynasty show, with dumpling dinner –to enjoy the city on my own, walking up the main street of Xi’an and buying dinner from friendly vendors. I end up with a rice noodle, meat and vegetable dish cooked before me in a giant wok, and a container of fresh fruit for less than $12. My comrades return from the show with less than glowing reports of the dumplings but rave about the show. I don’t feel I’ve missed out. No visit to China is complete without a visit to the Great Wall. iStock The ancient royal palaces building of the Forbidden City in Beijing. iStock



No trip to China would be complete without a journey to the Great Wall. After another bullet train journey from Xi’an to the outskirts of Beijing, we disembark for a three-hour bus trip to the Jinshanling section of the wall in Luanping County, Hebei Province. Our overnight lodging in a family-owned guesthouse is near an uphill path that leads to a beautiful serene section of the wall with green rolling hills stretching as far as the eye can see. There’s enough time to experience a sunset and a sunrise here before heading to the big smoke of Beijing. Tiananmen Square, the Forbidden City and lots of subway rides await. As we say farewell, we exchange emails to continue fledgling friendships and swap photos. But not the guy who travelled with his stash of hard currency. He hands everyone his address written out multiple times on tiny little scraps of paper. He might have just visited one of the most advanced technological countries in the world, but it hasn’t converted him. THE DETAILS VISIT

Australian passport holders do not need a visa for a stay of up to 30 days in China. FLY

Airlines that fly to Shanghai from Australia include China Eastern and Juneyao. See ceair.com; global.juneyaoair.com



Related Article Asia Australians are flocking to ‘the world’s most important country’ in record numbers TOUR

Intrepid’s eight-day China Highlights tour begins in Shanghai and concludes in Beijing and, depending on the date, costs from $2450. Groups number up to 16 and stay in three- and four-star hotels and a country guesthouse. Some breakfasts are included, as well as all bullet train, bus and subway costs. Also included are admission to the Terracotta Warrior display, the Great Wall, Tiananmen Square and the Forbidden City. See intrepidtravel.com.au MORE

cnto.org.au The writer travelled at her own expense.

World.title: ‘The pressure is astronomical’: Why this WA principal quit her job – and what it can teach us about our schools
World.content:
NationalWAEducation ‘The pressure is astronomical’: Why this WA principal quit her job – and what it can teach us about our schools Holly Thompson August 31, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jenny Cole was working as a principal at a Perth public school when she received a phone call that finally tipped her over the edge – she handed in her resignation and never went back. It was the middle of the day on a Wednesday and even though it is now 15 years ago, Cole remembers the moment clearly. Jenny Cole 15 years ago while she was still working as a principal. “I was at an Education Department event, where the minister was announcing a new behaviour management policy. During one of the speeches, my phone buzzed. There had been a critical incident at my school,” she said. “A nine-year-old boy had seriously injured one of my staff. The teacher was on her way to hospital.



Editor's pick Opinion

One Nation How Ben Roberts-Smith could help Hanson bring down a future Liberal leader George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general “I didn’t stay for the scones. I drove straight back and gathered the classroom team.” Cole, who was the leader at a specialist education support school, was in the middle of a case conference with her staff regarding the incident when she announced she was going to quit. At that time, she was also the head of the WA Education Support Principals and Administrators Association. “I thought ‘if I’m not getting any support, then who is?’,” Cole said.



“I just looked at my staff in that meeting and thought ‘I can’t make this better. I just cannot make it better, and if I make a decision, then somebody is going to be really adversely affected’.” She said the situation has become “significantly worse” with more teachers and principals burning out and leaving the profession than ever before. The build-up to Cole handing in her resignation had been years in the making. At one stage, 11 of the 28 teachers at the school were out on workers’ compensation. “It’s always devastating. No one comes to work to get hurt, and as a leader in a school you have compassion for the child, you have compassion for the staff who work for them, you have compassion for the parents, and so you’re holding a lot of people’s emotions,” she said.



“What has improved is there are now systems and processes for entering data, and there’s a lot more support for when things get to the very pointy end. Editor's pick Planning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback “But as a leader, you’re carrying everybody’s feelings, everybody’s emotions, and you’re just trying to follow the rules and policies and procedures at the same time.” Cole said the pressure on schools and teachers “has become astronomical” since she left. “I talk about how it’s like a frog in boiling water. Most teachers got into teaching and they loved it, and most people still do love it, but bit by bit, the pressure has risen to the point where teachers are drowning in boiling water,” she said.



“I work now as a leadership coach in the education space and I work with teachers and leaders who are all just teetering on the edge of burnout. “That’s the difference. There was one or two of us 15 years ago, and now teachers and leaders are working an average of 50 hours a week, which is completely unsustainable, and my DMs on Instagram are full every day of people who’ve said ‘I’ve just had enough’.” She said recent changes to NDIS funding would make the situation worse. “That pressure to be the support for parents and the community and therapists is now going to all fall back onto schools, just raising the pressure even more,” she said. “We need to rethink what schools look like.



“A lot of the responsibility for everything to do with kids is being pushed back onto schools.” In her work as a coach, Cole tries to help teachers and leaders create management strategies to keep them in the workforce. “When you’re overwhelmed and burnt out, you can’t see options – you just know that you’ve had enough, so while I have coached people to leave education, I have coached just as many to stay, but perhaps do it differently,” she said. “I want to say to every teacher drowning right now, your exhaustion is real, your overwhelm is justified. “The system is broken. Things need to change. Isn’t it time we listened to teachers?”



West Australian Education Minister Sabine Winton said the state’s teachers and school leaders worked “incredibly hard to support and nurture every student, including those with complex needs”. Editor's pick Analysis

One Nation The little coastal corner of Perth sending shivers through Australian politics “As a former teacher of 27 years, I know firsthand that teaching is a rewarding profession, but it can also be challenging,” she said. “That’s why the government is committed to supporting school leaders, teachers, and education support staff to reduce their workloads and ensure they have the resources they need to help children thrive.” Winton says the Workload Intensification Taskforce was progressing efforts to ease workload pressures for teachers and school leaders.



“This includes implementing complex behaviour support co-ordinators in 192 WA public schools, and small group tuition in 350 WA public schools, to provide targeted support for the students who need it most and reduce teachers’ workloads,” she said. “Last November, I also announced a $1.6 million funding injection to strengthen wellbeing supports for school leaders, providing targeted funding to give principals more choice to access wellbeing supports tailored to their needs. “This work is never done, and our government will continue to prioritise ways to support teachers to do what they do best – connecting with their students and helping them to reach their potential.”

World.title: Secret Harbour should be seen as a rallying cry for everyone who feels ignored
World.content:
NationalWAWA Parliament Opinion Secret Harbour should be seen as a rallying cry for everyone who feels ignored Kate Hulett Contributor August 31, 2026 — 3:00am

August 31, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The safe seat of Secret Harbour was WA Labor’s to lose in the by-election this weekend, and they deserved to lose it. By offering up a candidate who lives 60 kilometres outside the electorate and currently lobbies for Woodside, WA Labor showed an extraordinary level of arrogance, as well as disdain for the local community. Luke Herdegen is the first One Nation MP to be elected to WA’s lower house. Colin Murty As the dominant half of the “two major parties”, Labor appears to have become so utterly disconnected from ordinary working people that they haven’t noticed that life is increasingly tough and more people than ever feel like they’re being let down by the old parliamentary duopoly. We feel let down because we have been let down: another lane on the Kwinana Freeway won’t fix the problems of an electorate that’s been long ignored.



Time and time again, we see how the top end of town is prioritised by Labor over everyday folks. If you can pay, you can play – and by play I mean, directly influence legislation that will ensure the multinational corporation you represent, thrives. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Secret Harbour shellacking a warning for Labor, Coalition Just last week reporting showed corporate donations to Labor totalled over $1.6 million during the previous three months alone – and this didn’t include the $100,000 fundraising dinner the prime minister attended on Mosman Park’s “Millionaires Row” featuring the chairman of the region’s largest data centre provider, plus senior gas lobbyists, and mining representatives. The Secret Harbour byelection – triggered by the departure of Labor MP Paul Papalia – has been positioned as a litmus test of how suburban Australians are evaluating the performance of a state, and federal government, completely dominated by Labor. Having spent time in Secret Harbour every week during the campaign chatting to locals, it is a surprise to me that a by-election was required to perform this test. People are palpably pissed off, and they want change.



And now they have it with WA’s first lower house One Nation representative. What One Nation voters want, exactly, is unclear – no one I spoke with articulated any specific policies (including One Nation’s own MPs, as evidenced in Farrar last week). And while many One Nation voters are described as “anti-establishment”, Pauline Hanson has been a part of the political establishment for all of my adult life. We’ve also watched the organisations who once bankrolled the Liberal and National parties – including Australia’s wealthiest billionaire – now backing One Nation, which also gives “establishment” vibes. But here we are. The One Nation style of politics works when there is a broad feeling of discontent, and Labor are fuelling the feeling of discontent by ignoring the needs of ordinary working Australians. Over the past year, we’ve seen support across the nation for a tax on gas exports, a full ban on gambling advertising, more public housing, and a proper look under the hood of the AUKUS agreement – while at the same time, we watch the government shy away for these policies in favour of the wishes of corporate lobby groups.



With this in mind, Labor selecting a gas lobbyist as their Secret Harbour candidate makes perfect sense. It also makes a mockery of the idea that MPs are engaged to work for the people of their electorate. It’s no wonder voters were repelled. Related Article Updated

WA election ‘This is One Nation heartland now’: Labor shocked in bruising Secret Harbour byelection When you feel ignored, you look for attention elsewhere. If an elected representative isn’t going to work for you, it’s a good idea to vote for someone else who will. After all, we pay their wages. Time will tell if the new Secret Harbour representative will work day in and day out for his community – or if he will work for the top end of town funding One Nation. Lucky for us, we live in a democracy where we are compelled to give our MPs a performance appraisal at the ballot box every four years.



When Secret Harbour was called for One Nation, their candidate said, “There are no safe Labor seats in this country any more” – something I said myself after my community-backed independent campaign almost unseated a senior Labor minister in 2025. Secret Harbour should be seen as a rallying cry for everyone who feels ignored, and seeks change. I’m talking about all those people who seek change that is positive, constructive and collaborative, not focused on grievance but on a thriving, healthy future for all. The time is now to seek passionate, like-minded people in your community to support strong representatives, independent of corporate interests, that reflect you, your neighbours, and your hopes for our country. If we can do this, Labor’s loss in Secret Harbour could be a win for us all.

Caitlin Greiser has kicked a goal with 72 seconds remaining to lift Richmond to a thrilling five-point AFLW win over Essendon in a nail biting Dreamtime classic in Darwin.

In front of more than 4000 fans at TIO Stadium on Sunday night, Richmond kicked three goals in the third quarter to reduce a 14-point half-time deficit to just one point.

The final quarter was a tense affair, with no team able to kick a goal until Richmond struck at the death.

Beth Lynch sent the ball forward with a long kick before Katie Brennan picked up the crumbs from a dropped mark to fire a handball to Greiser at the top of the goal square.

World.title: Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPrivacy Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data James Massola August 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government will unveil a raft of changes to Australia’s privacy laws designed to keep pace with new technologies including smart glasses and artificial intelligence. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland will on Monday release the draft legislation, which will also include new online safeguards for identity documents, called IDLock, and a right to have personal information destroyed by social media and search companies. Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in a Ray-Ban eyewear store in Rome. Bloomberg Smart glasses look like normal glasses but can also photograph or film what the user sees, potentially without the consent or knowledge of other people. The Greens are already proposing new laws that would ban the import of the glasses for the next 12 months because of privacy concerns. The rise of AI, meanwhile, has seen tech companies shovel huge volumes of data into their systems to help “train” their AI models, with little regard for people’s privacy or copyright.



The law changes will include a right to erasure, so people can ask social media and search companies to have their personal information destroyed, rather than it being retained. The right to erasure will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles. Rowland said Australians deserved to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver’s licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online. “As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia’s approach must evolve with them. With the launch of IDLock, our government is taking the next step towards a stronger, more robust identity verification framework that expands the focus from responding after identity credentials have been compromised, to enabling Australians to protect themselves before identity crime occurs,” she said. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “Whether their driver licence details have been exposed in a data breach or they are concerned about scams and identity theft, IDLock will give Australians an accessible and simple way to have greater visibility, control and confidence in how their identity documents are used.”



After an initial trial, IDLock will be added to Australians’ myGov accounts in 2027 and will allow people to block, unblock and monitor the use of their ID documents. It will help people ensure they do not have their ID stolen or misused in scams and other identity crimes, while also allowing them to see whether their data has been subject to a data breach or hacking incident. IDLock builds on the Credential Protection Register, created in 2022 by the government, which is supposed to stop compromised identity documents from being used to falsely establish an individual’s identity. The register has blocked over 830,000 fraudulent identity verification attempts since it was established. After the release of the proposed new laws, the government will consult industry and look to introduce the laws into parliament by the end of 2026. World.title: ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
World.content:
Breaking SportVale ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death Sally Rawsthorne Updated August 30, 2026 — 9:56pm ,first published 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images and the name of a deceased Indigenous person. Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, age 75. The boxer, who is also the father of professional boxer and rugby league player Anthony Mundine, died at the weekend, sources close to the family have confirmed to this masthead. Three generations of the Mundine family, Anthony, Rahim and Tony in 2022. Jessica Hromas Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.



On Sunday night, Anthony Mundine said he was “broken” in an Instagram post. Anthony Mundine gets his hands taped by his father. Tony Mundine pictured at home in 1972. Antony Matheus Linsen/Fairfax Media “Dad I love you man my Allah bless your soul. I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time til we meet again... there’s only one Tony Mundine.” In 2024, Anthony Mundine described his father as his “biggest inspiration” in and out of the ring.



“You’ve shown me what it means to be a man of strength and integrity, and for that, I’m forever grateful. I wouldn’t be who I am without your sacrifices, your wisdom, and your unwavering support,” he wrote at the time. Tony Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984 and became a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 for services to sport, particularly boxing and Aboriginal youth. Anthony Mundine speaking at a press conference promoting his next fight with his father Tony Mundine next to him. A Bundjalung man from Baryulgil, just north of the NSW town of Grafton, Mundine moved to Sydney in the mid-1960s with the hope of becoming a first grade footballer. He played with the Redfern All Blacks and it was while doing some off-season training at a local boxing gym his talent was discovered.



Mundine had his first fight in Sydney in 1969 - competing in 96 bouts in a career that spanned till 1984 that also saw him travel the world and challenge unsuccessfully once for the World Middleweight belt in 1974. Upon his retirement from boxing, Mundine was heavily involved in a gym in the neighbourhood known as The Block in Redfern, on the corner of Eveleigh and Vine Streets. Mundine, the middleweight champion, did not raise a sweat as he disposed of Filipino Rapalo in two rounds in 1970. The gym had been set up inside an old shoe factory that had been acquired by the Aboriginal Housing Company and Mundine’s work had a positive impact on young Aboriginal people as the venue became a popular place for the community to spend time.
