World.title: The plastic pushing people
World.content:
Helen Kershaw of Killara is over the plastic hassle: “I was appalled to read ‘The Ooshies campaign has been a big winner for Woolworths’. Not a big winner for the environment, unfortunately – more plastic in landfills and more plastic in our oceans. Shame on you, Woolworths.”

“As a regular visitor to Parkes, we inevitably end up at one of the Chinese restaurants for dinner,” says Robert McElhone of Roseville. “This year, we knew it was the same restaurant as last year. When we sat down with our BYO bottle of wine, the waitress said the same thing as last year: ‘Would you like some glasses?’”

The licensing law-friendly culinary delights at the Chatswood Charles (C8) compares with that at the Decline Wine Bar (appropriately named The Decline Of Human Civilisation As We Know It) in Kingsford, usually full of UNSW students,” recalls Frans Boot of Gregory Hills. “At 8pm, staff brought out paper plates with tinned spag bol, sometimes even warmed up. You got a plate whether you wanted one or not. That must have added to the job of cleaning-up.”

“I’m chuffed to see the well-deserved accolades coming Boyd Exell’s (C8) way,” declares Keith Mayoh of Tathra. “He’s a graduate of Bega Public School where he learnt little about Four-In-Hand carriage driving but did very well in the more traditional subjects. His introduction to the sport came from the late, great Max Pearce, who was well known in the horsey world. As far as I know, the duke did not contribute to his success. Onya, Boydie!”

“My cousin, Mary Willsallen, was judging a Four-In-Hand driving competition in Britain where Prince Philip’s team suffered an equipment malfunction,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “The British judges also marked him down for, as a royal, swearing in public while encouraging the horses. Mary was insistent that he be judged on skill, not social status, and won the day.”

World.title: Decades on from backpacking, I nervously returned to a ‘challenging’ destination
World.content:
InspirationAsia Decades on from backpacking, I nervously returned to a ‘challenging’ destination Patricia Sheahan August 31, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The noodle soup I sit down to eat in a Shanghai restaurant is one of the best I’ve ever had. Full of fresh herbs and tender spicy lamb, it also represents a personal triumph of sorts. You see, I am flying solo in this city of nearly 30 million and, frankly, a bit nervous. The last time I travelled alone to what I regard as “a challenging destination” was as a backpacker 40 years ago. I’m out of practice at being out of my comfort zone. Paying for stuff was the first mental hurdle. I buy a bottle of water using Alipay, China’s “super app” (that does a zillion other things than just pay for goods and services) in a 7-Eleven, and it all works easily. A nearby eatery displays huge, colourful photos of its fare. I point at that delicious lamb soup and, before you can say “open sesame”, I’ve Alipayed it with my phone. Anxiety melts away. Like Sydney’s Vivid light show every night of the year: the Shanghai skyline. Getty Images My time alone soon ends as I join an Intrepid, eight-day “Highlights of China” tour. I’m en route to Europe, breaking my journey with the brisk tour that acquaints me with one of the world’s cultural, historical and political behemoths. Our group of 15 comes from almost every Anglophone country. Aboard bullet trains and buses, we will cover some serious territory in this vast country, from Shanghai travelling north-west to Xi’an and finally heading further north to Beijing.



Gavin Lee, our guide, is a local who polished his English-language skills with a stint in Africa. He seems nonplussed as the group vents about troublesome e-sims and apps. 



Leaving one of China’s most modern cities, we board a G-Series train that takes us 1500 kilometres to the ancient city of Xi’an in China’s north-western province of Shaanxi. After passing through a stringent security check at Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station (in China even bags are screened for a subway trip), it’s a comfortable five-hour, 40-minute journey, at up to 350 km/h and with full meals available on board. Far from Shanghai’s glittering cosmopolitan feel, this city – once the starting point for the Silk Road – feels more dusty and interesting. Xi’an is fortified by an ancient wall on which people stroll or cycle and is home to the AD 652 Buddhist Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and a busy, touristy Muslim quarter. The Terracotta Army attracts a crowd, but remains a must-see. iStock A stallholder in Xian’s Muslim Quarter sells pomegranate juice. iStock Thousands flock here mainly because it is the gateway to visit the famed Terracotta Army, thousands of life-size figures buried with China’s first emperor, Qinshihuang to protect him in the afterlife. The trip to the Terracotta Army begins by bus from our hotel in the centre of Xi’an. It is, rightly, one of China’s tourism highlights, but a visit can be a struggle and utter purgatory if you hate crowds.



Sheer visitor numbers – capped at 65,000 daily – mean lots of standing on tippy toes, the odd unintentional elbow to the head and patience while waiting to see the awesome two-football-fields-sized Pit One, in which the most spectacular warrior figures, many in the process of being repaired, stand. Three other, slightly smaller, pits contain, among other figures, horses and kneeling crossbow-men. Despite the hectic atmosphere, it’s a must-see. The next night, before the four-hour train journey to Beijing, I break from the group – most of them visit a Tang Dynasty show, with dumpling dinner –to enjoy the city on my own, walking up the main street of Xi’an and buying dinner from friendly vendors. I end up with a rice noodle, meat and vegetable dish cooked before me in a giant wok, and a container of fresh fruit for less than $12. My comrades return from the show with less than glowing reports of the dumplings but rave about the show. I don’t feel I’ve missed out. No visit to China is complete without a visit to the Great Wall. iStock The ancient royal palaces building of the Forbidden City in Beijing. iStock



No trip to China would be complete without a journey to the Great Wall. After another bullet train journey from Xi’an to the outskirts of Beijing, we disembark for a three-hour bus trip to the Jinshanling section of the wall in Luanping County, Hebei Province. Our overnight lodging in a family-owned guesthouse is near an uphill path that leads to a beautiful serene section of the wall with green rolling hills stretching as far as the eye can see. There’s enough time to experience a sunset and a sunrise here before heading to the big smoke of Beijing. Tiananmen Square, the Forbidden City and lots of subway rides await. As we say farewell, we exchange emails to continue fledgling friendships and swap photos. But not the guy who travelled with his stash of hard currency. He hands everyone his address written out multiple times on tiny little scraps of paper. He might have just visited one of the most advanced technological countries in the world, but it hasn’t converted him. THE DETAILS VISIT

Australian passport holders do not need a visa for a stay of up to 30 days in China. FLY

Airlines that fly to Shanghai from Australia include China Eastern and Juneyao. See ceair.com; global.juneyaoair.com



Related Article Asia Australians are flocking to ‘the world’s most important country’ in record numbers TOUR

Intrepid’s eight-day China Highlights tour begins in Shanghai and concludes in Beijing and, depending on the date, costs from $2450. Groups number up to 16 and stay in three- and four-star hotels and a country guesthouse. Some breakfasts are included, as well as all bullet train, bus and subway costs. Also included are admission to the Terracotta Warrior display, the Great Wall, Tiananmen Square and the Forbidden City. See intrepidtravel.com.au MORE

World.title: ‘The pressure is astronomical’: Why this WA principal quit her job – and what it can teach us about our schools
World.content:
NationalWAEducation ‘The pressure is astronomical’: Why this WA principal quit her job – and what it can teach us about our schools Holly Thompson August 31, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jenny Cole was working as a principal at a Perth public school when she received a phone call that finally tipped her over the edge – she handed in her resignation and never went back. It was the middle of the day on a Wednesday and even though it is now 15 years ago, Cole remembers the moment clearly. Jenny Cole 15 years ago while she was still working as a principal. “I was at an Education Department event, where the minister was announcing a new behaviour management policy. During one of the speeches, my phone buzzed. There had been a critical incident at my school,” she said. “A nine-year-old boy had seriously injured one of my staff. The teacher was on her way to hospital.



Editor's pick Opinion

One Nation How Ben Roberts-Smith could help Hanson bring down a future Liberal leader George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general “I didn’t stay for the scones. I drove straight back and gathered the classroom team.” Cole, who was the leader at a specialist education support school, was in the middle of a case conference with her staff regarding the incident when she announced she was going to quit. At that time, she was also the head of the WA Education Support Principals and Administrators Association. “I thought ‘if I’m not getting any support, then who is?’,” Cole said.



“I just looked at my staff in that meeting and thought ‘I can’t make this better. I just cannot make it better, and if I make a decision, then somebody is going to be really adversely affected’.” She said the situation has become “significantly worse” with more teachers and principals burning out and leaving the profession than ever before. The build-up to Cole handing in her resignation had been years in the making. At one stage, 11 of the 28 teachers at the school were out on workers’ compensation. “It’s always devastating. No one comes to work to get hurt, and as a leader in a school you have compassion for the child, you have compassion for the staff who work for them, you have compassion for the parents, and so you’re holding a lot of people’s emotions,” she said.



“What has improved is there are now systems and processes for entering data, and there’s a lot more support for when things get to the very pointy end. Editor's pick Planning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback “But as a leader, you’re carrying everybody’s feelings, everybody’s emotions, and you’re just trying to follow the rules and policies and procedures at the same time.” Cole said the pressure on schools and teachers “has become astronomical” since she left. “I talk about how it’s like a frog in boiling water. Most teachers got into teaching and they loved it, and most people still do love it, but bit by bit, the pressure has risen to the point where teachers are drowning in boiling water,” she said.



“I work now as a leadership coach in the education space and I work with teachers and leaders who are all just teetering on the edge of burnout. “That’s the difference. There was one or two of us 15 years ago, and now teachers and leaders are working an average of 50 hours a week, which is completely unsustainable, and my DMs on Instagram are full every day of people who’ve said ‘I’ve just had enough’.” She said recent changes to NDIS funding would make the situation worse. “That pressure to be the support for parents and the community and therapists is now going to all fall back onto schools, just raising the pressure even more,” she said. “We need to rethink what schools look like.



“A lot of the responsibility for everything to do with kids is being pushed back onto schools.” In her work as a coach, Cole tries to help teachers and leaders create management strategies to keep them in the workforce. “When you’re overwhelmed and burnt out, you can’t see options – you just know that you’ve had enough, so while I have coached people to leave education, I have coached just as many to stay, but perhaps do it differently,” she said. “I want to say to every teacher drowning right now, your exhaustion is real, your overwhelm is justified. “The system is broken. Things need to change. Isn’t it time we listened to teachers?”



West Australian Education Minister Sabine Winton said the state’s teachers and school leaders worked “incredibly hard to support and nurture every student, including those with complex needs”. Editor's pick Analysis

One Nation The little coastal corner of Perth sending shivers through Australian politics “As a former teacher of 27 years, I know firsthand that teaching is a rewarding profession, but it can also be challenging,” she said. “That’s why the government is committed to supporting school leaders, teachers, and education support staff to reduce their workloads and ensure they have the resources they need to help children thrive.” Winton says the Workload Intensification Taskforce was progressing efforts to ease workload pressures for teachers and school leaders.



“This includes implementing complex behaviour support co-ordinators in 192 WA public schools, and small group tuition in 350 WA public schools, to provide targeted support for the students who need it most and reduce teachers’ workloads,” she said. “Last November, I also announced a $1.6 million funding injection to strengthen wellbeing supports for school leaders, providing targeted funding to give principals more choice to access wellbeing supports tailored to their needs. “This work is never done, and our government will continue to prioritise ways to support teachers to do what they do best – connecting with their students and helping them to reach their potential.”

World.title: Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPrivacy Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data James Massola August 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government will unveil a raft of changes to Australia’s privacy laws designed to keep pace with new technologies including smart glasses and artificial intelligence. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland will on Monday release the draft legislation, which will also include new online safeguards for identity documents, called IDLock, and a right to have personal information destroyed by social media and search companies. Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in a Ray-Ban eyewear store in Rome. Bloomberg Smart glasses look like normal glasses but can also photograph or film what the user sees, potentially without the consent or knowledge of other people. The Greens are already proposing new laws that would ban the import of the glasses for the next 12 months because of privacy concerns. The rise of AI, meanwhile, has seen tech companies shovel huge volumes of data into their systems to help “train” their AI models, with little regard for people’s privacy or copyright.



The law changes will include a right to erasure, so people can ask social media and search companies to have their personal information destroyed, rather than it being retained. The right to erasure will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles. Rowland said Australians deserved to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver’s licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online. “As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia’s approach must evolve with them. With the launch of IDLock, our government is taking the next step towards a stronger, more robust identity verification framework that expands the focus from responding after identity credentials have been compromised, to enabling Australians to protect themselves before identity crime occurs,” she said. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “Whether their driver licence details have been exposed in a data breach or they are concerned about scams and identity theft, IDLock will give Australians an accessible and simple way to have greater visibility, control and confidence in how their identity documents are used.”



After an initial trial, IDLock will be added to Australians’ myGov accounts in 2027 and will allow people to block, unblock and monitor the use of their ID documents. It will help people ensure they do not have their ID stolen or misused in scams and other identity crimes, while also allowing them to see whether their data has been subject to a data breach or hacking incident. IDLock builds on the Credential Protection Register, created in 2022 by the government, which is supposed to stop compromised identity documents from being used to falsely establish an individual’s identity. The register has blocked over 830,000 fraudulent identity verification attempts since it was established. After the release of the proposed new laws, the government will consult industry and look to introduce the laws into parliament by the end of 2026. World.title: ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
World.content:
Breaking SportVale ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death Sally Rawsthorne Updated August 30, 2026 — 9:56pm ,first published 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images and the name of a deceased Indigenous person. Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, age 75. The boxer, who is also the father of professional boxer and rugby league player Anthony Mundine, died at the weekend, sources close to the family have confirmed to this masthead. Three generations of the Mundine family, Anthony, Rahim and Tony in 2022. Jessica Hromas Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.



On Sunday night, Anthony Mundine said he was “broken” in an Instagram post. Anthony Mundine gets his hands taped by his father. Tony Mundine pictured at home in 1972. Antony Matheus Linsen/Fairfax Media “Dad I love you man my Allah bless your soul. I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time til we meet again... there’s only one Tony Mundine.” In 2024, Anthony Mundine described his father as his “biggest inspiration” in and out of the ring.



“You’ve shown me what it means to be a man of strength and integrity, and for that, I’m forever grateful. I wouldn’t be who I am without your sacrifices, your wisdom, and your unwavering support,” he wrote at the time. Tony Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984 and became a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 for services to sport, particularly boxing and Aboriginal youth. Anthony Mundine speaking at a press conference promoting his next fight with his father Tony Mundine next to him. A Bundjalung man from Baryulgil, just north of the NSW town of Grafton, Mundine moved to Sydney in the mid-1960s with the hope of becoming a first grade footballer. He played with the Redfern All Blacks and it was while doing some off-season training at a local boxing gym his talent was discovered.



Mundine had his first fight in Sydney in 1969 - competing in 96 bouts in a career that spanned till 1984 that also saw him travel the world and challenge unsuccessfully once for the World Middleweight belt in 1974. Upon his retirement from boxing, Mundine was heavily involved in a gym in the neighbourhood known as The Block in Redfern, on the corner of Eveleigh and Vine Streets. Mundine, the middleweight champion, did not raise a sweat as he disposed of Filipino Rapalo in two rounds in 1970. The gym had been set up inside an old shoe factory that had been acquired by the Aboriginal Housing Company and Mundine’s work had a positive impact on young Aboriginal people as the venue became a popular place for the community to spend time. World.title: The plastic pushing people
World.content:
Helen Kershaw of Killara is over the plastic hassle: “I was appalled to read ‘The Ooshies campaign has been a big winner for Woolworths’. Not a big winner for the environment, unfortunately – more plastic in landfills and more plastic in our oceans. Shame on you, Woolworths.”

“As a regular visitor to Parkes, we inevitably end up at one of the Chinese restaurants for dinner,” says Robert McElhone of Roseville. “This year, we knew it was the same restaurant as last year. When we sat down with our BYO bottle of wine, the waitress said the same thing as last year: ‘Would you like some glasses?’”

The licensing law-friendly culinary delights at the Chatswood Charles (C8) compares with that at the Decline Wine Bar (appropriately named The Decline Of Human Civilisation As We Know It) in Kingsford, usually full of UNSW students,” recalls Frans Boot of Gregory Hills. “At 8pm, staff brought out paper plates with tinned spag bol, sometimes even warmed up. You got a plate whether you wanted one or not. That must have added to the job of cleaning-up.”

“I’m chuffed to see the well-deserved accolades coming Boyd Exell’s (C8) way,” declares Keith Mayoh of Tathra. “He’s a graduate of Bega Public School where he learnt little about Four-In-Hand carriage driving but did very well in the more traditional subjects. His introduction to the sport came from the late, great Max Pearce, who was well known in the horsey world. As far as I know, the duke did not contribute to his success. Onya, Boydie!”

“My cousin, Mary Willsallen, was judging a Four-In-Hand driving competition in Britain where Prince Philip’s team suffered an equipment malfunction,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “The British judges also marked him down for, as a royal, swearing in public while encouraging the horses. Mary was insistent that he be judged on skill, not social status, and won the day.”

World.title: Kiwi investors losing faith in property
World.content:
New Zealanders have lost faith in property investment as a way to generate returns, amid wider uncertainty about the political landscape.

ASB has released its latest investor confidence survey, which shows a record 40 percent of people are "very concerned" about how local political uncertainty will affect their investments.

Another 46 percent were "concerned".

More than half were also worried about global geopolitics and economics.

People were most confident in managed investments to generate the best return, followed by their own house and KiwiSaver.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

Only 10 percent thought the best returns would come from rental property, a level near a record low. Only bank savings accounts were lower.

ASB senior economist Chris Tennent-Brown said it made sense that confidence in property investment had "plummeted" over the quarter, given the property market had been flat for a while and political parties had raised several policies that could affect the market in different ways.

People whose main investment was a rental property were significantly more likely to be very concerned about the local political outlook, he said.

"The status quo won't mean a change but some of the parties' policies of removal of interest deductibility, a land tax in another instance, all are probably ... giving a sense of concern.

"At the end of 2025, we changed from thinking we're in an easing interest-rate environment to potentially a rapidly ... increasing environment. And we saw a flat property market.

"At the start of the year, there was optimism that the property market might start to pick up ... That's what we were forecasting. But now it's dipped back down."

Belief in the returns from the house people lived in had also drifted lower over time.

Overall investor confidence declined 5 percentage points to a net 1 percent.

Tennent-Brown said concern about offshore events related to "alarming" headlines.

"Locally it's probably about the potential for change because there is such a wide range of policies out there for both property and KiwiSaver that are all feeding into the mix."

Confidence in managed funds had improved while KiwiSaver declined, which he said probably highlighted concern about KiwiSaver settings as both funds would be performing similarly.

"We've seen sharemarkets perform incredibly well and that's actually flowed through to KiwiSaver returns."

But Tennent-Brown said the survey also showed that people were not making investment changes driven by their concerns, which he said was sensible.

"I think that the key thing is that the benefits of KiwiSaver are still there for employees to utilise and making sure that you're in the right fund, and you're focused on whatever your goal is … because elections do come along every three years. And they tend to throw up different ideas about what to do with things like KiwiSaver and the retirement age.

"But we can't invest on a three-year basis for someone that's got a long time to retire. So we have to look through this - as soon as we get our election out of the way, we'll be also thinking about what's happening in the midterms in the US. And then in another two years, there'll be a full presidential election in the US.

"So there's just always something coming along on the political front that you might like or dislike. But particularly for KiwiSaver, we've just got to focus on the long term. And that could be 30 or 40 years for some KiwiSavers."

World.title: All Blacks fan in South Africa told test match tickets didn't exist
World.content:
An All Blacks fan who missed out on A-grade seats at the weekend's test match says he and his group were told their tickets did not exist.

South Africa Rugby says it will pursue legal measures against travel agencies after claims SA Rugby was behind failures which saw fans miss out on tickets for the All Blacks' second test against the Springboks in Cape Town.

All Blacks fan Ant was one of 29 fans from Christchurch out on a tour in South Africa.

He had paid for premium seats, but was told the night before the game his tickets no longer existed.

"Everybody went into a bit of a meltdown, pretty upset," he said.

"The group's pretty disappointed about what happened."

He managed to get seats in the nosebleeds, but told RNZ he did not have a clear answer for what went wrong.

"We've been told a number of stories, and I've read some reports about what happened. There's a lot of fingers pointing in different directions at the moment," Ant said.

The 33-26 All Blacks loss did not help how they were feeling, he said.

Ant said the group was yet to be compensated, but there was talk about how they wanted to proceed.

"I guess that will work its way through, whether we go through our travel insurance or somebody comes to the party," Ant said.

All Blacks fan Ant managed to get seats in the nosebleeds for the weekend's big game, but still wants to know what happened to his premium seats. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

There was some worry ahead of the third test on Sunday, he said.

"There's a bit of concern amongst the group whether our tickets are legit," Ant said.

"I think the tour leader's gone out and bought another 29 tickets just to make sure that we are definitely going to get a seat at the game."

"Fingers crossed," he said.

In a statement, South Africa Rugby said travel agencies acted "illegally and recklessly" in selling tickets they did not have.

"In subsequent communication with disappointed clients, claims have been made that the issue lay at the door of SA Rugby. This is completely untrue.

"Agencies sold the promise of tickets they did not have - and could not secure - for the Test in breach of the events terms and conditions of sale, and without ever having been given access by SA Rugby or its ticketing agency.

"These companies acted illegally and recklessly in pursuit of their own commercial gain at the expense of their clients," the statement said.

World.title: Shane Jones accuses kiwifruit industry of 'slave practices', slams National over regional shakeup
World.content:
NZ First deputy leader Shane Jones has accused the Bay of Plenty kiwifruit industry of "medieval slave practices" at a public meeting, and called for a review of the laws governing Zespri.

The self-proclaimed champion of the regions has also promised New Zealand First will campaign on abolishing regional councils, and criticised National's approach - saying it has never had New Zealand First's backing and the mandate for it should be tested at the election.

Jones was railing against the India Free Trade deal and "blockchain migration" in his speech to about 130 people at the Victory Christian Centre in Lower Hutt when he turned his attention to "a deeper question".

"I don't know about you, but I'm sick to death of what I've seen up in the kiwifruit industry: medieval slave practices," he said.

"When the United States is calling out New Zealand as being responsible for the provision of goods and services that are associated with slave labour, look no further than the egregious cases of what we're seeing in the Bay of Plenty and the migrant groups that are being exploited there."

He said that could not be afforded and it was about time "we started to train more of our own young people".

Trade Minister Todd McClay in July rejected the United States administration's justification for newly reimposed 12.5 percent tariffs on the basis of "forced labour" in New Zealand.

"They are just looking for any means that they can to put tariffs back on... I strongly reject that there is any support at all in the New Zealand system for forced labour. We're not involved in it. It doesn't happen through our trade. It doesn't exist in New Zealand," McClay said at the time.

Jones told reporters after the public meeting that the kiwifruit industry "dominated by Zespri, is losing its social licence" and the next government should review the legislation which grants Zespri a legal export monopoly.

"It is riddled with cases of mediaeval labour practices, egregious taxation practices, and I fear that allegations of slave labour that are made from time to time by America against New Zealand are traceable back to migrant gangs exploiting the goodwill of Kiwis and ruining the reputation of an important industry called the kiwifruit industry. But that also can be shot home to the Zespri company and the orchard owners."

He believed "more systemic change" was needed than merely increasing the Labour Inspectorate's resources to deal with what he called "industrial-scale corruption".

"Casey Costello, who's been involved in this, has already got a model for us. It's the anti-corruption model," he said.

"All state agencies, as the IRD are now doing by issuing a red alert, should join forces and root out these cases of potential slave labour ... look no further than kiwifruit industry and those egregious cases that need to be not only terminated but the people associated with it, they need to be 501'd out to where they come from."

A Zespri spokesperson said the company had have extensive systems in place to both keep the wrong people out of the industry and remove them when they are found. Zespri

The NZ Herald reported last May on an illegal migrant allegedly exploited as a "money mule" to funnel more than $3 million through his bank accounts and withdrawn as cash.

At the time, Customs and Associate Police Minister Costello - a former police detective sergeant who later worked on investigating labour exploitation, and entered Parliament at third on NZ First's list at the last election - pointed to the Ministerial Advisory Group on organised crime she set up earlier in 2025.

"I saw these issues first-hand when I was working to prevent migrant exploitation before entering politics," she said.

"Numerous countries have introduced statutory requirements to ensure that wage payments are made through verifiable, electronic means, to enhance compliance and combat financial misconduct."

She had also called for an end to cash payments for professions like lawyers and immigration consultants, and a joint approach to investigations and prosecutions.

"It's time for a review of the Zespri legislation," Jones said on Sunday, "because I fear that they have trivialised their social licence, and we mean to do something about it if we come back into power."

Zespri responds

A Zespri spokesperson said the company wanted everyone in the industry to be safe and well looked after no matter where they were working.

"Any allegations of poor working conditions are taken seriously and investigated, with action taken wherever possible, including proactive on reporting to government agencies to consider further enforcement action.

"We have extensive systems in place to both keep the wrong people out of the industry and then to remove them when they are found."

The spokesperson said all growers supplying the company were certified to internationally recognised independent certification system GLOBALG.A.P and compulsory employer module GRASP which includes requirements for worker safety and health and welfare.

"All potential contractors go through a vetting process administered by independent private ethical labour investigators AIM CRI Ltd during the application process to assess if they will be able to meet the required standards.

"These contractors must also hold a CAV (Compliance Assessment Verification). To get this, they must show they have the appropriate systems in place to meet GAP and GRASP requirements including providing a safe work environment, with inspections taking place annually to observe that these systems are operating effectively."

Zespri said any who failed to comply were removed from its published list of approved contractors, and a separate list of such contractors was also published to the industry.

"To address issues when they arise, we work closely with government agencies and use AIM CRI Ltd to robustly investigate allegations of misconduct and to support a strong response. These investigations will often result in us passing files on to enforcement agencies to take action.

"To help ensure issues are brought to our attention Zespri also has a dedicated Speak Up Line in place for anyone who has concerns about poor practice taking place within the industry and we encourage anyone with concerns to contact this confidential information line. We also have a dedicated Industry Compliance team which continues its work to strengthen our compliance programme."

Zespri said its discussions with authorities about removing operators failing to meet its standards had previously led to successful prosecutions, "removing poor operators from the industry".

"The vast majority of employers in the industry look after their people. Any exploitation of workers is unacceptable and alongside the government and NZKGI we will continue to do everything we can to ensure an industry free from exploitation and one where people are valued, supported and safe in their jobs."

NZ First favours catchment groups to replace regional councils

Jones had also spoken of his party's plans to "do away with your regional councils", but would not "shoehorn you into a single model".

"That's on you, the community, to work with your ratepayer associations, to work with your community boards and your elected representatives to identify a type of reform model that improves not only responsiveness but your sense of confidence as to where you live," he told the gathered congregation.

"Other parties might be trying to force rapid change. We are going to campaign on it and then after the election we will feel - depending on the quality of the voting result - that we have a mandate."

Speaking to reporters, he said regional councils would be "no longer fit for purpose" thanks to the councils' "chequered history" and the changes to resource management laws.

Using Wairau as an example, he said far too much authority was placed with "distant bureaucratic offices such as Napier and Hawke's Bay".

"We're very taken with catchment boards and catchment groups having more authority. It worked in the past. It ensures that more local ownership is exercised for rivers, for other catchment features, rather than it being centralised in a bureaucracy," he said.

That contrasted with the government's approach to reforming regional councils, where National Party ministers Chris Bishop and Simon Watts had handed down an ultimatum for councils to "lead your own reform, or we will do it for you".

Watts this month confirmed to RNZ more than two thirds of councils had submitted proposals for reorganisation - but nearly 20 had not.

Jones on Sunday suggested that approach should have been campaigned on.

World.title: The geriatric giant growing by the hour
World.content:
The number of people with dementia in NZ is set to more than double in the next 25 years. Luckily, the medical world is learning more about treatment and prevention.

The geriatric giant growing by the hour The Detail Download MP3 24m

Every day, twice a day, at a level crossing in the Auckland suburb of Hobsonville, young and old gather with a mutual mission.

The young are on their way to school and the old, from the nearby retirement village, are tasked with getting them safely across the busy road.

Dr Cheryl Johnson sees it on a daily basis on her way to work, and as a geriatrician she celebrates it.

"They have a roster of people who help the kids cross the road," she says. "That's connection, that's sense of purpose, that's someone getting up in the morning to get these kids safely across the road."

Community connections and sense of purpose are among the key factors to ageing well and warding off dementia, which Johnson ranks as one of the 'geriatric giants'.

And it is a giant that's growing by the hour. Three people develop the disease every 60 minutes. By 2050, that number will rise to four, according to figures from Dementia New Zealand and University of Auckland.

The prevalence in Aotearoa is projected to grow from 82,945 in 2025 to 167,400 in 2050 with Māori, Pacific and Asian people experiencing faster-growing dementia rates. The economic cost is predicted to double from $3.2 billion now to $6.4b in 2050.

But among the grim figures are some heartening facts which show that people can do a lot for themselves, Johnson says. She's speaking to The Detail ahead of World Alzheimer's Awareness month in September.

A healthy lifestyle can play a big part in reducing the severity of what is also known medically as cognitive impairment. That includes a mediterranean diet, low or no alcohol, regular exercise - 30 minutes, five times a week - brain-stimulating activities from crossword to choirs to learning a language, social activities, and getting a hearing test.

According to the Lancet Commission on Dementia Prevention 2024, 40 percent of all dementia cases are attributable to modifiable risk factors that can be identified and treated.

According to figures from Dementia New Zealand and University of Auckland, three people will develop dementia every 60 minutes. By 2050, that number will rise to four. RNZ / Sharon Brettkelly

One in three dementia diagnoses are preceded by mild cognitive impairment, the window in which intervention is most effective.

Up to 23 percent of people referred with memory concerns are found to have a reversible cause, not dementia.

Studies also show that doing nothing is the most expensive choice. Johnson says too often people come to her in her public and private clinics too late.

"There was a study done in New Zealand that said the average time from the development of symptoms to diagnosis is three and a half years which is a really long time when you think about it.

"Lots of things are happening within that period. That statistic really struck me and what we see is that delay. I think people are scared or sometimes it's really subtle when it starts and then it becomes more obvious.

"And then when people come and see me, particularly in the public system, it is quite clear that they have dementia and the symptoms have been going on for a period of time."

She explains to The Detail that there are limited treatments available in New Zealand.

"We don't have disease-modifying therapies in New Zealand yet but they are coming."

Listen to The Detail to find out more about the tests for dementia, the latest treatments and why attitudes need to change.

World.title: Garage blaze spreads to two homes on Kapiti Coast
World.content:
Firefighters are battling a blaze that has jumped from a garage to two homes on Kapiti Coast.

Fire and Emergency said it was called to reports of a garage fire in Otaki shortly before 8pm on Sunday.

A FENZ shift manager said crews arrived to find the garage fire had spread to a house, which was engulfed in flames, and was also threatening a neighbouring property.

The fire was escalated to second alarm, pulling in crews from Otaki, Waikanae, and Paraparaumu, they said.

They said the fire at the second property has since been extinguished and the blaze was now contained.

World.title: Taiarahia documentary captures kotahitanga in action
World.content:
"Ko te wawata o te ngākau, kia mau te maunga i tana kākahu tawhito i mahue iho e o tātou matua, tātou koroua."

Our earnest wish is that the mountain should maintain her ancient raiments left since the days of our forebears.

Hiki Toko, 1985 (Te Māhurehure, Tūhoe)

For generations of Tūhoe, Taiarahia mountain in the Bay of Plenty settlement of Ruatoki Valley has stood as a sentinel landmark watching over them and welcoming them home.

Her cliffs once held the ancient pā of Tūhoe tūpuna, her presence sheltering the marae and hapū below, her dense forest sustains and protects native species.

As forestry plans loomed, the native forest of the maunga came under threat, galvanising a unified vision voiced by Te Mahurehure, Ngāi Tūhoe kaumātua Hiki Toko from the summit of Taiarahia.

"Ko te wawata o te ngākau, kia mau te maunga i tana kākahu tawhito i mahue iho ai e o tātou matua, tātou koroua.Ko tērā kākahu tawhito o te ngahere, kaua hoki e tangohia tērā kia whakamau i te kākahu hou anō mōna."

Our earnest wish is that the mountain should maintain her ancient raiments , left since the days of our forebears , that she should not be made to wear these new clothes.

Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito Docu Series Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

In 1985, Tasman Forestry began earthworks as part of plans to clear hundreds of hectares of native forest and replace it with pine.

The proposal, which was approved by the Tūhoe-Waikaremoana Māori Trust Board, triggered a six-month occupation that united and divided whānau, placing relatives on opposing sides of the argument.

Harata Day (Te Māhurehure. Ngāi Tūhoe) and Tame Iti Te Māhurehure Ngāi Tūhoe) - instigators of the occupation of Taiarahia. Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

Harata Day and Tame Iti initiated a unified response when the reality of the threat became stark - bulldozers were already tearing up the earth and felling trees on the maunga.

Their coordinated campaign combined direct action with strategic advocacy. Iti and others confronted the forestry operation on the maunga, while Harata worked behind the scenes, writing to ministers, politicians and organisations including Greenpeace and Forest & Bird to raise awareness and rally support.

In the months that followed, an enduring committment to kotahitanga overcame overwhelming odds to succeed in protecting the maunga.

Harata Day and two of her daughters Wikitoria Day and Ngarimu Daniels. Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

Taiarahia: Te Kākahu Tawhito chronicles the experiences of those caught up in the occupation in a seven-part documentary series co-directed by Harata's daughter, Wikitōria Day.(Te Māhurehure, Ngāi Tūhoe)

Day said one of its unique strengths was capturing the vastly different memories and emotions of generations who experienced the same event.

"Most documentaries are centred around a handful of kaikōrero. In contrast, this kaupapa captures at least 15 different perspectives, and what's quite fascinating is the difference in recollections across generations ."

The series includes the voices of those who experienced the occupation as children and are now pakeke with mokopuna of their own.

"Tamariki were very involved in the occupation, but they were sheltered from the confrontational aspects,and still quite naive to the significance of what was happening, "

"They saw it as a time of adventure and playing with their cousins, despite the emotional impact of the events, they were allowed to maintain that sense of naivety children often have around kaupapa like this."

In stark contrast to the perspectives shared by tamariki the series also captures the painful reality of whānau finding themselves on opposing sides of the argument. The impact still resonates with those involved.

Forestry provided employment when decent paying jobs were hard to come by and some of the Tasman Forestry workers sent to the maunga found themselves in stand-offs with whanaunga.

On one side was Tame Iti and his 'puna kiore' (rat pack) who were focused on protecting and upholding their obligation to the maunga, while on the other were whānau trying to protect jobs and feed their families.

Day described the result as an emotional rollercoaster.

"You hear anger, frustration and sadness. It's a real concoction of emotions, and that's what makes it really unique."

Beyond the occupation Te Māhurehure demonstrated the value of combining whakapapa, tikanga, strategy and collective action to build a movement around an extraordinarily complex issue.

Forty years after the occupation, Day said its enduring lesson was clear.

"The biggest and strongest lesson this provides is the power of kotahitanga."

"Kotahitanga can be achieved no matter how complex the argument, and the power of unity and kotahitanga can make a genuine and real difference."

After six months, the occupation ended in favour of tangata whenua and the native forest remained standing.

The feature-length version of Taiarahia: Te Kākahu Tawhito won the People's Choice award for best documentary at the Māoriland Film Festival.
